She is calling on the Government to reduce national insurance contributions. She wants to employ more young people, as does the whole of the hospitality sector. People in the industry want VAT, which those on the Labour Benches led them to believe would be reduced, to be reduced to 13%, and they want the charge on employment—the tax on jobs—to be reduced. The Government should reduce national insurance contributions.

The Government are quick to lecture Conservative Members about how to care for the most vulnerable, but at the very moment that Ministers say they want more people getting into work—as we have heard time and again this afternoon—they have increased the cost of employment. We all know that work is the best form of welfare, and Labour’s job tax is shooting the Government in the foot. Time and again, local businesses tell me that they can no longer afford to take on apprenticeships. The double whammy of higher employer national insurance contributions and the increase to the minimum wage has simply become too much to bear.

The Conservatives have made the argument that they would like to see a reduction in national insurance. Will the hon. Lady spell out, in pounds and pence, by how much the Tory party would like to see the minimum wage cut to achieve the outcomes that she is suggesting?

I thank the hon. Member for his question, but many questions of that nature have not been answered this afternoon. That is not what I am here to talk about. I am here to talk about the fact that businesses are currently dealing with this situation. What happens in the future is irrelevant; we are talking about what is happening while this Government are in power. We know that by next year the annual cost of employing a full-time worker on the minimum wage will have increased by more than £4,000 since 2024—a whopping 31% increase in just three years.

I will continue. It is little wonder that job opportunities have shrivelled up under Labour, as has been pointed out by Members on the Government Benches. Vacancies fell by 21,000 between July and September this year, and as we have heard, small firms are being hit the hardest. To get our economy moving again, the Conservatives would halve employer national insurance contributions for under-25s. We would help young people get a foot on the ladder by backing the businesses that are prepared to give them that first opportunity. Madam Deputy Speaker, you might be pleased to hear that there are more than 3,700 small and medium-sized enterprises in South West Devon, much like in Cornwall, which has been mentioned already. The south-west is home to many SMEs. Each one represents somebody who took a risk, invested their savings, employed local people and worked many long hours to build something of their own. In fact, that was my own experience. My dad regularly went out to work before I had even had breakfast, then came home and fell asleep—I never got a story or anything like that. He was out working six days a week, running his small business. When he was asleep, he was worrying about how the business was going to survive. For many sole traders and small business owners, there is no guaranteed safety net if their business fails. If they have no public sector pension waiting for them at retirement, they are in an even more precarious position. I was therefore genuinely astounded when a Labour Minister had the audacity to claim that employers are not working people. The employers I know work incredibly hard. They are, as we have heard many times today, the ones opening up before dawn and locking up long after everyone else has gone home. They are the ones managing staff, cash flow and contracts. They bear the ultimate responsibility when things go wrong. When a business goes under, the employees may be able to move on to another job—although given the examples this afternoon, that is perhaps less of a possibility—but for many business owners, it is not that simple. They are losing something they have devoted years of hard work to building. The Labour Government seem to forget that 99% of businesses in the UK are small and medium-sized enterprises, meaning that they have fewer than 250 employees. Saddled with ever higher costs, these businesses are now faced with difficult choices to raise prices, cut trading hours or make redundancies. Indeed, one local café owner told me that they have been forced to cut back deliberately on younger staff to protect the jobs of their employees who have mortgages and rent to pay. Added to that, they breed poultry, and they have had to increase the mid-year price of chickens, which will go on and lay eggs for people, for the first time in 18 years, which is driven by rising prices of animal feed, gas and fuel. One local electrician from Plympton has told me how he regularly sees about 10 other businesses at the wholesaler each morning. There was a time when the majority of them had an apprentice, but now it is just him, and he has one only because it is his son, so it is in his interest to keep the business going. Ministers seem to have forgotten that employers pay the apprentice when they are at college as well as when they are at work, and the costs are just too high. I have 670 construction businesses in my constituency, and one of them used to participate in an innovative scheme to support recovering addicts back into work. It partnered with well-loved Shekinah, a Plymouth homelessness charity, which provides employment support for people undergoing treatment for drug or alcohol misuse. These people would work for the company on a flexible basis, starting at a few days per week and building up gradually. After a few months, the workers would go on to gain full-time employment with other businesses. However, the company’s founders, Aaron and Sarah, say that it is impossible to continue offering th

When Labour campaigners knocked on doors at the last general election, they made a promise—a promise that they would not raise taxes on working people and that they would not increase national insurance—and people put their trust in them. Today, however, the shutters are coming down on our high streets, young people cannot get a foot on the ladder and the business owners, who were told that they had nothing to fear from this Labour Government, are now paying the price for that broken promise. Let no one pretend that this is a debate about abstract tax rates; it is about jobs, the future of our high streets and whether the commitments that this Labour Government made to the electorate carry any weight at all. Labour let the mask slip when the Chief Secretary to the Treasury said that employers are not working people. What an absolute load of rubbish. Of course, employers are working people—the café owner who starts work before dawn, the farmer who employs staff from the local community, or the pub landlord who has gone without their own salary to keep their staff in work. Each of them are working people, and each of them have been asked to pay more by this Labour Government, who promised that they would not. On broken promises and the rising cost of employment, Labour’s manifesto stated that it would not increase national insurance, yet in its first Budget the Government increased employer national insurance from 13.8% to 15% and cut the threshold at which it is paid from £9,100 to £5,000. The thresholds actively hurt part-time and lower-paid roles, which are precisely the jobs on which many young people depend. Ministers claim that this is not a tax on businesses, but it absolutely is a tax on businesses and working people. That has been seen throughout this debate. Then there is the increase to the minimum wage, which again stifled business growth. And that is before we look at the challenge of the Employment Rights Act 2025. Under this Labour Government we have seen higher taxes, higher costs and more red tape. Far from being the party of business, Labour is showing itself to be actively discouraging growth and killing the businesses up and down the country that are the very backbone of our economy. Let me turn to my own constituency. We have held many roundtables with many local businesses, and I thank Sarah Brookfield-Almond and Ryan Troy from the Ilkley and Keighley business improvement districts for helping me to organise them. The businesses who came along were retailers, hospitality businesses and independent traders. Employers of every size were present—people who have spent years building up their businesses and who give work to local people across my constituency. Their message was consistent and stark: they described the relentless pressure of the increase in employer national insurance contributions, the minimum wage increase with no support to meet their needs, the business rates that bear down on them and the uncertainty of the Employment Rights Act hitting their businesses hard. These businesses are not asking for special treatment; they are asking for a Government who understand and want to support them. One fantastic local business which has grown and expanded is Three Little Birds Bakery, owned and run by Bec Severs. She has a shop in Keighley, and recently opened one in Ilkley. Bec has been very clear about her views on the Labour Government’s most recent Budget. Taking to Facebook, she said: “This budget does nothing to help”. On the latest minimum wage rises, she says there is “absolutely no support” for how she will now have to pay that money to her employees. That has been heard loud and clear by the Turkey Inn, which has now reduced its working hours from seven days a week to four days a week on the back of this Government. Then we look at that hospice sector, which is being hit very hard, such as Sue Ryder Manorlands hospice in my constituency, by the rise in employer national insurance. Those people

Fewer sentences have caused such shock and reaction than when the Chief Secretary to the Treasury said that employers were not working people. I feel so saddened for all those small business owners across my constituency who have worked so unbelievably hard and sacrificed so much to give so many other people the opportunity of work. I think about Magda, who runs the Omorfi Nails and Beauty salon in Towcester. She does not only employ staff; while also bringing up her family, she is studying medical practice so that she can help people with diabetes—a matter close to my heart—through podiatry. It is an insult to say that she is not hard working and a working person. No matter how many examples we give, the Government simply will not listen. I wish they would engage. The voices from all the stories told here today are those of actual people from our constituencies who are living and breathing this. I implore the Government to take this issue seriously. At the very beginning of the debate, the Minister talked of breathing space. I think the only “Breathing Space” people recognise is the song by the Pet Shop Boys, but I think their version might be slightly more popular than the Chancellor’s. We ask businesses every single day to take risks. The contract must be that if we ask them to take a risk, we give them the confidence to be able to operate their businesses, not the shifting sands constantly coming from this Government and their Budgets. Actions ultimately speak far louder than words, because hope does not pay the bills, hope does not put food on the table and hope does not heat our homes. As we have identified, the people suffering most are our young people. We have heard many examples of people who are struggling to get opportunities and jobs. One of the pubs in my constituency—I have just run a pub of the year competition—said that it put up an advert for just a couple of hours of work at the weekend for those under 18. It received 200 applications for just one job. There are so many young people who are absolutely desperate to get into the working environment, but they cannot because those businesses cannot give them the opportunity. That is a travesty that has happened on this Government’s watch. Nearly 1 million young people are NEETs, with 60% of those being economically inactive—not just not in work but not even looking for it. There is a much deeper issue of youth detachment from the market, which hurts young people’s confidence, health and ability to earn an income, and it hurts the taxpayer, because it is incredibly hard for us to give young people opportunities if those jobs do not exist. That is why I welcome the Conservative proposal to halve national insurance contributions for the under-25s to get them into work. I will flag—as I did in justice questions this week—that the Employment Rights Act has introduced many powers that the Government laud, but with them we are going to start to see an increasing amount of red tape. With that red tape comes an issue with employment tribunals. When people are going through a dispute with an employer, one of the most difficult times of their lives, they are going to discover that there is a huge backlog for tribunals. There are already over 70,000 open single cases. In reducing the time from two years down to six months to bring a tribunal claim, the Act is going to increase the workload and the backlog in the courts by a third. That is madness. We are slowing down the economy with everything we do. The Employment Rights Act is exactly as the Conservatives describe: it is an unemployment rights Act. It is burdening our businesses and slowing down opportunities, but the Government and the Labour Benches just sit and stare. That is the problem: they are sitting and staring while hard-working people out there are trying to make a living. The Government need to start listening. My poor farmers were looking to the Budget for a little bit of help and assistance—88% of my consti

It is a pleasure to close this debate, and I thank every Member who has spoken across the House. That includes the hon. Members for Loughborough (Dr Sandher), for Truro and Falmouth (Jayne Kirkham), for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger), and for Norwich North (Alice Macdonald)—Norwich is a fine city. On the Opposition Benches, I thank my right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel), who took us on an excellent canter through the businesses in her constituency. I thank my right hon. Friend the Member for Daventry (Stuart Andrew), and my hon. Friends the Members for Central Suffolk and North Ipswich (Patrick Spencer) and for Mid Leicestershire (Mr Bedford). My hon. Friend the Member for Hinckley and Bosworth (Dr Evans) talked about the importance of the word “yes”, and I will hold him to that in future. I thank my hon. Friends the Members for Hamble Valley (Paul Holmes), for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith), for Keighley and Ilkley (Robbie Moore), and for South Northamptonshire (Sarah Bool), and my right hon. Friend the Member for Tatton (Esther McVey). My right hon. Friend the Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) gave an excellent speech about his business sense; he also talked about his sweaty palms, which explains some of his bowling when we are playing cricket. The most important contribution was from my hon. Friend the Member for Droitwich and Evesham (Nigel Huddleston), who talked about the reality of businesses failing, and the 662 jobs that have been lost due to the squeezed margins at Kanes Foods—we wish them all well. If this debate comes down to anything, it is two simple truths: if we tax growth, we get less growth; if we tax jobs, we get fewer jobs. That is not ideology; it is the exact logic that Government will use when they tax things such as tobacco. The difference is that the Conservatives would very much like to see more jobs. Let me be clear what I am talking about: employers are the café owner who opens at 6 am; the scaffolder out in the rain; the builder, the hairdresser, the gym owner and the hotelier; and the pub landlord, who on any given night is also the cleaner, the accountant and, when needed, the bouncer. They take the risk, they put their own house on the line, and then they do something remarkable: they give other people a job. They are the backbone of our high streets and our economy and we value them. In Bromley and Biggin Hill, I see them every week, in places such as The Oak pub in Bickley, Tip Top key cutters in Hayes, or the Spitfire Café in Biggin Hill. They are not asking for special favours; they are asking not to be charged more for doing the very thing that the Government say they want them to do, which is to give someone a job. That brings me to the remarks of the Chief Secretary to the Treasury on the first of this month, when she told GB news: “I don’t think employers are working people. They are companies.” I do not say this to be unkind. Every one of us has said something careless over the weekend that we have then spent Monday morning trying to explain—I certainly have. By the next day, it had fallen to the Science Minister to tell LBC that employers are working people. I have always believed in following the science, and I hope the Treasury will, too. I have met a great many companies in Bromley and Biggin Hill since then, and some were greatly distressed and hurt by that statement. These are hard-working people who felt undervalued, disregarded or that their work was being disrespected; some were angry; and most of them have a first name. They open early, close when the last customer leaves, and do the VAT return at the kitchen table on a Sunday night. If that is not working, I would love to know what is. This matters because of a promise. Before the election, Labour said in its manifesto that it would not increase taxes on working people, and that is why it would not increase national insurance. Businesses up and down the country were told again and again tha

Does the shadow Minister agree that the key difference between our increase and the Government’s increase is that in their manifesto to win the general election in 2024, they said that they categorically would not raise national insurance?

I thank my hon. Friend for his intervention. Saying one thing and doing another is something that we are getting very used to from this Government. What would we do? We would halve employer national insurance for workers aged 21 to 24, taking the main rate down to 7.5%. We are not inventing a new idea here. Under-21s and apprentices under 25 already pay no national insurance on most earnings. That was a Conservative reform and this Government have kept it, so I take it that they agree that it works. All we are asking is why that help should stop on someone’s 21st birthday, just as so many are leaving university or college and looking for a proper start. Nor is it only a Conservative idea. The cross-party Work and Pensions Committee recommended in July that the Government extend the relief to all under-25s. When a Committee with both Labour and Conservative Members agrees on something, it is usually worth a second look. Most of us in this House remember our first job and the person who took a chance on us. Mine was at the South London Press in Streatham—though, to be fair, I think they regarded that as a mistake pretty sharpish. For a lot of young people, that first chance comes as a job in a café, shop, pub or hotel. Those are exactly the businesses that this tax hits hardest and that our plans would help most. On business rates, we would give retail, hospitality and leisure businesses full relief—up to £110,000 each—so that our high streets have genuine room to grow and hire. We look at the whole bill that businesses face—not one line of it—because that is how the person running a business has to look at it too. Napoleon supposedly called us a nation of shopkeepers. I am sure he meant it as an insult, but as we know things did not go terribly well for poor old Boney after that, and I consider it a compliment—a strength, part of our industrious culture and something we can be proud of. The motion asks the House to agree with something that most of our constituents would think goes without saying: that the person who opens the shop, runs the pub or builds the extension and who pays the wages of the people working alongside them is a working person. If Members agree with that, they can say so tonight in the Lobby.

It is a pleasure to respond to the debate with you in the Chair, Madam Deputy Speaker. I join other Members in paying tribute to the work that entrepreneurs do in our country—to the sacrifice, long hours and sleepless nights that have been referenced. The right hon. Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) singled me out as being someone who has empathy with and an understanding of business. I do not know if that will result in him having to surrender his party card, or perhaps in me doing so, but I will take it in the spirit that it was intended. We absolutely understand the feeling of jeopardy that he talks about. My hon. Friend the Member for Loughborough (Dr Sandher) spoke powerfully about the feeling of responsibility that employers have, including his parents, towards their workers. For all the disagreement that there will be in this debate about how we do it, our job is to make that just a little bit easier, because it can be an all-encompassing and, at times, lonely enterprise running a business. I will endeavour to respond to as many points raised by right hon. and hon. Members around the Chamber as possible. Several made me hungry and reminded me that I skipped lunch earlier on today. The right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel) and my hon. Friend the Member for Truro and Falmouth (Jayne Kirkham) referred to fantastic food businesses in their constituencies, and even the reference to the prawn sandwich offensive from the hon. Member for Central Suffolk and North Ipswich (Patrick Spencer) brought on that feeling. I do, however, want to echo the remarks made by my right hon. Friend the Financial Secretary to the Treasury in his opening speech. The big macroeconomic picture for the UK is this: we were the joint fastest growing economy in the G7 in the first half of this year, the IMF has upgraded our growth for this year, and the IMF’s chief economist has called the UK the “stand out” economy for deficit reduction, with the lowest forecast deficit in the G7 by 2029.
Will the Minister inform us how many businesses have gone to the wall since Labour came into government?

It has been a dreadful decade for businesses, and for small businesses in particular. As I said at the beginning, our job is to make it easier to invest and to ensure that we are cutting red tape and increasing access to finance. I will talk about that in a moment. In the Budget, we took action to give the businesses that the right hon. Member for Tatton (Esther McVey) is concerned about and employers some breathing space. We continue to work on the long-term changes that are necessary to create good jobs and growth in every part of our country. As a result of that work, employment is up this year—it is higher than previously forecast in March—and, in fact, the UK has the third highest employment rate in the G7. Meanwhile, business investment—so often embarrassing under the previous Government—relative to the size of the economy remains at its highest level for a decade. Of course, as Members have said, there are global headwinds from the conflict in the middle east. [Hon. Members: “Ah!”] Conservative Members say “Ah”, and they do not like to be reminded of that, because they were calling for us to take part in that conflict. People and employers are seeing the impact of that conflict in their bills. We know that there is more to do, but this is a country that is turning a corner. With that, I turn to the points raised throughout the debate, starting with national insurance, which was raised by several hon. Members. The facts are these. Employer national insurance contributions are forecast to raise about £150 billion in 2026-27. That is a significant contribution to the funding of our public services. Why is that needed? Because we cannot have a strong NHS or strong public services without investing in them, investing in our country and rebuilding the crumbling infrastructure we inherited after 14 years of austerity.

The national insurance rises are really affecting hospices: in some cases, 40% of their beds are closing. Where will those people go? They will go to the national health service. How does that help our public services?

We recognise that and, as was mentioned, we are providing additional resources throughout the NHS and hospices to help with that. On relief for employers, hon. Members will know that the employment allowance was estimated to be worth £7.4 billion in 2025-26. That provides eligible employers with up to £10,500 a year towards their national insurance contribution bills. That is obviously not the only help that we gave to businesses in the Budget. As my hon. Friend the Member for Norwich North (Alice Macdonald) noted, we have lifted tens of thousands of businesses out of business rates. Several hon. Members raised concerns about youth unemployment.

Will the Minister acknowledge, because he not only has the ear of business but is a very honest Member of this House, that, notwithstanding the talk about support for business and the 70,000 businesses that have been mentioned, overall the Budget raised the tax on business by another £2.2 billion, on top of the £66 billion that came in the two previous ones?

We asked business, and banks in particular, to pay a little more so that we could give people help with their energy bills. We have heard in the debate, once again, that the Conservative party opposes that and so opposes that additional support that people are getting with their energy bills this winter. As has been said, no employer is paying national insurance contributions on under-21s up to a salary of £50,000 and similarly for apprentices who are under 25, which is a saving of around £6,700 at most for employers. We have doubled the employment allowance and ensured that 40% of companies do not pay national insurance contributions.
Has unemployment gone up or down on this Government’s watch, and what has caused it?

Unemployment is still lower than in comparable economies— [ Interruption. ] The hon. Gentleman asked the question, so I will answer. Employment is up and inactivity is down in this country. It is precisely because we are concerned about youth unemployment that we are introducing measures such as the £2,000 hiring payment for smaller employers to take on young people and the £3,000 jobs grant for those at risk of sliding into youth unemployment. As several hon. Members have noted, that is in stark contrast with the increase of a quarter of a million in youth unemployment and inactivity in the last few years of the Conservative Government.
I will give way to the hon. Member for Hamble Valley (Paul Holmes) for one last intervention and then I will make some progress.

The Minister has outlined the £2,000 payment to businesses. Does he think that it is best for a Government to administer that payment or to reduce taxation on businesses so that they can choose to employ younger people without that Minister getting in the way?

It is precisely because we recognise, as many right hon. and hon. Members have mentioned, that retail and hospitality give so many young people their first job that we are lifting so many of those businesses out of business rates and lowering the tax burden on those individuals. I will follow the Prime Minister’s lead and note that we agree on a lot despite the debate across the House. We agree, as many hon. Members have said, that small businesses in particular are the backbone of our economy, we agree that more must be done to support business to employ people, and we agree that young people should be supported.

I will make some progress. We agree that young people should be supported into work. However, we disagree fundamentally on how to go about that. The hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) spoke about the minimum wage, but told the House that she did not want to talk about what might happen in the future. I think I know why that is. It is because in a report from the Prosperity Institute, the shadow Business Minister in the other place committed to freezing the minimum wage for five years. That is a real-terms cut of 12% for the poorest workers that will not just take £8,900 out of the pockets of the poorest workers in the country, but take that money out of the tills of businesses in their communities. The way to fix the issue we have with youth unemployment is to increase the number of apprenticeships, increase the flexibility of those apprenticeships, invest in the growth sectors that will create the well-paid jobs of the future, ensure that those young unemployed people are more attractive to potential employers and take all the other measures that we are taking to invest in business. The Tory plan for those young people who have been rejected over and over again and who are close to being broken by the experience of being let down by the system is to punish them for that. We will not do that. The Conservatives offer only insecure hours, cuts to incomes and poverty pay. That did not work for 14 years, it did not work for employers and it will not work now. Question put .

I am grateful to have secured this debate and to raise an issue that is important not only to my constituents but to everyone who relies on the vital work of charities. It concerns whether the Charity Commission currently has the necessary powers and resources to respond effectively when charities are not properly governed. A charity’s ability to operate successfully and serve our communities depends on public trust. Well-governed charities can make an enormous difference to people’s lives, and trusteeship carries series legal responsibilities. Trustees are custodians of charitable assets, and they must comply with the governing documents and manage the charity’s resources responsibly to ensure that activities further charitable purposes. When charities are not appropriately governed, the consequences are significant, and it undermines public confidence and deprives the local communities they are supposed to serve. When trustees fail to meet their responsibilities, there must be an effective regulator with the powers and resources to intervene swifty and restore public trust in the charity sector, the vast majority of which does an excellent job. That is the role of the Charity Commission. I acknowledge the important work of the Charity Commission. It regulates more than 170,000 charities in England and Wales, overseeing a sector that is responsible for tens of billions of pounds in annual income and expenditure. It has a range of statutory powers, including the ability to investigate misconduct and mismanagement, to require information and documents, to issue official warnings, to suspend or remove trustees, and in appropriate circumstances to appoint interim managers.

I commend the hon. Lady for her assiduousness in bringing forward this issue. Although the Charity Commission should have teeth, does she agree that it is the job of enforcement agents such as HMRC, or indeed the local council, to take a bite out of those who are in breach? The delineation of powers must be clear, and that is one thing that charities perhaps needs some help with.

A wide range of powers are held by a number of organisations, and it is crucial that each one of those takes responsibility and has power to work within its own remit, as I am sure the hon. Gentleman would agree. There are serious questions as to whether the Charity Commission’s current framework is sufficient. A regulator’s ability to investigate concerns does not necessarily mean that it has the capacity to intervene swiftly or effectively enough, and there is a pertinent concern in my West Lancashire constituency, where I have been engaging with the Charity Commission over long-standing concerns about the management and governance of Scarisbrick village hall. In 1972, local people secured a piece of land and went about fundraising and building a village hall, a village green and a children’s playground. They then fundraised and erected a war memorial to the Scarisbrick residents lost in the world wars who had not previously been recognised. Many years went by, with the village hall being a valued community asset, including the village green and the children’s playpark. In recent years, however, concerns began to surface over the running of the hall and facilities. First went the children’s playpark, with trustees claiming that funds could not be found to maintain it. The trustees then changed the name of the village hall to The Venue Scarisbrick, marketing it as a function suite. Local organisations such as the Scouts were allegedly deprioritised, and regular slots that they had been using were changed, making it difficult for them to continue, forcing them to go elsewhere. The trustees then fenced off the village green, denying access to local residents, and renting the green space to a private sector petting zoo. The final straw came in July 2025 when the trustees proposed the permanent removal of the war memorial. I launched a petition to save the memorial, and wrote to trustees in August 2025 setting out my concerns and requesting a meeting. I received no response. I chased it in August and later in October, but I still received no response. Meanwhile, local residents became increasingly concerned about not only the trustees’ decisions, but their behaviour towards residents. It transpired that the trustees were using the hall as a base for their own private sector businesses and charging other businesses to use the address. When challenged, the trustees refused to meet local residents, refused to meet or correspond with me, and called the police when local residents protested at the proposed removal of the war memorial. On inspection, it transpired that the trustees have set up a limited company in the name of The Venue Scarisbrick, of which some of the trustees are directors. There is no indication of how that company relates to the charity that owns the building. They have also failed to register accounts for the charity for several years running. Residents demanded an annual general meeting, as one had not been held for some time and was long overdue. In February 2026, six months later than the governing document required, the trustees, despite receiving advice from the Charity Commission that they must hold the AGM in person, held an online broadcast, claiming that it was an AGM. There was no way to ascertain who was there, how many people were present or whether they were eligible to be there. There was no way to contribute unless explicitly invited to do so. When it came to so-called elections, the trustees were appointed by ballot by email. It was not secret, and there was no adequate scrutiny or transparency. Unsurprisingly, all the existing trustees were re-elected. Not only was the so-called AGM appallingly run, but the chair of the trustees took the opportunity to launch a 15-minute verbal attack on local people who challenged him. Local parish councillors have been threatened with legal action and intimidatory language on social media. While the war memorial was saved—at least for now—the village green remai

The hon. Lady is making a bold and brave case. As she knows, she has recently become a bit of a heroine of mine following a recent and well-publicised speech. Is not the problem here the Charity Commission? I do not know if it has the resources, the means or the legal powers required, but, in a variety of cases that I have drawn to its attention on woke causes—about which we might not agree—it seemed to be highly ineffective. She is talking about a very local case, but she is highlighting a bigger point in doing so.

I thank the right hon. Member for his contribution. That is the point that I am making: whether the Charity Commission has the powers, resources and ability to act. I fear that the story I am laying out today is far from unique across the country.

I congratulate my good and hon. Friend on securing this debate. There is a really key point about trust and accountability. Does she share the concerns of myself and other members of the coalfields group of MPs about the activities of the Coal Industry Social Welfare Organisation? It is a charitable body established by Parliament in 1952 to provide support to mining communities. Many former mining communities, including some in my own constituency, say that they are missing out on millions of pounds of investment from the sale of former miners’ welfare halls and outdoor welfare schemes. Does my hon. Friend agree that the public must have confidence that charitable trusts are held accountable for their actions? Will she support our efforts to ensure that the Charity Commission takes all appropriate action in the cases that we have identified?

I absolutely agree with what my hon. Friend has outlined. The Charity Commission should support all charities, because it is fundamental that public trust remains. That is why residents and I have engaged with the Charity Commission and raised concerns regarding the transparency and governance of Scarisbrick village hall and the decisions being made. The Charity Commission has begun an investigation. Following the February AGM, the commission confirmed that concerns about the failure to comply with advice and the conduct of the meeting itself had been escalated to its regulatory compliance team. Further concerns, including concerns around social media activity and questions about the transparency and integrity of the AGM ballot, have been added to its case records. However, by June, the commission confirmed that the case remained ongoing and was progressing. Last month, the commission advised that it had received a significant volume of further correspondence, including new concerns about the conduct of a trustee on social media. It also confirmed that it was continuing its investigation and planned to undertake a books and records inspection in the coming weeks. I appreciate that thorough investigations take time, particularly where there are complex governance issues to consider. However, this case illustrates the challenges of addressing concerns in a timely way, particularly where further issues and inappropriate conduct continue to emerge while an investigation is ongoing. Residents of Scarisbrick are concerned that the village hall will potentially be lost and its resources frittered away. Those concerns have been compounded by further developments. Two companies associated with the management of the village hall, The Venue Scarisbrick Ltd and Community Inclusion Projects Ltd, have appeared on Companies House as having active proposals to strike off. That raises even more questions about corporate governance and the protection of charitable assets and community facilities. Given that this case has been ongoing since last summer and I have been raising concerns with the commission for a year, I ask the Minister to consider what more the Government can do to ensure the commission can investigate cases of this nature promptly.

I am staggered by the story of Scarisbrick village hall—what the hon. Lady is describing is terrifying. It seems to me that the Charity Commission does not have the resources it needs to do any of its work. I have a constituent who is starting a charity, HeritageTies, and he has been told that it is going to take 23 weeks to register his charity. During that time, he cannot get a bank account, fundraise, or start the job he is trying to do. I am told that 3,000 new church charities have been added, so does the hon. Lady agree that we need a root-and-branch investigation of whether the Charity Commission has the resources it needs to do its job?

I thank the hon. Member for her contribution. This is an ongoing issue, and she will be aware that the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee’s report on the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman’s investigations of the Charity Commission more widely has raised similar concerns. It also questions whether the commission shows sufficient boldness in exercising its existing powers, and whether it has the powers it needs to regulate the charitable sector effectively.

I thank my hon. Friend for referencing my Select Committee’s recent report. Will she join our Committee in calling on the Government or the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee to hold a thorough consultation on the commission’s powers, both to identify whether it needs further powers and whether it is making the best use of the powers it already has, and particularly whether the legal advice it is getting is too risk averse?

I thank my hon. Friend for his intervention, and join him in that call. I would welcome an update from the Minister on the Committee’s report and on the Government’s plans to take forward its recommendations, particularly its proposal for a wider consultation on the powers of the Charity Commission. Is the Minister satisfied that the commission’s existing powers and resources are adequate to enable it to intervene at an earlier stage where there are persistent governance concerns and potential risks to charitable assets? Are there opportunities to strengthen the regulatory framework so that the commission can take effective action without unnecessary delay? Ultimately, this is about ensuring that the Charity Commission has the resources, powers and support it needs to fulfil its responsibilities, protect charitable assets and maintain public confidence in the charitable sector.

I am pleased to respond to this debate, and I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for West Lancashire (Ashley Dalton) on securing it. She is an incredibly powerful woman—such a powerful woman that she has been able to get the Secretary of State to attend the debate. She also shares powerful woman characteristics with my mother. I have to mention my mother today, because it is her birthday and, sadly, I am not able to be with her. Village halls and other such spaces are often the lifeblood of our communities, and I pay tribute to the army of workers and volunteers who selflessly provide vital services in them, to communities up and down the country. In the vast majority of cases, these spaces are well-run and treasured by their communities, but on rare occasions, problems can arise. My hon. Friend has raised concerns about Scarisbrick village hall in her constituency. Such cases highlight the important role that local Members of Parliament can play in resolving issues in their communities. I congratulate her on securing a positive outcome that protects and preserves the war memorial. On the ongoing concerns about the management of the village hall, I note that the Charity Commission opened a regulatory compliance case into the charity in February 2026. The opening of a case is not a finding of wrongdoing, but a step the commission can take to consider concerns in greater detail. The case is ongoing, and the commission is therefore limited in what it can say at this stage. However, I understand that the commission intends to meet the parties involved at the charity’s premises in the coming weeks. The Charity Commission for England and Wales plays a vital role in helping community charities, such as village halls, to thrive, and in supporting public trust and confidence in charities across the sector.

Trust is important, and I support the points made by my hon. Friend the Member for West Lancashire (Ashley Dalton), but further to the issues that I raised in my intervention, I point out to the Minister that we are expecting a judgment from the Charities Commission on the evidence provided to it by Members of Parliament representing coalfield constituencies. We gathered that evidence from local authorities, the National Union of Mineworkers, the Industrial Communities Alliance and around 20 locations across the UK coalfields. This is not an isolated issue, so does the Minister believe that the Charity Commission has sufficient powers to effect the change required to hold charities to account for their actions? If I may be so bold, will she agree to meet a delegation from the coalfields group to look at some of the evidence that we have gathered, which should raise concerns for the Charity Commission investigators?

I will come to the points that my hon. Friend raises later, but I will say that the Under-Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, my hon. Friend the Member for Barnsley South (Stephanie Peacock), met the Charity Commission when she was the Minister responsible for civil society to discuss CISWO’s support for coalmining communities. My hon. Friend the Member for Easington (Grahame Morris) cares deeply about supporting coalfield communities, and the Government and I share that sentiment. I would be happy to meet a delegation. We rightly rely on the Charity Commission not only to promote best practice and deliver knowledge for trustees, but to step in and act when issues arise. As a civil regulator, its core responsibility is to ensure that trustees comply with their duties under charity law, that charities pursue their charitable purposes for the public benefit, and that any misconduct or mismanagement is addressed. The Charity Commission has a range of statutory, investigatory and enforcement powers at its disposal to effectively regulate charities and address wrongdoing. The Government fully support the Charity Commission in taking proportionate action in such cases, but it is important to note that the Charity Commission can only take action where there is misconduct or mismanagement. Where a charity pursues its charitable purposes within the law and the terms of its governing document, the commission cannot intervene.

I am a member of the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee, and we have had the Charity Commission in to review matters, in the wake of its attempt to violate privilege in several cases that had been dealt with badly. Would it surprise the Minister to learn that the Charity Commission has expressed concern about the limits of its powers? One example was an incident in which a member of a charity board dealing with children had been asking for intimate photography of children. They resigned from that role, which meant that they could not be disbarred from holding an office in another charity in future, because the powers of the commission apparently did not extend that far.

I am interested in having a further discussion with my hon. Friend, because what he has described sounds extremely worrying. It is undoubtedly important to resolve disputes such as the one raised by my hon. Friend the Member for West Lancashire, for the benefit of local communities. Indeed, many of the points that she raised seem deeply concerning. However, with more than 170,000 registered charities to regulate, the Charity Commission takes a risk-based approach to regulation to ensure that no issue or complaint is overlooked, while also ensuring that it acts in a proportionate manner and uses its resources to prioritise the highest risks. That means that in some cases the commission cannot take action, or cannot take action as swiftly as those involved would like it to, and final outcomes of casework can depend on the complexity of each individual case. The commission experienced a 50% increase in the number of concerns raised about charities between August 2025 and 2026, which has left its resources severely stretched. It is important that we have a regulator that can act effectively to tackle abuse and mismanagement of charities.

There is a fundamental difference between others raising concerns and a Member of the House doing so. We do this all the time, do we not, in respect of public bodies, Government Departments and so on? That should be given an appropriate degree of weight by the Charity Commission, because we speak for our constituents.

I agree. The Secretary of State and I discussed the possibility of presenting this as a test case to establish why it is taking so long to be resolved, and we will explore that further. In the 2025 spending review, in recognition of all of the challenges faced by the Charity Commission, we gave it a 25% uplift in funding, which is backing a three-year transformation programme to manage rising demands on its services. I know that it has been criticised recently by both the Committee of Privileges and the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee for its approach to reports by the Public Service Ombudsman, which made findings of maladministration in two cases. The commission has apologised unreservedly to Parliament in response to the Committee of Privileges report, and has accepted the report in full. I have confidence in the commission’s leadership, and I know that the board is taking action to address the concerns raised by the reports and to learn lessons for its handling of similar cases. The Government keep the Charity Commission’s powers under regular review, and are committed to strengthening them where needed. On 14 October, the Government published a consultation proposing expanded charity trustee disqualification powers, which will help to protect charities from extremist abuse.

The Government are rightly consulting on those additional powers for the commission—which I welcome—to disqualify people from being trustees or senior managers if they engage in conduct that promotes hatred of people on grounds of race, religion or belief, but does the Minister agree that we should not limit the powers to those three grounds? We often see discrimination in the form of misogyny or homophobia, and discrimination against disabled people. Would the Minister consider extending her proposals to cover those as well?

We will indeed be happy to engage with my hon. Friend and look into his proposals. We will also consider carefully PACAC’s call for a broad review of the Charity Commission’s powers to ensure robust regulatory oversight, and will continue to engage closely with the commission on that. Let me again thank my hon. Friend the Member for West Lancashire for securing the debate, and genuinely thank all the Members who have contributed to it. I think that it has been enhanced by all those contributions. Question put and agreed to.

title: Physical Activity: Children and Young People

items.txt: 1. What steps her Department is taking to increase participation in sport and physical activity among children and young people.

The Government are highly committed to increasing physical activity for young people, which is why we are reforming the PE and school sports partnerships, strengthening links between schools, clubs and local communities, and investing in grassroots facilities. If I may say so, my hon. Friend is an outstanding advocate on this issue and an example of the amazing contribution that people can make throughout their lifetimes through sport. As an umpire for Wimbledon and someone who still plays tennis for her county, she is a shining example of what can be achieved through sport.

I thank my right hon. Friend for her kind words. At the recent Warwickshire youth conference, young people spoke to me about the challenges they face in finding work, from poor mental health to lack of confidence. Grassroots sport can help to break that cycle by building resilience and giving young people the skills to succeed. What steps is the Secretary of State taking to ensure that sport plays a greater role in tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training?

My hon. Friend will know that this Government co-produced with young people the national youth strategy, which we published last year. In that strategy we set out a commitment that all young people in this country should have somewhere to go, something to do and someone who cares. We are setting about rebuilding youth work and youth services, and putting my Department in the service of young people and that strategy through sports, art and other opportunities for them to live richer, larger lives. Next week we will publish the Milburn review to tackle the 1 million young people who are not in education, employment or training. The Prime Minister believes firmly—and I support him—that that has to include enriching activities for young people from an early age and all the way through their teenage years, so that when they go out looking for work, they have the resilience, confidence and skills to be able to benefit.

Reflecting on my time as Sports Minister, one thing that struck me is how much time we spent on the latest drama created by sports or governing bodies, and how little time we spent on promoting physical activity, to the extent that when we had meetings with Sport Ministers from around the world, it was striking that they were often members of a Department of Health, rather than some other body. Does the right hon. Lady agree that there is real merit in much closer co-operation, and perhaps even joint ministerial roles, in promoting physical activity and sports roles, with the added benefit of potential access to greater budgets?

I strongly support what the hon. Gentleman says. Less than half of children are getting the recommended 60 active minutes a day, and we as a Government are really concerned about that. I agree that this has to be a whole-of-Government endeavour. In particular, the Department of Health and Social Care, the Department for Education and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport need to work together much more closely. I have discussed this issue with the new Health Secretary and the new Education Secretary, but I am very keen to discuss it further with the hon. Gentleman and to get his advice as a former Sport Minister on how we might best achieve that.
2. If she will ensure that place-based funding for media and creative industries in the regions does not negatively impact London’s media sector.

Lifting the full potential of our city regions and clusters across the UK is a core objective not just of our modern industrial strategy, but of our plan for growth in every postcode. Place-based funding is helping to ensure that our city regions and high-potential clusters are able to unlock more growth, create more good jobs and continue producing world-class creative content. London is a global creative industries super-cluster, and we are committed to supporting its continued success as one of the 12 priority super-clusters identified in the creative industries sector plan.

My constituent Simon has built a media company in the heart of our creative sector in London, but at a recent surgery he told me that the Culture Secretary’s regional funding drive is destroying the creative industry in London and the south-east. Simon and his business partner employ 25 people, and they pay rent, business rates and service charges on top of their wage bill. We should be supporting this industry, not stripping it. What is the Minister doing to support the creative industries in the south of England?

I congratulate Simon on setting up his business. It is true that 67% of all creative industries activity happens in London alone, and an extra 18% in the south-east. The region is a super-cluster, and this Government are doing all we can to ensure that we support the industry right across the United Kingdom. The BBC has built hubs across the country, including in Cardiff, Bristol, Manchester, Newcastle and Glasgow, and they provide the ecosystem that allows companies to thrive. London will remain one of our super-clusters, and the funding that we are putting into the creative industries goes right across the country.

To get growth in every postcode, surely we must junk the Tories’ crude anti-London formula that saw the whole of the capital disadvantaged, including Ealing Studios—the home of comedy—and Acton’s Versa Studios, where “Big Brother” is made. Can Ministers start the rebalancing by introducing an unscripted tax credit? It has worked wonders in Ireland, where it is at 20%.

I do not know whether that was a question to me or a challenge to the hon. Member for Farnham and Bordon (Gregory Stafford), who asked the original question. The Government are fully committed to funding the creative industries wherever they are across the country. The Prime Minister has challenged all of us in the Government to create growth in every postcode, but in order to do so we need creativity in every postcode, because we know that there is talent everywhere, but not opportunity.
3. What assessment she has made of the adequacy of facilities for girls’ grassroots sports.

This Government are more committed than ever to championing women’s sport and inspiring girls to get involved. One of the great pleasures I have had in recent years is being presented with the challenge of a whole generation of girls coming forward to play sports such as football and rugby, inspired by the stunning success of the Lionesses and the Red Roses. That is why we have removed many of the restrictions on what grassroots facilities we are prepared to fund. The one restriction we have put in place is that women and girls must have equal access to priority slots when we invest in grassroots sports facilities. I would be delighted to discuss with the hon. Member what more we can do.

At Westminster Park in my constituency, girls want to play football and cricket, but there is nowhere suitable for them to change. For the Leopards, Westminster Park’s girls football team, that becomes a real barrier as the girls get older and move up to the adult pitches. Councillor Razia Daniels and I have been campaigning with local residents to get better facilities, and the council has commissioned a feasibility study, but it has no capital budget for this, and without proper funding the girls risk another season without being able to play. I would like to take up the Secretary of State’s offer, so will she meet me to discuss how we can work with the Department to ensure that the council, the Football Foundation and Sport England secure the funding so that no more girls miss out?

I would be very happy to ensure that officials follow up with the hon. Member to resolve that issue. She is right to point to changing facilities as one of the key reasons why girls do not stay involved in sport. We really have pushed hard to ensure that this is a priority for funding from the Football Foundation and others. A number of Members across the House have raised with me as Culture Secretary over the past couple of years the significant challenge of navigating these funding systems and the conditions attached to them. We are looking at how to make it much easier for councils and Members of Parliament to access that funding to solve the local problems that she describes, but I would be very happy to follow this up.

Will the Secretary of State please join me in thanking the volunteers at Junior Parkrun at Parc Bryn Bach in Tredegar. It has good facilities, but their hard work has doubled the number of girls and boys getting out to run on a Sunday morning. Having said that, research from Sky shows that girls in my constituency still do an hour and 16 minutes less sport each week than boys. Can she give us the wider picture of the steps that she is taking to close that gap and get more girls to be active?

I thank my hon. Friend for his advocacy for Parkrun, which has been one of the real bright spots on the sport landscape in recent years—I am a keen participant in my local Parkrun at Haigh Hall and across the borough. I take this opportunity to congratulate all the volunteers at Junior Parkrun, because without them these amazing events would not happen. He is right to point to the challenges we still have with women and girls’ participation. There is no single solution, but I can assure him that I and my hon. Friend the Minister for Sport are treating this as one of the top priorities in the Department.
4. What steps she is taking to support development of the new theatre in Swindon.

I was delighted to see £20 million allocated for a new cultural venue in Swindon via the growth mission fund, thanks to the tenacity of my hon. Friend and my right hon. Friend the Member for Swindon South (Heidi Alexander). Officials will continue to work on plans for the theatre with the new Conservative council, which I believe is assessing whether it should take this forward. The investment remains subject to a final business case demonstrating the project’s viability and affordability. I welcome this investment in the arts and communities in Swindon, and I thank my hon. Friend for his question.

I thank the Minister for his response. I am actively encouraging the Conservative administration in Swindon to proceed with the plans for a new theatre, following the funding successfully secured by my right hon. Friend the Member for Swindon South (Heidi Alexander) and me. In the interim, we have to think about our beloved Wyvern theatre. Is there any additional support to retrofit existing theatres in the interim?

There is. We are investing up to £425 million via the creative foundations fund for urgent capital works for not-for-profit cultural venues in England. The funding is already supporting older theatres, such as Scarborough Theatre Trust and Northampton Theatres Trust. I understand that Wyvern theatre’s activities involve Swindon borough council, a commercial operator and a charitable programme via Reach Inclusive Arts. I encourage local partners to discuss capital pressures with Arts Council England and my hon. Friend. I am sure that the Arts Minister would be delighted to meet him and his colleague, my right hon. Friend the Member for Swindon South (Heidi Alexander), to discuss that further.
5. What steps her Department is taking to support owners of listed buildings with the cost of essential repairs and maintenance.

Our listed buildings stand at the heart of our communities, and we are investing in heritage across the country with £230 million by 2030 to support listed buildings across England. That includes £75 million through the heritage at risk capital fund to support the repair and conservation of buildings at risk, and £92 million through the places of worship renewal fund for urgent repairs that keep buildings in use.

Many churches relied on the listed places of worship grant scheme to reclaim VAT paid on essential repairs and maintenance. The Government say that the new places of worship renewal fund will be targeted at areas with the greatest disadvantage and need. Can the Minister clarify the metrics being used and reassure my constituents that rural churches in areas such as South Northamptonshire will not be overlooked?

I am grateful to the hon. Lady and I appreciate that she is a huge champion for her local community, which has a rich heritage. The reality is that, under the previous scheme, 80% of those who got funding said that they would have done it anyway, so it was hugely under-targeted. The reality was also that more deprived areas simply could not raise the capital needed in the first place to qualify for the VAT rebate. Our places of worship renewal fund targets those places with the greatest levels of both deprivation and need.

Listed places of worship, such as St Mary de Haura in Shoreham, are not just places to pray; they are at the beating heart of our community. Following the listed places of worship grant scheme closing and being replaced by the more competitive and VAT-included places of worship renewal fund, my constituents are concerned about their ability to repair and maintain their places of worship. Will the Minister tell the House how the Government intend to ensure that our places of worship can continue to serve our communities long into the future?

My hon. Friend is right to point out how important they are to local communities. We have the places of worship renewal fund, which I have just spoken about. In addition, the Government have made available £230 million for heritage. Further, we have the National Lottery Heritage Fund and I also encourage him to engage with the Church of England.
6. What assessment she has made of the adequacy of the performance of the Independent Football Regulator.

The Independent Football Regulator is empowering fans and protecting clubs from unsuitable owners. In the 12 months since we appointed the football regulator, he has published the “State of the Game” report, which is an unprecedented assessment of football finances, and the biggest ever undertaken. He is involved in highly complex negotiations across the football pyramid. He has also been involved in meeting fans from a number of clubs, including Sheffield Wednesday and Morecambe, when problems have arisen.

The Labour donor and chair of the Independent Football Regulator has said that if Manchester City were to sue the regulator, the regulator would need to come to the Government to get more money. Given the interest that the Prime Minister has specified about Man City and his opinion on that, how much money have the Government put aside just in case Man City sue the regulator?

We have been clear from the outset that these are very serious allegations. Manchester City must have the right to a fair process, because it strongly refutes the allegations, but that is a matter for the Premier League. Its independent body will come to a determination about that—at which point, if the allegations are upheld, we will obviously all want to see action taken—but the process has to be allowed to run its course. I would just gently say to the hon. Gentleman that I am old enough to remember when he was putting out press releases welcoming the Independent Football Regulator, at a time when his Government were in power and intended to proceed with it, and when his Government had put the football regulator we later appointed on to the long list. If he thinks he is such a crony, he needs to ask why his Government decided to put him on the long list for the appointment in the first place.

Thanks to research by organisations such as the Black Footballers’ Partnership, we know that while roughly 43% of players in the English premier league are black, black people hold just 1.6% of executive and leadership positions in British football. Will the Minister agree to meet me and the Black Footballers’ Partnership to discuss how the Government can support football in closing this outdated gap?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising this issue, which I think in the two years I have been Culture Secretary has not been raised directly with me in the House. He is absolutely right to say that that must change. The Under-Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, my hon. Friend the Member for Barnsley South (Stephanie Peacock), and I have done a lot of work with football and other sports to ensure that women are in positions of responsibility within clubs and organisations. I would be more than happy to meet him to discuss what we can do to right this historical wrong.

I refer Members to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests and my ongoing engagement with the culture, media and sport sectors as a shadow Minister. In addition to this Labour Government’s tax increases on sport, we recently learnt that their new football regulator has already spent double what the Government promised it would cost clubs and fans. When challenged on that, the chief executive of the football regulator argued that he did not agree with the Government’s forecasts, with only £1 million set aside to repay £45 million of set-up costs. That leaves £44 million unaccounted for. When should taxpayers expect their money back, and does the Secretary of State believe that the football regulator is operating to the light-touch mandate it was given by Parliament?

Yes, I do. I strongly welcome the work that the Independent Football Regulator is doing, but that is less important than the fact that fans across the country strongly welcome the work that it is doing. The “State of the Game” report was a stark wake-up call to the whole of football. As the former Sports Minister, Dame Tracey Crouch, said when she established the regulator from the fan-led review, if we do not look after the foundations of football, then we will lose one of the things that brings joy to millions of people and is one of the UK’s greatest exports. It is right that we ask football to fund the regulator, it is right that we take action to ensure that there is fair financial flow through the game, and it is right that we set it up on an independent basis with a light-touch approach to ensure that we preserve the joy of football for generations to come.

The other part of my question was about the £44 million that is currently unaccounted for. If the football regulator was to charge clubs on a £1 million basis over 10 years, that would equate to £10 million, which still leaves £35 million unaccounted for. Is the Secretary of State saying that football clubs should expect bigger bills next year, and how does she believe that will help make them more financially resilient?

The shadow Minister has consistently stood at the Dispatch Box and challenged me and the Minister for Sport on ensuring that the football regulator is independent. We believe in that independence. The football regulator has offered him many meetings to discuss the various issues that he has raised in this House, and I am sure that it would be happy to meet to discuss funding.
7. What steps her Department is taking to support regional heritage and cultural venues.

Through our Arts Everywhere programme, we are investing £1.5 billion into culture and heritage infrastructure in places with the greatest need. That includes funding the Art Centre Penryn in my hon. Friend’s constituency, which was awarded project development grants through the heritage revival fund.

Cornwall Museum and Art Gallery is essentially the national museum for Cornwall. While £7 out of £8 of DCMS’s museum funding goes to our 15 national museums, which are free to enter, the Cornwall museum charges a fee, does not get funding from the local authority any more and, as it is trustee run, is not eligible for many funding streams. What options are there for the Cornwall Museum and Art Gallery in Truro to close that funding gap?

I thank my hon. Friend for her advocacy on that issue. As an Arts Council England accredited museum, Cornwall Museum and Art Gallery is eligible to apply for the museum estate and development fund, which provides capital funding for urgent repairs and infrastructure maintenance. For other funding opportunities, the museum could also explore Arts Council and national lottery project grants and support from philanthropic organisations.

Essex and the Witham constituency have a range of fantastic heritage houses, museums and venues for people to visit. It will come as no surprise to the Minister and the Front Bench team that those venues are struggling because of increases in employment taxes and some of the other burdens they are now facing. Has the Department done a cumulative impact assessment on what that means for the sustainability of some of those big cultural heritage sites, and what more can the Government do to assist them?

The right hon. Member is a strong advocate for her constituency. This Government are investing in heritage across the country, with £230 million committed by 2030. I am sure the Minister for Heritage would be delighted to discuss it with her further.

Before I answer the question, I say to the hon. Gentleman that we stand fully with him after recent incidents online, with him having received tens of thousands of disgusting messages and death threats. This Government and everyone else in this House—maybe with the exception of a few Members of Parliament —take a zero-tolerance approach to racism and those kinds of threats. We stand with the hon. Gentleman. Local journalism is vital to society and democracy, including titles such as the Eastbourne Herald and the Eastbourne Reporter in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency. We published the local media action plan to help the sector adjust and thrive in the digital age. Our actions include a local news fund with up to £12 million, a campaign to inspire the next generation of journalists and readers, and an updated plan for journalists’ safety, both here and abroad.

I thank the Minister for his comments. It should not be controversial to say that you do not have to be white to be English. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear.”] Much of social media has become a cesspit of abuse and disinformation, but local journalism can be an antidote to such poison. Local journalism in Eastbourne is thriving, with the likes of Adam and Ivana recently joining the Eastbourne Herald and Paul Gibson’s Eastbourne News expanding, too. Will the Minister tell us a little more about what he can do to support local journalism in the fight against disinformation and misinformation?

We have the local news fund and the local news strategy. This is an issue right across the country, and we need to ensure that we have a thriving local journalistic community so that we can get those stories to people and so that the news is trusted and trustworthy. The BBC obviously plays a key role in that, and the BBC charter process is investigating how it can support that infrastructure and ecosystem across the country. I would be very happy to work with the hon. Gentleman in sharing his experience to see what we can do to help his local area and areas across all regions across the country. I want to emphasise from the Dispatch Box, too, that you do not have to be white to be English—the hon. Gentleman is right to say that—although you do have to be tight to be Scottish. [ Laughter. ]

From Scotland to Harlow, Mr Speaker. Online news sites like Your Harlow, which has provided thousands of news articles to Harlow residents across the years, rely on people visiting their site for advertising revenue, but there is a danger posed by AI summaries, particularly when some of those summaries are wrong. What thought has the Minister given to the impact of AI summaries on local news sources like Your Harlow?

The Government are actively looking at this issue, because we know from experience—we always use the Southport example—that when there are incidents or crisis moments across the country, people turn to their local news outlets and the BBC to find the truth because they are sceptical of what they are reading. In the meantime, anyone who is reading these AI summaries online should double-check with their local newspapers and the sources they are given to ensure that that information is true. What happens, of course, is the old adage: a lie is halfway around the world before the truth has got its boots on. That happens much faster now with social media. I am delighted that my hon. Friend has broken his habit in the House by at least mentioning Harlow in his question.

Vibrant local news is essential to our democracy, but plans for the Government or a state quango to pick what is a source of trustworthy news content and is prioritised over other publishers risk undermining that sector. Does the Minister agree that the approach of picking winners, with the state deciding what can be trusted, is a dangerous course and should be abandoned?

I disagree with the hon. Gentleman on this basis: the media Green Paper to which I think he is referring is trying to deal with the issue of misinformation and disinformation and to answer the exam question posed by the hon. Member for Eastbourne (Josh Babarinde) about how we promote the local trustworthy news that the public are crying out for and have a massive thirst for. It is an ecosystem that we have to try to support. The Green Paper is rightly posing these questions, and we will have the answers for the White Paper shortly.

The Minister has not given an answer and has declined to rule out going ahead with the proposals in the Green Paper for the state or a quango to decide what is trustworthy news. Will he at least rule out that only news publishers that sign up to an approved regulator under the press recognition system could qualify?

These are questions that have been asked in the Green Paper. The White Paper will be published soon, and I am not going to pre-empt it at this Dispatch Box. The hon. Gentleman will just have to contain himself until then. The big, fundamental issue here is how we deal with the misinformation and disinformation in this country that is undermining our democracy and society and doing the kinds of things that have been experienced by the hon. Member for Eastbourne. Those are the kinds of questions the Green Paper is trying to address. It is in all our interests—the interests of every Member in this House—to get misinformation and disinformation out of our ecosystem so that we can have a thriving democracy and thriving communities.
9. What steps her Department is taking to support volunteering.

I thank my hon. Friend for her support for volunteers who strengthen communities like Blaydon and Consett, and I pay tribute to her first-hand experience as a Samaritan. This year we provided £300,000 for the Big Help Out, promoting nearly 5 million volunteering opportunities across the country. We extended the know your neighbourhood fund, providing an additional £4.5 million to voluntary organisations. We also worked with the Open Data Institute and civil society partners to create a simpler system for advertising opportunities across a range of platforms.

In two weeks’ time, I will hold my annual red kite awards, ensuring that volunteers in Blaydon and Consett know the value of their work—they go above and beyond to help save lives and support whole communities. But for many voluntary organisations rising costs and reduced funding are making that good work ever more difficult. What steps are the Government taking to support voluntary groups and ensure that they are able to continue that vital support?

First, I congratulate my hon. Friend on all the work she does to ensure that the red kite awards take place. This Government are backing a strong and sustainable voluntary sector, as outlined in the civil society covenant, through VAT reliefs on donated goods, updating charity thresholds, which will save £47 million annually, and the £2 million better commissioning pathways programme. We are supporting voluntary organisations to build resilience and deliver vital support.

This year, Harrogate International Festivals is celebrating its 60th anniversary. It relies on a small army of volunteers to make it happen, with the fantastic leadership of Sharon Canavar as chief executive and Fiona Movley as chair of the board. Increasingly, arts festivals like Harrogate International Festivals are coming under strain, and we need to do more to make sure that we recruit the next generation of volunteers so that it is there for the future. Will the Minister meet me to discuss what more we can do to ensure that the festivals have another 60 years and beyond?
I congratulate the hon. Gentleman on all the work he is doing to celebrate the 60th anniversary of his local festivals. I would be more than happy to meet with him to discuss it further.
10. What steps her Department is taking to improve online safety for children.
