We are working closely with the Polish authorities on the case, as well as providing the appropriate consular support to the family in what is a deeply distressing and appalling time. My thoughts are with them. My hon. Friend is absolutely right to praise my hon. Friend the Member for Cowdenbeath and Kirkcaldy (Melanie Ward) for her past work and advocacy on those issues before joining the Government. It is crucial that we listen to the actual experiences of those who have seen the reality on the ground in Gaza, as well as organisations and others. That is exactly what the Foreign Secretary and I have been doing, and I will listen to what they have to say about the reality of what is happening and respond accordingly.

Would the Minister agree that the Palestinian-majority parties, which have scored a record number of seats in the most recent Israeli elections and have now said that, despite profound differences, they will give Eisenkot support in trying to find a new Government, so that there might be a change of policy in the Israeli Government, show us all what extraordinary grace is needed if we are to find a lasting and inclusive peace in the region? I have to say, it is a grace that seems to be totally missing from the Conservative Front Bench today. Will the Minister also give us an update on the latest with the so-called board of peace, which was meant to be brokering the aid into Gaza, but seems to be totally missing from the conversation?

On the Israeli elections, obviously the formation of any future Government is a matter for the parties and people in Israel and for their system of government. We will of course work and engage with any Government formed, and our asks of that Government and demands in relation to the situation will be same: get the aid in; support the two-state solution; stop the illegal settlement expansion; and stop the violence and settler terrorism that we have seen. Our message will be very clear whoever is in power and we will engage accordingly. The hon. Lady talked about the board of peace, which does important work. We are not a member of the board of peace, but when I was in Egypt a few weeks ago, I met with the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, which is the body that has been set up to look at the administration of Gaza going forward. The House will note the comments of the board of peace in relation to the current situation in Gaza, and the condemnation and criticism that has come from all parts. That shows the scale of the challenge, and that the Israeli Government need to respond.

Last night, six Palestinians including a surgeon, Dr Rizk Abu Shaira, were slaughtered in an airstrike on Gaza’s Nasser medical complex. It is the sixth attack on the hospital in just three years, and part of the systemic healthcare destruction in Gaza that UN experts have called a “medicide”. Can the Minister confirm whether this Government are tracking Israel’s use of the F-35 parts that are still shamefully being exported to Israel from the UK, and whether they are being used to deliberately target Gaza’s last remaining hospitals?

I share my hon. Friend’s horror at the reports coming in overnight, and we have been attempting to get clarity on the situation there. A hit on a medical facility, after so many doctors, humanitarian workers and others have lost their lives, been injured and been put at risk by the actions in Gaza, is absolutely appalling. I have heard the appalling experiences of a number of doctors in recent weeks. I assure my hon. Friend that all of our arms exports are kept under constant review, and we are convinced that we have the right measures in place to ensure that they are done in accordance with the law.

Almost 2 million people are now forced into 30% of the Gaza strip. Israel continues to bombard them, to allow them to die and to refuse aid going in. How is the British Government’s aid going to get there, and what sanctions will the Minister place against Israel, as the illegal occupying power of the Gaza strip, for its refusal to allow it in? Will the Minister, for once, make it absolutely clear that there is no further military or security co-operation whatsoever with Israel because of its behaviour in the west bank and its killing of almost 100,000 people on the Gaza strip?

I was very clear about what needs to happen on Gaza: we need to get all that crucial aid in. The aid that we have provided has made a difference, but it cannot make the difference that we wish it to have, and all items cannot get in, because of the blockages we have seen. The right hon. Gentleman rightly points to Israel’s responsibilities as an occupying power. It needs to adhere to them—there are clear legal grounds for that—and we will continue to urge it to do so. I have been very clear about the position we have taken on arms exports and the number of licences that we have refused and revoked. We will continue to keep all those under constant review.

I thank the Minister for his statement this morning. I have to say that I have been saddened by the approach of the those on the Opposition Front Bench, particularly as the Minister was addressing what is a climate catastrophe and two breaches of international law by a so-called democratically elected Government. In a meeting earlier this year with COGAT—Co-ordinator of Government Activities in the Territories—a cross-party delegation from this House and I were appalled at the perverse way in which the definition of dual-use items was being used, as it includes things like tent poles that can by no means be considered to be dual use. I very much welcome the sanctions the Minister has talked about, but will he be very firm in his conversations with COGAT, as I know he will be, in ensuring that that definition is consigned to the history books once and for all?

I can absolutely assure my hon. Friend that the absurdity of some of the restrictions is at the heart of the conversations we are having with COGAT, and indeed other authorities. She quite rightly points out the climate aspects of this situation, too. The tragedy is that we knew those conditions were coming, and from previous examples we have seen we knew the impact they could have. Like others, including the United Nations, we issued warnings, and yet that crucial aid and assistance was not able to get in at the necessary levels, and large numbers of tents, tarpaulins and the equipment to put tents up still remain outside Gaza.

The blocking of aid has previously been cited by a UN commission as evidence of a genocide in Gaza, and stopping infant milk reaching starving children certainly sounds like that to me. Are this Government committed to working with the UN to provide the necessary evidence to prove that what is happening in Gaza is a genocide?

The Foreign Secretary and I have set out our position on this matter on a number of occasions. We will, of course, continue to work and support the work of the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court and other bodies and listen very carefully to all evidence provided.

I welcome the Minister’s statement and the promise of the further £5 million. The devastating flooding in Gaza has compounded the intolerable suffering of the Palestinians. Israel’s continued obstruction of humanitarian aid, including vital flood relief materials, is indefensible. When will the Minister and the Government not simply ask for but demand the immediate entry of emergency shelters, drainage equipment and flood relief supplies, press Israel to remove all restrictions on humanitarian access and work with international partners to establish a funded, long-term reconstruction programme to prevent further avoidable suffering?

My hon. Friend clearly and passionately sets out the situation in Gaza. I hope I have been very clear today that we are making demands, and that it is not just us, but the United Nations and other countries doing so. We will be bringing together other people in that demand in New York today.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza is absolutely horrific. The Minister says that he is here today to send a clear message to the Israeli Government to let in the aid, but as he himself has pointed out, he and others have been sending that same message and predicting this situation for months and indeed years. Unless asks are accompanied by action, they will be ignored, as they have been over and over again. The Minister talks about contributing more UK aid, but what is the point if it is just going to sit on the border, blocked from getting through the border crossings by the Israeli Government? I welcome the expansion of the global human rights sanctions regime to cover blocking delivery of humanitarian aid; surely deregistering 37 humanitarian organisations and stopping tents getting through to people facing horrific flooding counts as that. How much longer does the Minister need to wait until he acts?

With the greatest respect, we are acting, we have acted and we will continue to act. Ultimately, the responsibility here lies with Israel as the occupying power. It is failing to deliver on those requirements, and we are going to hold it to account in every way possible. We have taken powers and announced additional money today. We will continue to demand directly with Israel, and with others publicly, and to build international pressure and consensus around that. That is exactly what we are doing in New York today—bringing together other countries and ensuring that that pressure is brought to bear on Israel to uphold its responsibilities.

Against the backdrop of a war that has seen a record number of orphaned child amputees, the news that equipment to alleviate the devastating floods in Gaza is being blocked at the border continues a pattern that we have seen with medicines and baby food. Does the Minister agree that without actual evidence that this is being done for military purposes, it looks like collective punishment? Will he restate our adherence to the ICJ process and use maximum pressure? Change of Government or not, a change of action is needed.

A change of action is absolutely needed. I have heard the same reports as my hon. Friend about medicines, prosthetics and other items being denied entry. She will note that I announced what we are doing, particularly on the issue of prosthetics. Of course, we also need to get access for people to be medically evacuated, as we have already done with a number of severe cases, including here to the UK. We need to open up new routes for people to get treated in the region, too. Most crucially, hospitals in Gaza need to have the equipment and capability necessary to function as hospitals and not to face devastating attacks that kill their personnel.

In 2024, the ICJ issued three legally binding orders requiring Israel to allow entry of shelter, food, fuel and medical supplies and to keep those crossings open for as long as possible. We often hear warm words from the Dispatch Box supporting the principles of international law, and we have heard talk again today of expanding sanctions, but the real question is, when? What work is the Minister undertaking with international allies to ensure that those ICJ orders are upheld?

It is crucial that ICJ orders and positions are respected, which is exactly why we work with international partners to raise attention to that and to hold Israel to account. That is exactly the sort of work we are doing in New York in our role on the Security Council; it is exactly the work we are doing today, bringing together different international partners as part of our call to action on humanitarian access. We will continue to hold Israel to account.

The recent flooding in Gaza has made an awful situation even worse. Some 1.4 million Gazans living in tents and thousands of families have lost what little shelter they had. We need to get as much aid into Gaza as possible, and Israel continuing to block that aid seemingly breaks international law. I ask the Minister what practical diplomatic action we will take if Israel continues to block the flow of aid into Gaza.

We have already taken practical diplomatic action this week, including in Tel Aviv and here in London and, crucially, in galvanising other countries around the world. I hope to be able to share with my hon. Friend such work later on today in New York to hold Israel to account on these very issues.

I cannot recall another conflict where the occupying and illegally invading force has used adverse weather, starvation and hypothermia as a weapon of war. The comments from those on the Opposition Front Bench were absolutely disgusting. Our compassion should be equal for Israeli civilians and Palestinian civilians. We should not differentiate in our humanity based on ethnicity or nationality. Israel has used Lavender AI systems to target and execute thousands of Palestinian children, women and men. According to the Financial Times , the IDF is now in talks to deploy 1,000 AI robots to police and potentially engage in combat in Gaza. The humanitarian crisis is only worsening, with the future of technology being used to annihilate the civilian population, while Israel’s tech sector is booming. What steps are the Government taking to ensure that the UK can no longer invest in Israeli companies or co-operate with Israel, as these tools are used to cause the misery and death of Palestinians?

I am not aware of the specific systems that the hon. Gentleman refers to, but I would be very happy to write to him on that issue. What I can assure him of is that we have, I would argue, the most robust export licensing system in the world and we have huge amounts of scrutiny and controls on it. We consider all export licences in that regard.

I welcome the Minister’s statement and condemn the shadow Foreign Secretary’s comments. The situation in Gaza is dire. Flooding has damaged or destroyed thousands of shelters. Heavy rain has disrupted education for around 55,000 children across at least 55 learning spaces, while flooding and damaged infrastructure are putting children’s health, safety and access to basic essentials at serious risk. Enough is enough. What discussions has the Minister had with his American counterparts, who have real influence over the Israeli Government, to try to broker a deal to ensure that aid flows fully into Gaza?

We engage closely with our American counterparts on a range of issues every day, as my hon. Friend will know. While we are not part of the board of peace, we have engaged closely with it and the efforts on the 20-point plan. It is crucial that that is able to move forward. Part of that is making sure that there is humanitarian access for aid supplies. We will work with all partners internationally to address these appalling issues on the ground, which she rightly described.

I am also genuinely shocked that the shadow Foreign Secretary would use a horrific humanitarian crisis in an attempt to score cheap political points. The flooding in Gaza has added more suffering to what was already a horrific and deteriorating situation, if that were even possible, and the Israeli Government preventing aid from getting in is making life even worse for elderly people, sick people and children. I very much welcome the Minister’s commitment to further aid and the condemnation of the Israeli Government’s actions, but could he highlight what specific actions are being taken by us and our allies to ensure that Israel does allow aid in, including any further sanctions and when those will be imposed? Will the Israeli ambassador be summoned to No. 10 by the end of today?

The hon. Gentleman has already heard what I said about our engagement directly with the Israeli Government in Tel Aviv and here. I can assure him that multiple conversations are going on. I could not be clearer publicly, let alone privately, about what needs to happen. We are conveying that in every way possible and working with international partners. I reassure the hon. Gentleman and other colleagues about the humanitarian funding we are providing to Palestine overall. Of the £78.3 million we already announced, £74.9 million has been disbursed to partners already, including in Gaza and the west bank. I assure him that the work we are doing is making a difference. Given the scale of need that he describes and what we saw at the weekend, so much more needs to get in and so much more needs to be done. That is what we are pressing for.

I think many Conservative voters in Edinburgh South West would be disgusted by the shadow Foreign Secretary’s comments. The only reassurance I can give them is that when he made the comments, behind him were four fully empty Benches—perhaps those Members had prior sight of the right hon. Gentleman’s comments. Eman attended my constituency surgery on Saturday; she has probably attended more of my surgeries than any other constituent. She was in tears talking about this issue, not because she has watched it on TV or seen pictures on social media but because she has lost friends and family in this conflict. She is an amazing woman, and it is always fantastic speaking to her. On her behalf, I want to ask a couple of questions. First, I know that it is a very congested site, but is there no prospect of airdropping aid into Gaza? Secondly, Netanyahu has said that this is nothing to do with Israel—that it has no responsibility. Was there any acceptance in the diplomatic talks that Israel is partly responsible at least and holds the keys to resolving it?

I thank my hon. Friend for conveying so powerfully the views of his constituent. It is those direct connections that we often hear about so passionately in our constituencies. Indeed, in my own surgeries in Cardiff South and Penarth I have had individuals who have family in Gaza, and I know humanitarian workers who have worked there as well. Airdrops are an extraordinarily complex logistical operation to pull off. The best way to get aid in is by reopening those crossing points and making sure that there are no restrictions on dual use. That would have the maximum impact that we want. I could not have been clearer: Israel ultimately has the responsibility. As the occupying power, it has the legal and moral responsibility to allow in this lifesaving aid. We urge it to do so.

We watched this genocide with more than 64,000 Palestinian children murdered and maimed by the 2,000 bombs that rained on their heads. We watched this genocide while Palestinian children were murdered through starvation while piles of food sat a few hundred metres away. We watched this genocide while Palestinian children were butchered by Israeli snipers, drones and tanks. Here we are again, for the fourth winter, watching this genocide while Palestinian children are being drowned by sewage-filled rainwater. Does the Minister agree that we, the UK, have a legal and moral obligation to help, and can he confirm that all options are on the table, including naval assets in the region ready to help to ensure that we stop watching and start acting?

We are acting, we have been acting, and we will continue to act. I am proud of the fact that we had already pre-positioned support and resources with some of the organisations that can make the difference on the ground. That has been making a difference, but there needs to be much, much more. That is why I have today announced the additional £5 million of funding to UNICEF.

I thank the Minister for his statement and express solidarity with my hon. Friend the Member for Cowdenbeath and Kirkcaldy (Melanie Ward) on the Front Bench. A little over a year ago, a ceasefire was agreed, and that offered people a glimmer of hope that finally the horrors we have seen over the past few years were coming to an end. Given that 1,600 men, women and children have been killed since that agreement, it is clear that this is a ceasefire in name only. Will the Minister condemn the ongoing violence and urge all parties to come together and finally honour the commitment of a ceasefire and move towards a lasting peace?

I absolutely will. My hon. Friend sets out the case very convincingly; we have to get back to that 20-point plan, and we have to get back to getting the aid in, stopping the violence and moving forward with a governance that no longer involves Hamas.

I welcome the statement by the Minister. In it, he outlined the new settlement sanctions regime that was announced earlier this year. I appreciate that he says that work is under way at pace, but can I press him for a timetable for when it will come into force?

I set out a timetable earlier. The Foreign Secretary was clear that it will be six to nine months, but we will try to do it at the earlier end of that scale. I want to be clear with the House that that is because we need to make sure that this regime is designed effectively, so that it will have the impact that we are aiming for. We have incredible teams of sanctions officials who work on these issues. We are very successful in that the regimes that we run around the world have an impact as well as being legally and evidentially sound. It is important that we get it right, but we want to see this brought in as soon as possible.

The Government have rightly described Israel’s occupation of Gaza and the west bank as illegal. In the light of this, surely Israel’s control of Gaza’s territorial waters must be in some question. Can my hon. Friend the Minister give his thoughts on what pressure this Government and the international community can bring to bear on Israel to ensure that aid can come in, perhaps through a naval route and indeed other routes?

Matters that ultimately relate to maritime delimitations and so on must be done in line with the United Nations convention on the law of the sea. We are a firm defender of that principle. My hon. Friend rightly talks about different routes through which aid can get in. I would draw him back to what I said earlier, which is that the best thing that can be done is to reopen Erez, to make sure that Kerem Shalom is open fully and to ensure that those dual-use restrictions are removed. That will make the tangible difference on the ground right now.

Like myself, my constituents in Hyndburn and Haslingden are deeply concerned about the situation in Gaza, with 950,000 displaced people urgently in need of aid. Unlike the Conservatives, I am very proud that we have committed £88 million to support the Palestinian territories and an extra £5 million today. Could the Minister say more about the expansion of the global human rights regime and how that might help to get the aid into Gaza that is so desperately needed?

I set out the message on that new regime at the end of my statement. We are sending a very clear signal that—not just in relation to Gaza but in relation to a number of other conflicts and situations around the world—we can take action against those who deny humanitarian assistance and lifesaving aid when it is most needed. My hon. Friend speaks with great passion on behalf of her constituents, and I thank her for the support that she has given us today.

I thank the Minister for his statement. Like, I suspect, every Member of this House, I have received countless emails from my concerned constituents—residents of West Dunbartonshire—who regard the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, made worse by the recent deadly storm, as utterly unacceptable and entirely the fault of Israel and its restrictions on aid getting in. Will the Minister tell the House what level of UK lifesaving humanitarian aid is blocked, and who have we specifically sanctioned, and when, for actions in blocking UK aid?

On the last point, we have only just taken the powers in recent weeks, and I will not comment on future designations. On the aid that has been provided to date and what items we think are being blocked, I do not how much granular detail we can go into for operational reasons, but I will certainly try to write to my hon. Friend with some more information about the types of items and others that we have funded. I saw with my own eyes huge amounts of aid from a range of different donors sitting in warehouses in Egypt, unable to be delivered because the Israelis had denied it.

I am grateful to the Minister for his statement. Last night, my two-year-old daughter fell asleep next to me in a warm, dry home. In Gaza, mums and their two-years-olds were not sleeping; they were surrounded by flood water, frozen and drenched. As mums like me watch this from our living rooms in the UK, I am sure that I cannot be the only one thinking, “There but for the grace of God go I.” What new steps are being considered following Israel’s recent elections to make it clear that withholding the vital aid that we are providing, including to toddlers and babies, will not be tolerated now or throughout the extremely difficult winter still to come?

My hon. Friend speaks with the passion and clarity of any parent in this House or, indeed, in Britain when looking at those scenes. That is fundamentally what should be motivating us in our efforts and in our commentary on this situation. Most importantly, we have to act, and that is exactly why we are going to use every route we have—directly with the Government of Israel, directly with the different agencies and authorities, at the United Nations, in our sanctions regimes, and ultimately in the direct aid and assistance that we can provide—to ensure that children do not have to go through the experience that she so powerfully described.

I refer Members to my declaration in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests as a trustee for a humanitarian children’s charity that sends aid to hospitals and families in Gaza at this time. I thank my hon. Friend for his statement. He knows that humanitarian organisations are working tirelessly on the ground to try to save lives. More than 77,000 Palestinians have lost their lives in this abhorrent war, including 17,000 children, yet even after the so-called ceasefire, still more than 1,600 have lost their lives. We know from the reports from the UN and its independent commission that Israel has committed war crimes and genocide against the Palestinian people. What further action will the Government take to protect civilians, including children, in Gaza and to secure a lasting peace?

International humanitarian law and principles need to be upheld. We are resolute in defending those principles internationally and in the accountability that we expect. We communicate that directly to the Government of Israel and to all other parties, and we will continue to stand up for humanitarian workers and all those who do incredible work. I want to pay tribute to them, because I have met so many over recent weeks. They often put themselves in harm’s way, knowing the risks, and still go out there driven by the pure humanitarian impulse to try to make life better for people who are suffering so much. My tribute today is to them.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. The right hon. Member for Tonbridge (Tom Tugendhat) has acted shamefully during this session. First, he suggested that an hon. Member was siding with Hamas, a proscribed terror organisation—a disgraceful slur, which the right hon. Member needs to withdraw. Then, from a sedentary position, he suggested that another one of my hon. Friends was being antisemitic. Will you provide advice, Madam Deputy Speaker, as to how to ensure that the record is corrected and such awful accusations are not allowed to stand?

I thank the hon. Lady for her point of order. She and all Members will know that good temper and moderation are the characteristics of parliamentary debate, and they should prevail even from a sedentary position.

We now come to the Select Committee statement on behalf of the Health and Social Care Committee. Layla Moran will speak for up to 10 minutes, during which there will be no interventions. At the conclusion of the statement, Members may ask questions on the subject of the statement; those contributions must be questions, not speeches.

On behalf of the Health and Social Care Committee, it is a pleasure to present to the House our report on the obesity moonshot, our sixth report of this Parliament. It is also the final report in a series from our inquiry on food and weight management, drawing together our two previous reports on the food environment and obesity treatment. What if I said that there was a life-limiting condition that affects a third of adults in this country—one that costs the Government at least £74 billion a year, and for which they have no coherent plan? I am afraid to say that this is the case for the relapsing, remitting condition that is obesity—a condition that, if left untreated, is associated with dozens of others, from cancer to diabetes to heart disease and fertility problems. Why have we got here? In short, it has happened because of an enduring underlying stigma that that condition is in some way a personal failing of individuals, rather than a largely preventable and demonstrably treatable disease that society and the Government need to take as seriously as any other. In July last year, we launched our inquiry into food and weight management to better understand the public health challenge of rising rates of obesity. We asked why, despite there being at least 14 Government strategies and nearly 700 individual policies since 1992, efforts to reverse the tide of the country’s obesity crisis have failed spectacularly. The latest Government policy—the so-called moonshot—was announced in the Government’s 10-year health plan, with an ambition to “end the obesity epidemic.” That is certainly a laudable aim, but it faces the unfortunate pitfall of lacking any real substance, and our concern is that, without significant work, it is doomed to fail. We want this to succeed. If we are going to call it a moonshot, let us look at its destination, at its flight path and at who is in command. Can you tell that I am a Star Trek geek, Madam Deputy Speaker? Obesity is a crisis. Among reception-age children, it has now reached a level of 10.5%. That is the highest it has ever been. It is a shocking figure. When we asked Ministers what they expected from the trajectory of the moonshot—do we expect the rise to stop, level off or go down, and over what period and with what targets?—we did not get any coherent answers. That is just not good enough. How do we know if we are reaching where we want to go if we have not even defined the destination? Next, let us look at how we might get there: the flight plan. We found a muddled relationship between prevention and treatment in conversations about obesity. I hear this all the time. If someone is living with obesity, immediately the conversations about it turn to the food system. However, the fact of the matter is—and this is the bit that I think most people do not understand—if someone has lived with obesity for a long-enough period of time, their underlying physiology changes. It is no longer enough simply to point to lifestyle changes or to ask for changes in the wider environment. There must also be a clinical pathway that those people can follow, and that is simply not what happens. Let us take another example that is not dissimilar. A bariatric surgeon told us, “I still see lung cancer every day in my clinical practice, and I have to treat it…Nobody questions whether those patients should get chemotherapy”. But if someone presents with obesity, that is exactly what happens. We do not tell someone living with cancer to stop smoking—it is too late by that point. Yes, ideally, we stop them in the first place, but we also need to be able to treat the problem in front of us. One reason we have not turned the tide on obesity so far is the failure to treat prevention and treatment as distinct but interoperable. Let us take each in turn. On prevention, our report on “Fixing the food environment” focused on the action that the Government must take to prevent people from living with obesity in the first place, bea

Taking part in this inquiry was eye-opening. It was interesting to see the Public Health Minister’s predecessor tell the Committee that we would treat obesity in future as a relapsing-remitting condition. I hope the current Minister will undertake to follow through on that so that we can update all our guidance. Does the hon. Member agree that central to the problem of how we treat obesity is that we see it as a one-time thing? Like a broken leg, it is treated once, the people lose the weight and then we let them go, with the result that too many people get GLP-1s without the support on diet and lifestyle that comes along with them, and they are not followed up on. Would it not make a lot more sense if the health service treated people in a person-centred way and helped them recover from this relapsing-remitting condition of obesity?

I am extremely grateful to the Committee member for his question—he is absolutely right. We had a roundtable with lived experience witnesses and they all said the same thing. Even though many had had aspects of treatment over the years and had tried every conceivable diet, what was disheartening was that they would go to their GP and face that wider stigma from the GP themselves, who would tell them that they just needed to tweak things in their modern life. It just does not work that way. Naming it as a relapsing-remitting condition, putting it up there as the public health challenge it is and focusing in on it in the way that we are so good at doing when we want to in this House is the answer—I completely agree with him.

I was pleased to see the wealth of experience that the Select Committee drew upon, including from organisations such as Diabetes UK and Yorkshire Cancer Research. The report asks for a target to cut obesity. That is welcome, but does my hon. Friend the Chair of the Select Committee agree that we need to have additional sub-targets and metrics to ensure that progress is equal across all our regions, because we know a north-south divide still exists and there are persistent issues when it comes to health inequalities, including obesity?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for his point. He is exactly right that there is a huge disparity. We know that healthy food is too often out of reach for those on the poorest incomes, especially so when it comes to children, and that is not reflected currently. That is what we hope the modern service framework might start from—how we close that patchwork of services across the country and make inequality one of the core missions of this Government through this policy.

I thank the Chair of the Select Committee for her statement. Most of the House will know—I have spoken about this publicly—that I have had a lifelong battle with obesity. It was only when I was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at 33 years old last year that the NHS stepped in to help. Since then, I have lost seven and a half stone through the diabetes path to remission programme. My plea to the Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety, who I know is listening intently, is that those of us with lived experience of obesity and overweight are included in the conversation about how we tackle this, because for too long people who have not experienced it have dictated to those of us who have, about how best to go forward. The path to remission programme for type 2 diabetes is referenced in the report and its conclusions because it is a proven weight loss intervention, but it is currently only available to a small subset of people with type 2 diabetes. Does she agree that this cost-effective and efficient way to help people like me to lose weight should be rolled out to people living with obesity nationally?

I pay enormous tribute to the former member of the Committee. I can entirely understand why he was elevated to other things, but he was very much my right-hand man through the obesity side of this inquiry. I completely agree with him—it was stark. We know what works, and the path for how we do this is clear, but what was missing was a joined-up approach, not just across Departments but within the NHS itself. He is completely right that there are things that work and we know what we need to do, but at the moment we are not seeing that joined-up approach that we need Government to take to achieve it.

Given that child obesity is at record levels, what single intervention does my hon. Friend believe would make the greatest difference to preventing children from developing obesity in the first place?

I am extremely grateful to my hon. Friend for his question. The rising rates of obesity among reception-age children should give us real pause for thought. If we ever wanted proof that obesity is not an individual failing, it is the fact that it seems to be most acute among that population. There is no silver bullet—that is the trap we fall into—despite the lobbying not to do this or that, whether that is about the food industry or advertising. It will never be one thing. It will be a suite of measures that we put around children: stopping fast food joints being on their walk to school; supporting their families with sustained funding, so that they can have healthy food at home; and bans on advertising, which we know works on children, because otherwise, why would the companies do it?

Many moons ago, in 2009, long before I had the pleasure of meeting you, Madam Deputy Speaker, or anybody in this Chamber, I used to be 17 stone. I was a big fat pudding—I am calling myself that. I was eating Chinese food five nights a week with two bottles of Coca-Cola. It was the wrong recipe, with lots of stress. When I became a type 2 diabetic, I realised I had to lose weight. I lost 4 stone, and I have kept it off. I tell that story because sometimes we do not know things are happening until the doctor tells us. I think of the children in school. I am very fortunate to have six grandchildren. The wee ones especially—the six-year-old and the four-year-old—eat their fruit and veg every day, all day, which is really good. My question is, does the hon. Lady agree that if we want to change habits, we must engage and educate our young people about eating fruit and veg, and if they cannot have it at home, they need to have it at school, starting at primary level?

All credit to the hon. Gentleman. As I said, I have faced a similar journey, and it is hard to keep the weight off, because once we have lived with it for a long while, our underlying endocrinology changes. People need to appreciate that if we allow young people to live with obesity, it affects their whole life. With any luck, we can avoid the point where they end up with diabetes, which can be reversible, as we know. He is completely right: this needs to happen in school, but it is not just about school. We need to recognise that when those children are at home, their families need help. We need to drive down the prices of healthy fruit and veg, and that needs a joined-up strategy with the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. That is why we are calling for a cross-Cabinet Committee—because if any one Department tries to do this on its own, it will continue to fail.
I thank the Select Committee Chair for her statement and all Members who shared their stories.

We now come to the Select Committee statement on behalf of the Defence Committee. Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi will speak for up to 10 minutes, during which there will be no interventions, and there will be questions for 10 minutes at the end.

I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting this statement on the Defence Committee’s report, “Defence in the High North”. The High North is a priority theatre for the UK, as well as a particularly challenging and hostile environment in which to operate. Russia is seeking to dominate and exploit the High North, potentially turning the region into a major vulnerability for the UK. The UK is a near neighbour of the High North. Indeed, parts of northern Scotland are closer to the Arctic circle than to the channel, while the strategically important GIUK gap spans Greenland, Iceland and the UK. The region is changing rapidly. As temperatures rise and ice melts, new access routes are opening up, making the High North more congested and contested. Most critically, the High North is home to much of Russia’s strategic nuclear, naval and undersea sabotage capability and provides a base from which Russia can project military power into adjacent regions. That extends to UK territorial waters, where there has been a significant increase in hybrid threats to subsea critical infrastructure. In recent weeks, the Royal Navy has intercepted a Russian intelligence ship off the coast of Scotland. Our report concluded that the UK has glaring capability gaps in the High North that leave us vulnerable. Without intervention, those gaps are set to widen, further weakening the UK along its northern flank. Evidence of low availability among frigates, destroyers and attack submarines raises serious questions about whether the UK can meet its High North commitments before new capabilities enter service. The Ministry of Defence also has a serious gap in its anti-submarine warfare capability measured against its own military requirements. Currently, there are 11 frigates and destroyers in service. That is just over half of the requirement for 19 vessels. Of the required 13 frigates, eight should be fitted with towed array sonar for anti-submarine warfare. At present, this capability is limited to the remaining five Type 23s. That weakens the UK’s ability to respond to Russian submarines and underwater sabotage. It is a worrying picture. The Royal Marines’ Arctic experience is a significant national strength, but it cannot compensate for shortfalls in the naval platforms needed to deploy, protect and sustain operations in the region. The Government are already rightly investing in the hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion, including the £90 million investment announced this week in new drones and sensors to counter undersea threats. We know that the Government are aware of the growing threat in the High North. Our concern is not that nothing is being done, but that the necessary capabilities will not be available fast enough. Given the critical role of anti-submarine operations in the High North, the Committee called on the Government to ensure that no further towed array-equipped Type 23 frigates leave service until they are replaced one for one by the new Type 26 vessels. Addressing our own capability gaps is fundamental, but the UK must also be able to deploy flexibly to the High North, whether acting alone, with partners such as Norway, or through the joint expeditionary force or NATO. That brings me to the joint expeditionary force—the JEF—a UK-led force of 10 like-minded northern European nations. Although the JEF was originally conceived as capable of operating across the full spectrum of conflict, its role has become increasingly focused on countering sub-threshold and hybrid threats, on the assumption that NATO would deter any escalation to warfighting. But with less certainty about the US commitment to collective NATO defence, the JEF’s comparatively limited capabilities could be seen as less of a deterrent. That could leave it exposed if an incident threatens to escalate. We heard from some during our inquiry that the JEF was a “jack of all trades” and therefore master of no military tasks. The Government should therefore reassess the JEF’s c

I congratulate the Committee and its Chairman on the production of such an important report. One section that most struck me was that beginning at paragraph 84 on submarine under-ice capability. I was surprised to learn that Astute-class submarines do not have the capability that their predecessors, the Trafalgar-class submarines, used to have. Can the hon. Gentleman tell us a little more about when that capability might be acquired, and can he throw any light on the fact that, as has become painfully clear over recent weeks and months, the existing Astute-class submarines, some of them very new, are not at sea? Is that a manning problem, is it a technical problem, or is it both?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman, a former Chair of the Defence and Intelligence and Security Committees, for his perceptive and incisive remarks. Under-ice capability is key for the UK to effectively deter and defend in the High North. Unfortunately, we have allowed our under-ice capabilities to lapse precisely at the time when they are most needed. That is why a previous Defence Committee report advocated for the hardening of hulls. This report recommends that we rapidly re-establish those under-ice capabilities, because if we do not, Russia will not be deterred from its activities. In fact, it will be further emboldened, because we will not be able to protect those transatlantic supply routes.

I thank the Committee Chair for presenting this report on the High North to the Chamber. Does he agree that it underscores how acutely important our submarine programme is, and the value of what we do in Barrow-in-Furness? Does he also agree that we need a massive increase in funding to help deliver those changes rapidly?

I thank my hon. Friend, a fellow member of the Defence Committee, for her strong and positive contributions to this report, and her other work. Indeed, it was a pleasure to visit Barrow-in-Furness and to see some of those submarine capabilities. She is right: as a nation, we need to invest at pace because of the lack of availability of those submarines, and that is portrayed strongly in our report.

I thank the Chair of the Defence Committee for his remarks, and I very much enjoyed going with him on our various visits to make this report. Did he feel, as I did, slightly awkward when we were visiting the Nordic states? We know what we are spending on defence. We know that Norway is spending 3.35% of GDP, Denmark 3.5%, Sweden 2.8% and reaching 3.5% by 2028, and Finland 2.85% and reaching 3.3% by 2032, yet we have not yet committed to the Committee’s preferred 3% by the end of this Parliament. That created a certain unease. Does the hon. Gentleman remember that when we visited Norway, we were told by its Chief of Defence that every time the Prime Minister of Norway makes a speech, he mentions the threat from Russia? Does he agree that we must advance the so-called national conversation if we are to take the British public with us, and explain the threat to them, as well as the capability and investment that we need to counter it?

I thank the hon. Gentleman, a fellow member of the Defence Committee. I very much enjoyed going with him on various visits to increase our knowledge and understanding of what is happening out there, and to get that perspective from our allies. He rightly highlights the significant increases in defence spending among our European allies, which is why some of us have been vocal in our advocacy for the position that the UK must not be left behind, and that we need to reach defence spending of 3% of GDP by the end of this Parliament. Indeed, as Committee members will be more than aware, we made a joint statement to ensure that the Government focus their attention on that issue. I could not agree more with the hon. Gentleman.

I thank the Chair of the Committee for his magnificent statement. As the Arctic becomes increasingly contested, with growing Russian and Chinese activity, does he believe that the UK armed forces are adequately equipped, trained and prepared to operate effectively in extreme Arctic conditions, or are there significant gaps in capability and readiness?

I congratulate the hon. Gentleman, a fellow member of the Defence Committee, on his recent elevation to Lib Dem defence spokesperson for veterans and people. No doubt he will give our former Committee member, now the Minister for Veterans and People, good scrutiny in the future. The hon. Gentleman rightly highlights that there are significant capability gaps, and those need to be addressed. As I said earlier, while we can be proud of the expertise and capabilities of the Royal Marines, those are no substitute for naval vessels or for having the platforms through which they can project that expertise.

Unlike the Secretary of State for Defence, Conservative Members listen to the Chair of the Defence Committee, and indeed to his colleagues who have produced an excellent report, “Defence in the High North”. As I must be brief, I wish to ask about the report’s warnings about the lack of operationally available assets in the Royal Navy, both surface escorts and attack submarines. As the report states on page 29: “According to several media sources, all five Astute Class nuclear attack submarines have recently all been tied up in dockyards at the same time, with none deployed.” That point has been mentioned by several Members this afternoon. The Astute class was once described to me by a naval officer as being like a Formula 1 racing car—great on the track, but a bitch when it gets into the pits. The hon. Gentleman mentioned serious capability gaps, so when does he think Ministers will finally come clean about why all five of our nuclear attack submarines have been tied up for months?

I thank the shadow Minister for his kind words about the work of the Committee. Capability gaps, particularly with regard to submarines, were mentioned by the Committee at length, and my hon. Friend the Member for Barrow and Furness (Michelle Scrogham) was also forthright in making that point. The capability gaps in the delivery of future subs must be addressed urgently. For example, we received evidence suggesting that the production of certain assets was advancing at a “leisurely” pace. That needs to be addressed. Ultimately, as the Committee’s report on AUKUS highlighted, the next-generation SSN-AUKUS is incredibly important and we must ensure that we are investing at pace so that our Australian friends also have that capability at pace. For much of the time at present, we are left in a situation where many of our assets, including submarines, are in either maintenance or deep maintenance.

I commend the Chair of the Defence Committee and his colleagues for a tremendous report. As he rightly mentioned, Scotland is effectively on the frontline of the new potential battleground of the High North. Will the Chair be circling back to the report to see whether there has been progress? Scotland is critical to closing the frigate gap; BAE Systems on the Clyde and Babcock in Rosyth on the east coast are building warships even as we speak. I am concerned by recent comments made by Scotland’s First Minister, John Swinney, who claimed that Britain is in some way abandoning Scotland to the Russian threat, when in fact one of the real threats to national security in this country is the Scottish National party’s separatist agenda: it is not sure whether it wants to be in NATO or out of NATO, and it wants the nuclear submarines out of Faslane. It is a strange picture, so I wonder whether the hon. Gentleman might go back to that?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his incisive comments. He will be pleased to note that Scotland had several mentions in our report, as well as in the wall-to-wall coverage that the hard-hitting report attracted. There was much mention of the need to strengthen our capabilities in Scotland. Obviously, the Scottish Government need to make sure that they are aligned with some of the investments that are being made by the UK Government. That is really important, because during our visits to Scotland we saw that many of those working in the industry, as well as those serving, are very much looking to the UK Government and the Scottish Government to work in partnership. The hon. Gentleman mentioned NATO. Let nobody be in any doubt that NATO is a cornerstone of British defence. I therefore fully concur with his views on that question.

I thank the Chair of the Defence Committee and the Committee for all they have done. The Chair outlined the training that the Royal Marines receive to carry out their duties in the High North. If there is a war—we hope there will not be—the Royal Marines will not fight that war on their own, because the Royal Irish Regiment, along with all the other regiments in the British Army, will fight alongside them. What has been done to ensure that the Royal Irish Regiment and other regiments have the same training as the Royal Marines in the High North?

Thank you for that steer, Madam Deputy Speaker. I thank the hon. Gentleman, who is ever present in the Chamber, for his question. The Committee did not look into the capabilities offered by the Royal Irish Regiment, but it is true that it needs to be strengthening their capabilities and training because Britain can only succeed if all regiments are fighting together, just as we can only succeed more widely if we are fighting alongside our NATO allies. We need to deter the threat before there is any conflict or crisis.
I thank the Chair of the Defence Committee for his statement and his excellent timekeeping.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. May I ask your advice on whether Mr Speaker has received any notification that the Prime Minister intends to correct the record following his response to my question at yesterday’s Prime Minister’s Question Time? He said: “on the very day that the National Wealth Fund has committed £1 billion of funding to support offshore wind off the east coast of Scotland”, —[ Official Report , 11 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 172.] when no such UK Government investment in Scotland had been announced or committed.

I thank the hon. Member for his point of order and for having given notice of it. He will be aware that ministerial answers, including the Prime Minister’s, are not a matter for the Chair, but I am sure that Members on the Treasury Bench have heard his comments and that if an error has been made in this instance, the Government will seek to correct it as soon as possible.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. We have just had a very important statement on an extremely good Defence Committee report. As you have a perfect view of the Chamber from the Chair, could you confirm for the record that throughout the proceeding no Reform Member of Parliament was present?

The right hon. Member will know that that is not a matter for the Chair. He has put his point on the record. Bill Presented Residential Use Class (Planning Permission) Bill Presentation and First Reading (Standing Order No. 57) Ben Maguire presented a Bill to introduce a requirement for a grant of planning permission to change a primary residential home to a short-term let or secondary residential home in England; and for connected purposes. Bill read the First time; to be read a Second time on Friday 26 February 2027, and to be printed (Bill 181).

I beg to move, That this House has considered the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme. It is a great privilege to open this debate as we mark the 110th anniversary of one of the most defining battles of the first world war. For 141 days, between 1 July and 18 November 1916, British, Commonwealth and French forces fought along the River Somme in northern France. Around 3.5 million men took part. By the time the fighting ended, well over 1 million men on all sides had been killed, wounded, captured or were missing. Those numbers are almost impossible to comprehend. Perhaps the figure that remains most deeply embedded in our national consciousness is that of the first day. At 7.30 on the morning of 1 July 1916, whistles sounded and tens of thousands of British soldiers climbed from their trenches and advanced towards the German lines. By the end of that day, the British Army had suffered 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 men killed. It remains the bloodiest day in the history of the British Army. Yet even those extraordinary figures can distance us from what actually happened. Statistics convey the scale, but do not tell the stories: every single one of those 19,240 fatalities is a unique story—each a family tragedy; an empty chair at a table; potential left forever unfulfilled. Madam Deputy Speaker, you may have seen some of those stories projected on to the face of the Elizabeth Tower on Sunday to mark Remembrance Day. I thank the Speaker and his office for their work with the Commonwealth War Graves Commission in making that wonderful spectacle happen. The battle of the Somme did not begin as the predominantly British offensive that it became. In December 1915, the allies had agreed a strategy of co-ordinated offensives against the central powers. Britain and France would attack on the western front, while their allies attacked elsewhere, making it more difficult for Germany and Austria-Hungary to move forces between theatres. Then, in February 1916, Germany attacked Verdun. The enormous demands of that battle meant that the French contribution planned for the Somme was dramatically reduced, while the British commitment increased. By the end of May, one of the principal purposes of the Somme offensive had become relieving the immense pressure on the French at Verdun. The British Army that prepared for the attack was very different from the small professional force that had gone to France in 1914. It had expanded rapidly following Lord Kitchener’s call for volunteers, and many of the men preparing to fight had relatively little experience of battle. For seven days before the attack, allied artillery pounded the German positions. More than 1.5 million shells were fired. It was hoped that the bombardment would destroy the German defences and cut the thick belts of barbed wire protecting their positions, but in many places those defences survived. German troops had deep dugouts in which to shelter, and when the bombardment lifted, they emerged to meet the attacking infantry. So began those 141 days of fighting. Names that had once meant very little to people in Britain, and what would become the wider Commonwealth, became part of national memory: Beaumont-Hamel, Mametz, Delville Wood, Pozières, Guillemont, Longueval, Courcelette and Thiepval. Today, anybody who visits the Somme discovers that those places are not simply names in a history book. The battlefield is marked by cemeteries and memorials, many standing on or close to the ground over which those men fought and died. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission commemorates 1.7 million casualties of the two world wars in more than 150 countries. Of those, 140,000 died in France during those bloody months of the battle of the Somme. Around 61,700 have an identified grave, while approximately 78,950 are commemorated by name on memorials to the missing. Commonwealth casualties from the battle lie in more than 400 cemeteries across the region. I should declare an interest

The hon. Lady is making a powerful and moving speech. I can remember being a child at high school and going on a trip to world war one battlefields. My little sister, who is 15, has never had that opportunity. Does the hon. Lady agree that we should do more to ensure that the memory lives on, by making sure that our children, grandchildren and future generations get the same opportunities to understand what happened at the Somme and throughout the world war?

I agree with the hon. Gentleman 100%. I did not get to visit a cemetery site when I was young either, so I appreciate the situation his sister is in, but I got to when I was working for the commission. I pay tribute to my former colleagues, the public engagement co-ordinators at the commission, who go out to schools right across the country to ensure that the next generation can understand and hear some of these stories.

Before my hon. Friend concludes her powerful speech, may I, from the Dispatch Box, commend the work that she has done for the Commonwealth War Graves Commission? She mentioned those who served from around the world at the Somme. Will she also pay tribute to the 36th Ulster Division, who broke through five rounds of trenches and managed to storm the Schwaben redoubt, in the course of which, on one morning, they earned five Victoria Crosses?

I thank my right hon. Friend for that story; five Victoria Crosses is, of course, some contribution to the war. The Irish Regiment played a huge role, and I have seen some of the graves of the Inniskilling Regiment in Northern Ireland—once you have worked for the commission, you find yourself visiting cemeteries and graves on every trip abroad. I wholeheartedly agree with him.

The hon. Lady is making a powerful speech. This week, I had the honour and privilege of laying a wreath at the Poppies to Paddington remembrance service, which commemorated the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme. Does she agree that Great Western Railway should be congratulated for holding that service and for giving a prominent role to the 1914 Sikhs and the King’s Gurkha Artillery unit, commemorating the incredible contributions of those from around the world to the war effort?

I absolutely agree. I use the GWR train line. I usually put a wreath on the train from Ivybridge—a place I have mentioned several times—but I am grateful to my friends at the Royal British Legion in Ivybridge, who this time laid a wreath while I was here in Westminster. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission works very hard to recognise the role of Sikhs. They have their own headstones to ensure that that is visible to the public. I hope that today’s debate will play a small part in our remembering those words: the Somme. I also hope that it will remind Members of the vital work of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission in caring for the graves, cemeteries and memorials of those who died, and ensuring that their stories continue to be told. The commission maintains a stories portal, called For Evermore, which will allow Members to upload their own stories of family members, constituents or others who fell. I urge Members to do so, and to add to the 13,000 stories already told there. I look forward to hearing the contributions of Members from across the House.
Order. I regret that there will be an immediate five-minute time limit.

I commend the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for keeping alive the memory of those brave souls to whom we owe so much. There are moments in history when forgetting becomes an injustice, when silence becomes a betrayal, and when remembrance becomes not only a simple act of respect, but a duty. The battle of the Somme is such a moment. As has already been mentioned, on 1 July, after just one day, 19,240 British soldiers lay dead. The battle continued for another 141 days, until 18 November 1916, when more than a million men across all sides had died. Today, I want to speak about men whose extraordinary contributions have often been overlooked; those Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs who fought under the British flag and endured the same horrors and shed the same blood. Their sacrifice was no less, their courage was immense, and their place in British history must be permanent. One extraordinary example of their courage came on 14 July 1916 at High Wood, during the battle of the Somme. Across the open fields of northern France, the British 7th Dragoon Guards advanced alongside the 20th Deccan Horse of the British Indian army, which was basically full of Sikh cavalrymen. Picture the scene: German machine guns concealed in trenches and standing crops, artillery exploding all around, and Sikh soldiers thousands of miles from the Punjab charging forward on horseback, armed with just their swords, into the face of modern machine guns. Above them, a Royal Flying Corps aircraft helped to identify concealed German positions, assisting the cavalry as they advanced. The horsemen reached enemy positions and captured prisoners but suffered terrible casualties, and the ground could not be held indefinitely. Many fell, horses fell, and families thousands of miles away would never see their loved ones again. Those Sikh cavalrymen demonstrated extraordinary courage in one of the most remarkable mounted actions of the Somme offensive, yet how many British schoolchildren know their story? I was once one of those children, and I was never taught it. How many know that Sikh soldiers charged across the killing fields? How many know that Hindu and Muslim soldiers also fought and died for Britain, and not only at the Somme, but across the wider world war? How many know that the history of Britain’s Asian communities did not begin with immigration after 1945, but began long before? That history was written in the trenches of Flanders and on the banks of the River Somme. It was written in the blood of men who travelled halfway around the world. A Sikh mother’s grief was no different from a British mother’s grief. A Hindu father’s sorrow was no different from a Muslim father’s sorrow. The blood of an Indian soldier was no less precious than the blood of any other man who fell. However, their recognition has not always been equal. Indeed, investigations by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission have acknowledged historical inequalities in the commemoration of predominantly non-European servicemen. We must not just confront that, but rectify it, because remembrance cannot be selective. We cannot celebrate the achievements of the British empire while forgetting the people of that empire who made those achievements possible. This is not simply Sikh, Hindu or Muslim history; it is British history, and it belongs to every one of us. That is why the contribution of Indian soldiers must be properly recognised in our schools, our museums, our memorials and our national commemorations—not as a footnote, or a token gesture, but as an inseparable part of our shared national story. Some 110 years later, the fields of the Somme are peaceful. The crops grow where soldiers once fell, and the birds sing where artillery once thundered. The silence of those fields must never become the silence of our history. We owe those men more than a wreath once a year; we owe them the truth, we owe them recognition and we owe them a permanent place in British national memory.

It is my solemn duty to break to right hon. and hon. Members that “Blackadder Goes Forth” is not a documentary. As we recall the charnel house that was the first day of the Somme, we must consider the reality and not the fiction that today surrounds the generation who suffered and sacrificed so much in the great war. To truly understand what our forefathers went through, we should look to great works such as “Tommy: The British Soldier on the Western Front” by the late Professor Richard Holmes. I was lucky enough to meet the professor, famous for his “War Walks” television series, during my own minor attempts to study military history. He told me that the two biggest barriers to earnest study of the first world war were the war poets—although he conceded that their testimony was valid, since they served—and “Blackadder Goes Forth”. Those final frames of “Blackadder” captured the awful reality of death on an industrial scale—but showing every private soldier to be an economic conscript, every officer a public school toff and every general ensconced in a chateau far behind the lines? It simply was not like that. Take every public schoolboy and there still would not be enough numbers to officer the giant British Army on the western front alone. While “‘Forward!’ he cried from the rear And the front rank died” is a lovely line from Pink Floyd, the “lions led by donkeys” narrative, which is set in stone today, is really a canard from the 1970s. The creeping barrage on the first day of the Somme campaign, with the shells falling just ahead of our advancing infantry, was a failure. There is no disguising it, but it was a genuine attempt to change the tactics of a war of attrition and to give advancing infantrymen the edge in an era where technology had outpaced tactics. Our troops moved more slowly than expected, and co-ordination with the artillery in the infancy of battlefield radio communications was difficult. As we have heard, the shells failed to cut the wire in front of the German trenches, whose deep dugouts proved devastatingly effective. General Douglas Haig would carry the can for the failure of the Somme to deliver the hoped-for decisive breakthrough, yet “the Chief”, as he was known, remained popular with his men. The reality is that the British were hard-pressed for experienced troops and matériel. Haig’s strained relationships with David Lloyd George meant that his reputation was tarnished, perhaps deliberately, as Lloyd George sought to insulate himself from blame for the Somme’s failure and the awful toll of dead and wounded. The two men observed an uneasy truce in the immediate aftermath of the armistice, and it was only after Haig’s death that Lloyd George launched his political assassination in his multi-volume war memoirs. He accused Haig of a lack of vision and flexibility, and blamed him for the “ghastly slaughter”. It was odd, though, that the Welsh wizard kept his counsel and did not depose Haig at the material time as the war raged. None of that takes away from the huge sacrifice of British and empire troops throughout a war that spanned the globe. Perhaps the saddest aspect is that today we seem unable to answer the question of what it was all for. Ask the French. Ask the Belgians. They were invaded, and there is no whitewashing the atrocities committed against civilians by the Germans in 1914. The great war was then a war of liberation. I leave the final word not to British generals, but to one American and one Prussian. William Sherman’s march to the sea in the American civil war saw him unleash total war on civilians. He said, “War is all hell, boys”, and, “you cannot refine it.” That is a truism echoing through human history, but what of the hellish Somme? General Erich Ludendorff, whose doctrine of an elastic, flexible defence cost us so very dear, said in his autobiography, “My War Memories”: “As a result, we were completely exhausted on the Western Front”. We paid a high price in blood and treasure,

I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for bringing this debate to mark the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme coming to an end. That is 110 years since young men from Ipswich, Suffolk and communities across Britain bravely went into battle, facing extraordinary danger in the service of their country, but many never came home. More than a century has passed, but the sacrifice that they made and the loss suffered by their families must never be forgotten. For many men, the Somme would be their final battle. Back home in Ipswich and Suffolk, families waited for their fathers, sons, brothers and husbands to come home; instead, they were left with the devastating news of their deaths and the knowledge that the lives they had imagined for them and with them would never be lived. They were soldiers who answered their country’s call with extraordinary courage, but they were also young men with hopes, ambitions and their whole lives ahead of them. For so many, their lives were cut tragically short on the fields of Europe. For the families left behind in Ipswich, the war did not end when the guns fell silent; it ended with a telegram through the door, an empty chair at the dinner table or a photograph of a loved one who would never come home. More than 100 men from Ipswich lost their lives during the Somme offensive—more than 100 families in our town were left to live with a grief that no passage of time could ever fully erase—and I want to put some of their names on the record today. Private Harold Bailey was just 19 years old when he was killed—an age at which so many young people begin their adult lives, make plans and dream of their futures. Private William Attewell was 21. Private Vivian Bradley was 19. Private Walter Fiddaman was also 19. Those young men served in the Suffolk Regiment and came from our town and our county. They grew up on our streets and belonged to our communities, but they never came home. On 3 January 1916, the 7th Battalion, Suffolk Regiment took part in a devastating attack on Ovillers. The battalion suffered 470 casualties, including all its company commanders. Among the Ipswich men lost were Benjamin Baker and Arthur Holmes. Just 12 days later, on 15 July 1916, the 4th Battalion suffered more than 200 casualties during the fighting around Bazentin Ridge and High Wood. Seventeen Ipswich men lost their lives that day. Among them were Samuel Jennings, aged 19, and Robert Lloyd, aged just 18—a young man who had a whole life ahead of him. More than 1 million men were killed over the four-month period that the fighting raged, but every single one of those deaths was a life extinguished and a family devastated. This week, I joined hundreds of people in Ipswich to pay tribute at Christchurch Park and the fields of honour in Ipswich Old Cemetery. As the “Last Post” sounded and our town fell silent, I thought about the young men from Ipswich who had been killed on the battlefield. Ipswich and Suffolk have a proud and enduring history of service to our country, from the Suffolk Regiment on the Somme to the radar pioneers at Bawdsey. Our town and our county have given so much to the defence of our nation, but remembrance is not simply about pride and honour, as crucial as they are; it is about grief. It is about recognising the terrible human cost of war and understanding that the freedoms we enjoy today were secured by people who paid such a heavy price that we can scarcely comprehend. They gave their tomorrow for our today, and we will remember them.

Over a century after the appalling losses on the western front, historians still debate whether any alternatives existed. Some blame political intrigue and poor generalship; others emphasise technology, with the battlefield dominated by interlocking fields of fire, which ensured that slowly advancing troops would be mown down by machine guns before making any worthwhile inroads into the enemy’s trenches. Minor advances that were occasionally achieved were usually reversed by counter-attacks or simply absorbed into a new, static confrontation a short distance from the original one. We heard echoes of some of those controversies, with the pendulum ascribing guilt and responsibility swinging first one way, then another, in the very perceptive speech of my hon. Friend the Member for Dumfries and Galloway (John Cooper). I was first influenced by a work of fiction—a rather more in-depth work of fiction than the immensely entertaining television series to which he alluded. It was a book by a Sheffield journalist and writer called John Harris, entitled “Covenant with Death” and published in 1961. In 1961, the people who had fought on the Somme were still living, and John Harris interviewed many of them. He says in the introduction to his great novel that although the characters are fictitious, the real people will recognise many of the incidents that he describes. The story is based on the Sheffield City Battalion. On 1 July 1916, the battalion sent 700 men over the top. The majority of them—nearly 500 men—became casualties, half of whom were killed, and only four of their officers survived the battle.

My right hon. Friend is giving an incredibly powerful speech. He is recognising quite properly those who were in teeth arms and running towards the ballistics and bullets coming at them, but will he also recognise the military medics? They were so important and often ran into danger, and they included Captain Noel Chavasse, who won not only the Military Cross and bar but the Victoria Cross in the Somme.

Yes, indeed. I believe I am right in thinking that he won the VC twice overall—one of three people to do so—and I am delighted that my hon. and gallant Friend has put that on the record. In more recent years, there has been a swing of the pendulum that has tried to justify the scale of loss on the Somme by saying that it was necessary for lessons to be learned for the ultimately successful campaigns of 1918. Some of the people who have put forward that proposition undoubtedly know more about the history of the first world war and its battles than I do, but I simply do not buy that. You should not have to waste the lives of tens of thousands of soldiers to learn lessons, some of which ought to have been obvious from the beginning. One of those lessons was the need for surprise. Before 1 July 1916, there was a seven-day bombardment by British artillery on the Somme. Everybody knew what was going to happen and where it was going to happen. In 1918, at the start of the successful 100 days offensive—the phenomenal, brilliantly fought campaign that led to Germany suing for armistice in November 1918—everybody had secrecy impressed on them. Every officer and man had a passbook in which it was deemed essential that they must not say anything about what preparations were being made. Similarly, when the Germans mounted their spring offensive in March 1918—which, for a while, looked as if it could have put Britain out of the war—one of the reasons it succeeded was that they too had an element of surprise. They had three alternative plans and decided on one of them, the Operation Michael attack, very much at the last minute before it was launched. You did not have to be a strategic genius to know that you needed an element of surprise in order to achieve tactical success. Similarly, the lessons of the Somme were not learned very quickly, because the same thing happened again in April 1918 with the second battle of Arras and, later in the year, with the third battle of Ypres, known as Passchendaele. Let me conclude by quoting someone who was not an amateur historian: a man called Sholto Douglas, who later became Marshal of the Royal Air Force. He stated that, as he looked down from his aircraft at the field of Passchendaele in 1917, his mind was full of the sort of questions that many people have asked about the futility of the tactics. He said then, and I agree with him now, that those questions are very, very difficult to answer.

I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith), both for securing this debate and for the way in which she introduced it. In Edinburgh South West, we have the Heart of Midlothian memorial clock, something that defines Haymarket. If Members do not know, Heart of Midlothian is perhaps Scotland’s finest football team—or even the UK’s. [ Laughter. ] Sorry, I should not have laughed there. Every year, former Hearts players gather at the memorial clock alongside club staff, fans from across the city and local Gorgie residents to remember the incredible sacrifice that Hearts players and fans made on the frontline. For those who are not familiar with the story, Hearts players led by example when Sir George McCrae, a popular Edinburgh figure and former MP—he was in this place between 1899 and 1909—announced that he would raise a battalion to fight in the war, the 16th (Service) Battalion of the Royal Scots. In November 1914, Hearts comfortably led the first division, having started the 1914-15 season with eight straight victories, including a thumping defeat of the reigning champions Celtic—even in a time-limited debate, I had to mention that. That streak coincided with the beginning of world war one and a debate about whether or not football should be taking place at all.
