Sixteen Hearts players signed up, along with players from Hibernian, Raith Rovers, Falkirk, Dunfermline Athletic, East Fife and St Bernard’s. McCrae’s was the first of the so-called footballers’ pals battalions to be raised during the war. Some 500 Hearts supporters and ticket holders enlisted, alongside 150 from Hibs, rugby players, cricketers, swimmers, hockey players, golfers and even a bodybuilder. Then came the Somme. None could have expected that McCrae’s battalion would suffer 229 dead or missing on the first day, with a further 347 wounded. That was a small part of the tens of thousands who were killed or wounded on that first day, but the toll on Hearts and the wider Edinburgh community was immense. Many bodies were never recovered, including the remains of Harry Wattie, a Hearts striker and arguably the best inside forward in Scotland at the time.

The hon. Member is making a very eloquent speech about the sacrifice of Scottish football. Did he share my disappointment at the weekend when the two-minute silence at Celtic was interrupted after only 13 seconds?

I thank the hon. Member for that intervention. I heard that news from someone in this place who had also heard about it—somebody who does not live in Scotland—and I was absolutely ashamed to hear it. The 16th Royal Scots made great inroads into the German line, more than any other British battalion, but that was little comfort to the families who lost their sons. The losses of McCrae’s battalion were a small but significant component of the 1 million casualties in the 141 days of that battle. When Hearts unveiled the memorial clock at Haymarket in 1922, a crowd of 65,000 people gathered to honour that remarkable sacrifice. They were told that the nation owed a debt of gratitude to Hearts that could never be repaid. At the weekend, I was proud to attend a service at the memorial clock alongside hundreds of other people. Many of them were Hearts supporters—Jambos—but many of them were people who just live locally and wanted to take part in an act of remembrance. I was proud to be at that remembrance service, but I was even more proud to see pupils from Tynecastle high school, Balerno high school and George Watson’s college take part in it. A few days before, I attended another remembrance service at Firrhill high school in Edinburgh South West, which was entirely led by the young people there, apart from a small introduction by the headmaster. What is special about that school is that it is directly across the road from Redford infantry barracks. The young people who led the service read out the names of people who had died on that day, 6 November, during the first world war. All the names were of people who were 17, 18 or 19 years old, some of them perhaps even younger than the pupils who were reading out the names, and most of them just a few months or years older. Taking part in that service and being so close to the barracks was a real reminder of the impact of war. We talk about conflict, perhaps within 1,000 days, but I would hate for any of those young people to have to take part in a war. It was a reminder to me that in this place, we should always focus on peace, not war.

It is a privilege to rise in this House today to speak on behalf of the good, decent, salt-of-the-earth people of my constituency of Strangford, and indeed for the loyal people right across Northern Ireland. When we look at the history of our Province, there is a golden thread of loyalty, duty and unyielding resolve that runs from the fields of France in 1916 right through to the present day. Over a century ago, when King and country called, the men of Ulster did not hesitate. They stepped forward in their thousands—from the shipyards of Belfast, the farms of the Ards peninsula and the towns and villages across Ulster—and on 1 July 1916, at the battle of the Somme, the 36th (Ulster) Division paid the ultimate price. They charged into the teeth of the German guns at Thiepval wood and the Schwaben redoubt. Over 5,000 men were killed, wounded or missing in the first 48 hours alone. They shed their blood so that tyranny would not prevail, and so that this United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland might remain free. To truly understand the soul of Ulster, one does not need to read a history book; one only needs to walk through the towns and villages of the constituency of Strangford and look at the names carved into the stones of the war memorials. Every name tells a story of a young life laid down on the altar of freedom. Picture, as other Members have done, 1 July 1916 in the damp, chalky trenches of Thiepval wood. Imagine a young lad from Newtownards—let us call him Lance Corporal David John Thompson.

The hon. Gentleman is giving a typically impassioned speech. Will he join me in reflecting on not just the service of those who fought in the Somme, but their families left at home, who were thinking of them at those most difficult of times?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for giving me that chance to gain some composure. Picture Lance Corporal David John Thompson, serving proudly with the 13th Battalion, Royal Irish Rifles—the County Down volunteers. As the clock ticks towards half-past 7 in the morning and the deafening roar of the British artillery barrage shakes the very earth beneath their feet, young David’s mind is not in France; his heart is back home in County Down. He can almost smell the air drifting off Strangford lough—there is nothing quite like a breath of air from Strangford lough. He remembers the quiet mornings walking past Scrabo tower, which stands sentinel over the town; the warmth of his mother’s kitchen; and the familiar faces in Conway Square in Newtownards. He longs for the peace of home, for his Sunday morning service at First Ards Presbyterian church, and for the simple, honest life he left behind when he answered his King’s call. Yet, as he looks down the trenches at the pale, mud-streaked faces of the young men under his command—fellas he grew up with in Newtownards, Comber and Donaghadee —fear gives way to duty. He knows that the whistle is about to blow. He knows that climbing over the parapet means walking into a storm of German machine gun fire. He has no desire to die in a foreign land, yet he is entirely prepared to do so. Why? Because Lance Corporal David John Thompson understands that the freedom of his family back in Newtownards, the preservation of the British way of life and the defeat of tyranny are worth a great price. He is willing, along with others, to pay that price for that which he honours more than his own life. So, when that shrill whistle blows, 19-year-old Lance Corporal Thompson does not hesitate. With his Lee-Enfield rifle gripped tight, standing beside his brothers in arms with Orange sashes beneath many of their tunics, he climbs into no man’s land, shouting over the din to rally his boys forward. He leads them across the cratered earth towards the Schwaben redoubt, not out of hatred for the men in front of him but out of an unshakeable love for the home and the country he has left behind. He pays the ultimate price at 19 years of age. That is the calibre of the men of Ulster: young men who loved their homes fiercely, yet loved their duty and their freedom even more. Captain Wilfrid Spender said: “I am not an Ulsterman, but yesterday, the 1st July, as I followed their amazing attack, I felt that I would rather be an Ulsterman than anything else in the world. My pen cannot describe adequately the hundreds of heroic acts I witnessed. The Ulster Volunteer Force, from which the Division was made, has won a name that equals any in history. Their devotion deserves the gratitude of the British empire.” What lovely words from a man who witnessed that attack of the 36th (Ulster) Division. The blood of those who fell at the Somme runs through the very veins of the people I represent. We carry their legacy with pride and their resolve in our hearts. Come what may, the people of Ulster will continue to stand unbowed and unbroken for freedom, for the rule of law, for our Christian faith and for God, and for this precious United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. For us, “We will remember them,” is not just a phrase; it is always our promise.

It is a real honour to follow the moving speech of the hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon). It is a privilege to speak in the debate marking the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme. As is the case for many hon. Members in the Chamber, the impacts of the first world war are still felt in my constituency generations later. It is with a sense of sorrow and pride that we see family members’ names on those war memorials. We promise to remember them and their sacrifice and never to allow such a tragedy to happen again. The scale of the lives lost at the Somme is larger than most of us can comprehend. We commend the strength and bravery of those who sacrificed their futures to protect our country and honour them by marking the anniversary of this battle. For my constituency, this anniversary has a special significance, because the town of Ulverston is twinned with Albert, a town at the heart of the Somme in France. The relationship between the two towns stretches back decades and has been built on friendship, exchange and a shared commitment to remembering those affected by the war. Every year, people from Ulverston travel to Albert, and residents of Albert often visit Ulverston, not simply to commemorate but to strengthen the ties between our two communities. What began with remembrance has grown into genuine friendship. One of the most remarkable links between our towns was the discovery of the Ulverston trench near Albert. During research into the battlefields, an historical trench map was found showing a trench bearing the name of Ulverston. A memorial now stands there, serving as a lasting reminder of the connection between our community and the Somme. I am immensely proud that that site, once associated with conflict, has become somewhere people can come together in remembrance. More than a century on, British, German and French people come together as friends, determined to ensure that the sacrifices of the past are not forgotten. The twinning of Ulverston and Albert shows how remembrance can bring people together and how communities can build lasting bonds, even from the darkest chapters of our shared history. I will take the opportunity to commend our brave service personnel currently deployed around the world. We are grateful for the service and sacrifice that they and their families make on behalf of this country. The Government recognise that our duty to those who serve does not end when they leave the armed forces. That is why we are working to strengthen support for our veterans through better access to housing, healthcare, employment and welfare services. I particularly welcome the roll-out of the Valour programme in Cumbria, which will help create a more joined-up and accessible network of support for veterans and their families. My fellow Cumbrian Labour MPs and I have been campaigning for stronger, locally delivered veterans’ services, so it is encouraging to see the commitment backed with investment and action. Programmes such as Valour recognise that many veterans face challenges long after their service has ended and that support should be easy to access. As we remember those who served at the Somme and in conflicts throughout our history, it is right that we also reaffirm our commitment to the men and women who serve today and to the veterans who continue to make such a valuable contribution to communities across our country. I want to commend my former school, Ulverston Victoria high school, which has done incredible work over the years not only by commemorating the war through remembrance services, but by bringing together the lives of all those we lost in Ulverston—all those young boys and men who went to war—and looking at their backgrounds, their histories and where they worked before they joined the Army. Just for one moment, over the couple of weeks before Remembrance Day, it brings the lives of those young men back together in a way that the students at the school can understand. I pass on
Order. Unfortunately, we have to go down to a four-minute time limit.

I pay tribute to the hundreds of thousands of soldiers who lost their lives during the battle of the Somme, one of the deadliest battles ever fought. I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for her opening remarks, and the Members who have spoken before me. On Sunday I attended the service of remembrance and reconciliation at Christ church in Coalville. The most poignant part was when I heard the roll call of the people from the community who paid the ultimate price. It was moving to see the Elizabeth Tower lit up over the weekend to commemorate the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme, and to share five personal stories from across the country. Thanks must go to Mr Speaker, alongside the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, which organised it. Mr Speaker said: “Seeing the faces of these brave people from the Somme on the most iconic landmarks in the country is incredibly moving—faces of ordinary folk who had a future, only for it to be cut short by war.” One of those folk was Esmée—Barbara Esmée St John— who was from my constituency. Esmée was born in Ashby and volunteered with the Red Cross during the first world war, serving in the No. 26 General Hospital at Etaples, on the French channel coast, which made up the largest centre for medical care of British and Commonwealth service personnel on the western front. Following the opening of the battle of the Somme, Esmée managed a 35-bed surgical ward, working 13-hour days with only a young orderly, just 17 years old, to assist her. Only a few months later, Esmée tragically caught scarlet fever and died from complications. She was buried with full military honours at the Wimereux communal cemetery. Sadly, the infectious nature of her illness meant that her burial could not be delayed for her family to attend, as was the case for so many. In 1918, Esmée’s father supplied her photograph to the Imperial War Museum, expressing pride that she would be among the brave women and hard workers who will never be forgotten. Esmée’s story is just one of the many examples of the brave women who worked tirelessly and courageously to help soldiers on the frontline, and I am pleased that her vital contribution was recognised. As North West Leicestershire is home to a rich mining heritage, I also want to talk about the role that miners played in the battle. I read a 2016 article from Mining Magazine about tunnelling companies, which were specialist units in the British Army that were formed to dig under enemy lines. Among them were the “Famous Fifty”—specially selected volunteers from the Coalville area of Leicestershire who went to fight on the western front in 1914. They marched from St John the Baptist church in Hugglescote to the train station in Coalville, with thousands of people cheering them on. Because of their mining background, many of the men became tunnellers, but only 22 of them ever returned. Miners had a particularly useful skillset in the battle of the Somme, because the harder chalk formations under the ground were more suited to their expertise. The volunteers were exceptionally brave and typically worked in spaces that were about 60 cm wide and just over 1 metre high, with the constant risk of the tunnel collapsing. At the start of the battle of the Somme, two separate tunnels were painstakingly dug, with 900 men working on each. They packed 40,000 lbs of explosives in one and 60,000 lbs in the other, with the blast intended to rip through the ground creating a 450-foot-wide crater. However, German soldiers had detected the tunnelling. The blast was so powerful that the German soldiers were killed, but as the British infantry flowed over the top, they were massacred by German machine guns. With honour, I dedicate my speech to the miners and women who were at the battle of the Somme, whom we will never forget and who, alongside our brave military personnel, paid the ultimate price.

I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for bringing forward this debate, and for her work on behalf of the all-party parliamentary group for the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and commemoration. The Somme carries particular significance for north Cumbria because of the Lonsdale Pals, formerly the 11th Battalion of the Border Regiment. Raised by the 5th Earl of Lonsdale shortly after the outbreak of war, it was one of the earliest pals battalions authorised by the War Office. Men from Carlisle, Penrith, Workington, Whitehaven, Kendal and communities across Cumberland and Westmorland enlisted together. They were neighbours, workmates, fellow parishioners, but they trained together and went to war together. That bond gave the battalion a powerful identity, but it also meant that, when casualties came, entire communities shared the loss. It was my privilege to lay the wreath at the county memorial last weekend on behalf of all Cumbria’s MPs, who represent the former counties of Cumberland and Westmorland. On the opening day, the 11th Battalion attacked the Leipzig salient near Thiepval and suffered devastating casualties. Among those killed was Corporal Stephen Putland, who was born and lived in Carlisle. His name is recorded on the Upperby war memorial in Carlisle and on the Thiepval memorial to the missing. He was not the only man to be lost that day. John McDivitt, John Nevin, James Jardine Wilson and Company Sergeant Major John Sewell were also lost. On the battle’s final day, further tragedy struck the pals. The battalion attacked German positions at Redan ridge, and among those killed was Colour Sergeant Major Robert Lorimer. His body was never recovered, and his name, too, is commemorated at Thiepval. Another man whose story is particularly personal to me is Harry Wilfred Lowthian, who served with the Lonsdale Pals during the Somme. My research suggests he would have been a distant relative of mine, and also the brother or nephew of Ernest Lowthian, Labour’s first candidate for the parliamentary seat of Carlisle. Earlier this year, I had the privilege of visiting France and Belgium with the Commonwealth War Graves Commission. I visited Thiepval and several other sites, including Serre Road cemetery No. 2, which deserves a particular mention. It is the largest cemetery on the Somme battlefields, and standing among its rows of headstones is a powerful reminder of the immense loss in that battle. The visit also gave me a much deeper appreciation of the work of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, which cares for 1.7 million Commonwealth service personnel—not their graves, but the personnel—who died in battle. It maintains graves, cemeteries and memorials at more than 23,000 locations in over 150 countries. I was particularly struck by the work of the commission’s recovery unit in recovering and identifying those still being discovered on battlefields today, more than a century later. The team carefully excavate, record remains, examine personal possessions and match them with military records, battalion diaries and wartime maps. Matching that with DNA can often establish the soldier’s identity over 100 years later. It is painstaking but vital work. As we mark 110 years since the Somme, we remember Corporal Stephen Putland, Robert Lorimer, Harry Wilfred Lowthian and the men of the Lonsdale Pals. We remember all those from across Cumbria, across the United Kingdom and throughout the Commonwealth, and our allies, who served and sacrificed. Their names live on in memorials and family histories, and through the work of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission. It is our duty to ensure that their stories continue to be told and that their sacrifice is never diminished by the passage of time.

I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for giving us this opportunity to speak on behalf of our constituents, past and present. I am honoured to speak on behalf of the people of South Derbyshire and to remember those who gave so much. I am particularly moved by the story of brothers Henry and William Barnett, both of whom died on the first day of the battle of the Somme. Their parents were William and Geraldine Barnett of 37 Market Street in Swadlincote. William, the younger brother, who was a shop assistant, was the first to join up. He enlisted in Church Gresley, and by 25 June 1915 was in France. Henry, who was a sink maker, enlisted on 26 March 1915, and when he was posted to France in December 1915 the two brothers were reunited on the western front. Both served as privates in the first line of the 5th Battalion of the Sherwood Foresters, and they were both killed during an attack on the German positions at Gommecourt. They are commemorated alongside one another on the memorial to the missing at Thiepval. In May, I was invited by Shelly Lynn and Joanne Abbassi, two volunteers for the charity In From the Cold Project, to visit the Commonwealth War Graves Commission site in Church Gresley in my constituency. The In From The Cold Project was formed more than 20 years ago to research and identify all servicemen and servicewomen missing from the official Commonwealth War Graves Commission list of casualties from the first and second world wars. Their task is to get these soldiers, sailors and airmen their due recognition, even after the passing of so many years. I was moved by the dedication and diligence of the volunteers in ensuring that all the fallen have a marked Commonwealth war grave, but a passing comment about council charges that are paid out of the volunteers’ own pockets sent me and my team off into a conversation with the Local Government Association to see whether we could seek agreement from local authorities to waive the fees in these special circumstances. I want to give special recognition and a shout-out to Antony Cobley, in my team, who helped make that happen. I am pleased to share with the House that an agreement was reached with the LGA and its new guidance is that fees should be waived across England. Council Matt Boughton, who is chair of the LGA’s safer and stronger communities committee, said: “Preserving the links between local communities and those who served and died in conflict is an important part of ensuring future generations continue to understand and remember their sacrifice. While often modest, charges for record searches can present an additional barrier to organisations trying to identify the final resting places of service personnel. Lifting these charges where they relate to service personnel, which many councils have already done, is a good way to help ensure those who lost their lives in service receive the recognition and commemoration they deserve.” We will never know where so many servicemen and servicewomen from the Somme, world war one, world war two and subsequent wars rest, but all parties are committed to working to ensure that as many unmarked graves are now marked so that we can commemorate those lost for so long. We will remember them.

On the first day of the battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916, 19,240 British men lost their lives. It was the single bloodiest day in the history of the British Army. The Sherwood Foresters, some 2,000 men from across Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, started the battle with an assault on Gommecourt. I have been able to identify at least 12 names of young men from across Ilkeston, Long Eaton and Sandiacre, who were killed on that first day alone. The eldest, James Mann, was 41. He worked in the lace industry and left behind his wife Flora and their five children. The youngest man who was killed, Arthur Robinson, had only just turned 20. He lived with his sister and her family at 105 Bennett Street in Long Eaton. Looking over these lists, it was seeing exactly where they lived that struck me the most. The first world war was so long ago now, it is almost a different world. The numbers of dead and wounded at the Somme alone are so large as to be incomprehensible, squeezing from view the individual, human stories that were lived by each and every one of the people who were there, but the thing about knowing which house Arthur lived in is that that house is still there. I have knocked on that door. I have delivered leaflets through it. Twenty-year-old Arthur Robinson knew the streets that I know. He lived across the road from my mates Howard and Margaret. Long Eaton has changed a lot, certainly, in the more than a century that has gone by since he gave his life, but it is still the same place. I get similar feelings when I look at the list of young men killed from Ilkeston. I see Naylors and Beardsleys and Mees, local surnames that I still see regularly everywhere, from my Facebook comments to our council ballot papers. It should not be a surprise that this information exists and is there to be found. Despite the first world war having ended so long ago, we make a vow every November that we will remember them and we hold true to that vow. The two world wars draw further into history all the time, but I think our remembrance events in Ilkeston, Long Eaton and the surrounding villages are better attended every year. In Draycott, the homes of soldiers who died in the first world war are marked with their own small, individual memorials on each doorstep, reminding us of the time that our world was their world. They were sent off from terraced streets in Derbyshire to the fields of France and Belgium, where they endured the most unbelievable hardships; suffering so great that the very least we can do now is remember them. There is plenty of history written about grand acts of strategic brilliance or incompetence, depending on one’s opinion—about noble generals and the aristocrats and industrialists who dominated this place at that time, and the balance of power between the great empires fighting over who got to have the biggest navy or which African colony they got to control—but that is not why people piled into Ilkeston and Long Eaton town centres on Sunday. What we pledge to remember are the hundreds of thousands of working-class men, so many of them so young, who were sent abroad to fight in those great wars. We should remember who they were: their names, what families they came from, where they lived and where they worked. We should remember them not just for dying but for living—for being the people that they were. We should remember that for as long as we can, no matter how long ago it was. If we remember them like that, then the history stops being faraway and abstract; it stays real in our hearts and minds and helps us prevent such tragedies from ever occurring again.

I want to talk about the Cornish men and women who were in the Somme and involved in the first world war. There were 6,300 deaths of people from Cornwall in world war one. Many of them signed up to the Duke of Cornwall’s Light Infantry. There were a number of battalions from Cornwall that fought in the Somme, and the 63rd (Royal Naval) Division fought in the latter stages of the war as well. There was an article in the Royal Cornwall Gazette on 26 October 1916, which was an account sent by someone from the front, who said that they were mocked by the Germans because they knew where they were from; the Germans asked them if they had any Cornish pasties. Even over there, the Cornish were known and recognised. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for North West Leicestershire (Amanda Hack) for talking about the tunnellers. They were coalminers where my hon. Friend is from, but those from Cornwall were tin miners. The Royal Engineer tunnelling companies worked in silence so that they were not heard; they could hear the Germans above them, apparently sometimes talking about how long it was since they had held their wives—they were that close. On the first day of the Somme, 19 charges were detonated under German frontlines, many of those tunnels having been built by the miners from my constituency and my hon. Friend’s. The saddest thing is that many of those who managed to survive the Somme and the first world war came back to Cornwall and carried on working in the mines, and only a year later, on 20 October 1919, five of them were killed in the Levant mining disaster, in which 31 people died when the mine collapsed. It is a terrible sadness. I know some of those stories because last week I saw the historians of Penair school, who have won the Western Front Association Malcolm Doolin local history prize for bringing the stories to life in a magical way. They used AI to make films about some of the people who fought in the Somme and the first world war—tunnellers from Cornwall—and said they had become very close to the men because many of them were only a year or two older than they are now. The way they brought them to life was magical. I am proud of the historians from Penair. They have been here for the past couple of days; they went to the ceremony at the Cenotaph yesterday and paraded there. I am contributing to this debate simply to remember the men of Cornwall who died in the Somme, of whom there were many, and to give our great thanks for all that they did and all that they gave.

I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for securing this debate and for her powerful opening speech. I join her in thanking all those Members of this House, along with House staff, who gave their lives for our freedom in the battle of the Somme and in the entirety of the first and second world wars. One of the great things about speaking last is having the opportunity to reflect on what has already been said in the debate. It is telling that we are talking about events that happened 110 years ago, yet the emotion from those who have spoken has been raw, real and clear to see. That highlights the enormity of the battle and of the sacrifice made by those men who lost their lives. My interest in this topic was first awakened when I visited the war graves in France—like many—with my parents when I was younger. Like the hon. Member for South West Devon, I was struck by the graves that did not have names—the unknown soldier—and by the graves, quite concerningly, that had more than one soldier in them. That was incredibly powerful. I apologise, Madam Deputy Speaker; I have got my information from trusted sources, but my numbers might be slightly wrong. In stark contrast to the constituency of my hon. Friend the Member for Erewash (Adam Thompson), Harlow in 1916 was, it is fair to say, a very different place from today. In fact, my constituency was a collection of villages under the banner of Epping. Members will all know who the Member of Parliament for Epping was during the second world war. According to the information I have from a trusted source, 13 men from Harlow were killed in the battle of the Somme, with two killed on the first day—two of the 19,240 British soldiers killed on that first day. However, looking at all the villages that have since combined to become Harlow, I suspect that the numbers were greater. Among those who died, some of whom were from Potter Street, were Private Walter Wheeler of the Essex Regiment, Private Thomas W. J. Baldock of the East Surrey Regiment and Private Henry Ayton. I want to focus specifically on one soldier who died in the battle of the Somme. Eight years ago, to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the end of the first world war, Your Harlow, our local online newspaper, brought together local councillors and community champions to read out the stories of the individuals who had lost their life in the first world war. I am running short of time, but I just want to mention Thomas Lewis, who was born in Great Parndon in 1895. He was one of 10 children, one of whom died at birth. Private Lewis enlisted at Warley and joined the 1st Battalion of the Bedfordshire Regiment. His regiment was involved in the battle of the Somme, specifically the attack on High Wood on 20 August 1916 and the capture of Falfemont farm between 3 and 6 September 1916. Thomas died of his wounds on 13 September at the age of 21. I want to quickly thank the Harlow branch of the Royal British Legion for the commemorative service that it held over the weekend. It was particularly poignant to hear the names of Thomas, Cyril and Francis Riley—three brothers who died in the first world war. We will remember them. I apologise for going over time, Madam Deputy Speaker.
Which brings us to the Front-Bench contributions. I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

I thank the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for introducing this debate, for her work on the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and for her powerful speech. Of course, we have heard powerful speeches and testimonies from all Members today. The significance of today’s debate on the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme is something on which Members from across this House can agree. It is an opportunity to remember, to honour and to commemorate those who fought, suffered and gave their lives in the service of this country and in defence of the freedoms that we enjoy today. The battle of the Somme was not simply a battle fought in a distant field in northern France; it was a moment that reached into every town, every village and every family across our country, changing lives forever. Communities across my constituency felt that loss as keenly as anywhere else. It was one of the largest and deadliest battles of the first world war. More than 1 million soldiers were killed or wounded during the campaign, and the first day remains the bloodiest day in British military history. Despite taking place more than a century ago, the Somme retains a powerful place in our national memory, symbolising not only the terrible human cost of war and the loss of so many young lives, but the extraordinary courage of ordinary men. Across the country stand memorials to those who served and those who never came home. In my constituency, memorials stand in Walton-on-Thames, Thames Ditton, Long Ditton, Esher, Claygate, Hersham, East Molesey, West Molesey and Oatlands. The names engraved on those memorials are more than inscriptions on stone—they were sons, brothers, husbands, workmates and neighbours. Each name represents a life cut short, a family left to grieve, and a community forever changed. This history is woven deeply into the history of my constituency. At Hare Hill in Walton-on-Thames stood the Australian auxiliary hospital, where thousands of wounded Australian and New Zealand soldiers were treated during the war. Walton-on-Thames became a place of recovery, rehabilitation and refuge, forging lasting links between our community and the Anzac story that endure to this day. Hurst Park played an important role in the war effort, as troops assembled and trained before deployment overseas. The roads, parks and open spaces of my constituency became part of a national effort that touched every aspect of local life. The East Surrey Regiment played its own role in the Somme campaign. On the opening day of the battle, Captain Wilfred Percy Nevill encouraged his men to kick footballs across no man’s land as they advanced towards the German lines as a way to boost morale and remind the soldiers of home. It is an important reminder that these men were ordinary people from communities like ours, whose courage, comradeship and resilience carried them through. We should never lose sight of the individual lives behind the figures. That is why commemoration matters. On Remembrance Sunday, I had the pleasure of visiting the Molesey Royal British Legion, and I shared a glass of port with the veterans from the Royal Artillery. Paul Morriss, the secretary and treasurer to the committee, and I spoke for a while about the remarkable work of Richard Dunning, who is the founder of the Lochnagar Crater Foundation. He is a Surrey man who in the 1970s purchased the Lochnagar crater—one of the most significant surviving sites of the Somme battlefield. He visited Lochnagar in the early 1970s, spoke of a feeling of profound connection to the site and determined that it should be protected. He acquired the crater and dedicated himself to preserving it as a permanent memorial. Today it ensures that future generations understand not only what happened on those battlefields, but why it matters. I am pleased that my son, who is in year 9, visited the Lochnagar crater this year, as so many schoolchildren across the country do. I pay tribute to my local scho

It is an honour to sum up this debate on the day after Armistice Day, although it is a genuine shame that, yet again, no Reform MP has chosen to take part, especially as some of them regard themselves as authorities on world war one. Fortunately, my hon. Friend the Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) was here, and she clearly really knows what she is talking about. The battle of the Somme took place between 1 July and 18 November 1916, during which both sides between them suffered over 1 million casualties. Of that total, over 400,000 were British and Commonwealth troops, including over 130,000 who were killed. The strategy for an Anglo-French offensive had been agreed between the respective commanders, Lord Haig and General Joffre, at the Chantilly staff conference some months previously. However, when the attack was launched in July, it was a costly failure. In the 110 years that have passed since, a great deal has been written about what happened. However, the fundamental reason for the failure of the Somme offensive, especially in the British sector, was the highly over-optimistic assumptions about the effect of artillery on prepared defensive positions that had been skilfully chosen by German generals and engineers months previously. As John Keegan, in his authoritative history of the first world war, summed it up, the Germans “had driven dugouts thirty feet below ground, impervious to artillery fire, provisioned to withstand siege and linked to the rear by buried telephone cable and deep communication trenches….They had made themselves secure.” Moreover, the German defenders regularly rehearsed dashing up from their well-protected dugouts to man their defensive positions and, crucially, setting up their machine guns with carefully calibrated interlocking fields of fire in rapid time. It was a feat that the allied planners thought impossible, as they believed that all such positions, including dense belts of barbed wire, would effectively have been destroyed by a massive preliminary bombardment —one that also effectively surrendered any element of strategic or even operational surprise. Even worse, many of the shells failed to explode. For many men, the Somme was their first experience of combat, and their last. The 19 or so British divisions that took part in the initial assault were a mixture of old soldiers and new. Four divisions—the 4th, 7th, 8th and 29th—comprised largely veterans, including men who had survived the original battles as part of the British Expeditionary Force in 1914, or had served at Gallipoli. As a former Territorial Army infantry officer myself, I should also point out that four more—the 46th, 48th, 49th and 56th—were territorial divisions, whereas the bulk of the remaining 11 divisions largely comprised idealistic civilian volunteers who answered the famous call from the Secretary of State for War, Field Marshal Lord Kitchener: “Your Country Needs You”. Many of those men comprised Kitchener’s army and volunteered to fight alongside their fellow workmates or townsfolk in the so-called Pals battalions, enticed into the recruiting office by the promise that those who joined together would serve together. On 24 June, British artillery commenced a seven-day bombardment of the German defences, utilising around 1,000 field guns and almost 500 heavy artillery pieces. During that preparatory barrage, approximately 1.5 million shells were fired and confidence was high among British commanders, with General Sir Henry Rawlinson reportedly stating: “nothing could exist at the conclusion of the bombardment in the area covered by it.” Tragically, he was wrong.

I will be brief. As the right hon. Member mentioned the shells, I want to put on the record our gratitude for the many women back home who made those shells—the Canary Girls—in highly dangerous work and whose skin became discoloured as a result. Does he back my campaign for those women to have a memorial at the royal arboretum?

Without hesitation. Captain Siegfried Sassoon MC, one of the famous war poets, wrote in his diary on 1 July 1916: “We had breakfast at 6.—the morning is brilliantly fine—after a mist early. Since 6:30 there has been hell let loose. The air vibrates with the incessant din—the whole earth shakes & rocks & throbs—It is one continuous roar—Machine guns tap & rattle—bullets whistling over head—small fry quite outdone by the gangs of hooligan shells, that dash over to rend the German line”. On a personal note, as a student on the King’s College London MA war studies course studying the first world war, I went on a departmental tour to the Somme battlefield in 1987. I was then aged 22. We were awakened early in the morning, given a hot breakfast, taken out to the site of the then British frontline, given a tot of rum and then listened as whistles were blown at H-hour at 0730. It was exactly as it was intended to be: a deeply affecting experience and one that I will never forget. Given the relative inexperience of around half the assaulting divisions, British tactical instructions placed considerable emphasis on troops advancing steadily in line so as to maintain order and discipline. Troops were generally ordered to walk and not run on the assumption that the defenders would either have likely been killed, or so stunned as to be incapable of offering effective resistance. However, in the southern part of the British sector, some British officers who were sceptical of their artillery’s ability to suppress the German defenders ordered their troops to lie out in the open just prior to the assault, and then rush the German lines as soon as the barrage had lifted. Some of these units achieved at least local tactical surprise in reaching their initial objectives before the well-drilled German infantry could react in time. Sadly, however, that was the exception rather than the rule. In the majority of cases, the German defenders, exactly as they had rehearsed many times, won “the race to the parapet” and then rained down a literally murderous fire on the slowly advancing British infantry, who had been assured by their senior commanders that what they were about to experience could not happen. Even among those units who made it to the German lines, they frequently discovered the wire still uncut while being raked by multiple machine guns, still stuck in no man’s land. The eventual outcome in terms of loss of life was catastrophic. On the first day alone, over 19,000 British and Commonwealth soldiers were killed and a further 38,000 became casualties in what to this day represents the single bloodiest day in the history of the British Army. By that evening, some battalions, in particular the inexperienced pals battalions, had effectively ceased to exist. Despite the failure of the initial assault, British commanders pressed on over the next several months, resulting in a number of heroic actions, such as the Australians at Pozières and the South Africans at Delville—or Devil’s—Wood. Nevertheless, by the time the offensive was finally abandoned on 18 November, the maximum limit of the advance was some seven miles, for which the British Army alone had lost some 130,000 British and Commonwealth soldiers killed and more than twice as many wounded. In total, including combatants on all sides, over 1 million men were either killed, wounded, taken prisoner or went missing over the course of the battle, which lasted a total of 141 days. One of those wounded on the German side was a Bavarian corporal named Adolf Hitler. Men of all ages bravely fought and died, in many cases literally side by side, during the Somme. The oldest confirmed British fatality was Lieutenant Henry Webber of the 7th Battalion, South Lancashire Regiment, who was 67 when he was killed on 21 July. Members of this House and the other place also lost their lives, as did Lieutenant Raymond Asquith, son of the Prime Minister Herbert Asquith, who was killed in action on 15 September.

It is a great privilege to follow the right hon. Member for Rayleigh and Wickford (Mr Francois). He routinely reminds us of the absence of certain Members of Parliament in such debates. It reminds me that it is serious parties and a serious Parliament that present a united point of view on matters such as this, and it is not Governments alone that fix or address our security, but Parliaments. We must come together in our resolve to ensure that we pay these matters respect when they are brought to the House. I am grateful to the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) for securing this very important debate at a very important time, and to all Members for their worthy contributions. The hon. Member for South West Devon captured not only the colossal scale of the loss but the extent to which it covered her constituency and all our constituencies, right here to the doors of Parliament. I am very grateful for her work for the Commonwealth War Graves Commission. I reflected that perhaps the Devonshires did not just hold ground; they also held her heart. As I prepared for this speech, I was struck by the extent to which every community was touched by this battle, which was a seminal battle in the first world war but also a seminal moment in our nation’s psyche. As I stood in front of the Cenotaph yesterday, it felt as though the whole nation had joined us in silence, reflecting and remembering. That, for me, is what remembrance is about: unity. They came from every nation in our Union, every village and town in every region, forming something like 50 divisions. Every soldier fought, many giving their lives. I was incredibly touched by the stories of the Pals. In Leyton, 41 players, staff and supporters from my beloved Leyton Orient—known then as Clapton Orient—led by the club captain Fred “Spider” Parker were enlisted as the 17th (Service) Battalion. Many of them never came home, including three sons of Leyton: Richard McFadden, William Jonas and George Scott. It was incredibly powerful to create a bridge and a link with my hon. Friend the Member for Edinburgh South West (Dr Arthur), who spoke about the 16th (Service) Battalion, and my hon. Friend the Member for Carlisle (Ms Minns), who spoke lovingly about the Lonsdale Pals, reminding us of the proximity of our people who gave so valiantly in this campaign. But Britain did not fight alone. We are the great convener. We are the home of democracy, and at moments like this, our friends came to our aid. Some tens of thousands of Commonwealth soldiers are buried in military and civilian cemeteries. In Thiepval, the Memorial to the Missing of the Somme bears the names of 72,000 British and South African men who died at the Somme and have no grave. It was incredibly powerful when I heard those stories in the speeches by the hon. Member for Esher and Walton (Monica Harding), and my hon. Friend and colleague the Member for Ilford South (Jas Athwal). They spoke about the contributions of all those nations, and reminded us that courage has no religion and sacrifice has no colour. The Commonwealth Air Forces memorial is a poignant reminder of that sacrifice, because those who came to fight alongside us from the Commonwealth, from places like Africa, from where I came, were Christians, Muslims, Jews, Hindus, Sikhs and many others, looking after our birthplace, looking over Runnymede. I suggest that all hon. Members go there and take some of that in. Over the past couple of days I have had the honour and privilege to host my opposite number from Australia, the hon. Matt Keogh. Yesterday I presented him with a poppy forged from barbed wire recovered from the battlefield of the Somme, as a sign of the shared sacrifice that our two countries made and which the Liberal Democrat leader— [ Interruption. ] Correction; perhaps in the future—the hon. Member for Esher and Walton spoke so powerfully about. Around 6,800 of the Australian Imperial Force were killed at the Somme, and 18,000 more were

As the Minister will know, many of those who died in the Somme were buried close to where they fell, so there is a whole line of cemeteries across the Somme battlefield that mark out the very limited extent of the allied advance. Across the Dispatch Boxes, will he join me in together paying tribute to the amazing work of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, which tends those graves to our fallen so respectfully and brilliantly?

I thank the shadow Minister for those powerful words. I agree with him, which is why I took the time to go to the grave of the Unknown Warrior. I will ensure that any Member of the House who wishes to do the same is able to do so, and I urge all hon. Members to take up that invitation. The local and personal nature of the battalions who served in the first world war was reflected in a powerful contribution from my hon. Friend the Member for Ipswich (Jack Abbott), who spoke about loyalty and reminded us that freedom has a cost. My hon. Friends the Members for Harlow (Chris Vince) and for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) spoke about the importance of preserving those links and reminding ourselves what war is for. Before I finish and the hon. Member for South West Devon sums up the debate, I want to return to something she said about the amount of time that has elapsed since the battle of the Somme. Given that the battle was 110 years ago, it is easy for us to think that the time for remembrance has passed. However, as veterans will know, remembrance is part of the continuum of service. This year we remember the 20th anniversary of the loss of XV230 and the 14-person crew from 120 Squadron, the Royal Marines and the Parachute Regiment. We remember their loss and we will never forget their sacrifice. In closing, the legacy of the battle of the Somme unites us in remembrance, no matter where we come from and no matter our religion, race or politics. The sacrifice of men and women—including the Canary Girls in Woolwich and Carlisle, who bonded over the colour that stained their hands—is the same, from the Somme to Afghanistan, from Gallipoli to XV230. We remember their loss and we will never forget their sacrifice.

I am incredibly grateful to all those who have contributed today and to the Commonwealth War Graves Commission for helping to prepare for the debate. We have heard many individual names and about people of different nationalities and religions. We have heard about the role of women, the pals battalions, sports teams, miners and medics, and we have heard examples of immense bravery. Reflections about the human cost of war have brought emotion across the Chamber as we have shared the sheer scale of the losses at the battle of the Somme and allowed it to sink in again. One hundred and ten years ago, the young men who fought on the Somme would have had no idea that Members of Parliament would still be speaking their names in this Chamber more than a century later. Perhaps that is exactly what remembrance requires of us. The most meaningful thing that we can do as we approach 18 November, the 110th anniversary, is simply to tell their stories again, because remembrance cannot be passive; it has to be renewed by every generation. Those who fought on the Somme entrusted their memory first to their families, then to the memorials and cemeteries that were built in their names, and ultimately to us and all those whom we represent. We will remember them. Question put and agreed to. Resolved, That this House has considered the 110th anniversary of the battle of the Somme.

I beg to move, That this House has considered the Nolan principles. I thank the Backbench Business Committee and the co-sponsors for bringing this important debate to the House. It is a pleasure to follow the debate on the battle of the Somme led by the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith). It reminds us of the sacrifices made by so many so that we can enjoy our way of life today, which we cannot take for granted, and which the Nolan principles help us to protect. Recent polling has shown that just 9% of people trust politicians to put the interests of the nation above the interests of their own party, and recent British Election Study research found that around three quarters of people had low or no trust in MPs. Frankly, I am horrified that people might look at me in that way. For years, I operated in the community as a volunteer and activist, and later as a local councillor, and I was viewed in my community as a trustworthy source of support. Now I am proud to serve that community as the Member of Parliament. I know that most of my colleagues in this place and across public service are in it for the right reasons—to serve their constituents and communities. More than 30 years ago, Lord Nolan set out seven simple principles that must be followed by people in public life: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership. The principles represent not just rules for us to follow, but an agreement and understanding between the public and those they trust to serve, represent and protect them. We have all read about the headline-grabbing failures—partygate, when the rules our constituents followed were broken in Downing Street, or the questions over Peter Mandelson’s appointment as ambassador in Washington—but sometimes we do not know about the devastating consequences for our constituents when these principles are not followed. We do not always know how the pernicious creep of the ignoring and bending of the rules has reached into public bodies that people deal with every day: councils, the police and our schools. In my Mid Dunbartonshire constituency and across Scotland, schools operate a software system called SEEMiS. Most hon. Members will not have heard of SEEMiS, but it is the system used by Scottish schools to keep pupil records—the formal records of a child’s education journey. Importantly, the records include notes on bullying incidents. Following a bullying incident in a school, a constituent told me about the difficulties they faced in trying to gain access to the data in their child’s record on SEEMiS. This resulted in a devastating breach of trust. After the incident badly affected the education journey of their child, they asked to access their child’s records. East Dunbartonshire council told them that the incident involving their child that they wished to view had been properly logged at the time, and that records could not be changed afterwards, but that was not the truth. My constituent was forced to go to court to access their child’s records, and only after a court ruling did the council hand them over. This lack of transparency is deeply worrying, and the willingness of the council to spend taxpayers’ money on a court case, which it lost, shows little objectivity and poor accountability. To add to my constituent’s ordeal, they found not only that the notes were inaccurate, but that they had been altered. They did not find that out because they were told or because it was recorded in the notes; they had to access stored metadata—information that is not readily available and that requires a high level of technical expertise to access. When my constituent complained to the Information Commissioner’s Office, now the Information Commission, they were told that the actions of the school and the council did “not meet with the obligation to be transparent”. The ICO told the council that it should change the system so that notes cannot be backdated. The council has said

It is poignant that this debate follows a debate on the battle of the Somme. I was reflecting yesterday on remembrance and thinking about the sacrifice of my grandfather in the second world war and our great-grandfathers in the first world war, and I reflected on what they might think about politics today. I think they may be quite disappointed in the democracy that we have built, particularly in the coarsening of public discourse, the amount of times that people engage with others as their enemies, rather than their opponents, and some of the falling standards in public life.

I was going to make this point to the hon. Member for Mid Dunbartonshire (Susan Murray), but she had finished her speech. My hon. Friend the Member for Bishop Auckland (Dr Rushworth) talks about the behaviour of Members of Parliament, which is really important. I visit schools quite regularly in my constituency and talk about the debates that we have in this place, and it is really important that when the debates end, we treat each other with respect and courtesy; I think the majority of Members do that in this place. Does he agree that it is disappointing when some Members of this House do not treat other Members with the same respect?

I agree 100%. There is a responsibility on all of us, frankly, to do better. Why? The point has already been made very well, but there is a decline in trust in politicians. I naively thought when I was elected to this place that if I just told the truth all the time, worked incredibly hard and acted with integrity, it would shine through, but it does not. I have many constituents who do not trust me and think that I am a liar, not because of anything tangible that I have done, but because they think the whole political class is not to be trusted and that the moment somebody becomes a politician, they fall into that class. That is why it is so important that we do more to uphold and strengthen standards in public life. It is important that we address a couple of areas in particular. One is around stronger safeguards that give our constituents confidence that when we choose to put ourselves forward and become elected to this place, we genuinely have their interests at heart and are not using this place to enrich ourselves. For example, we have to get rid of second jobs. I am not talking about medics maintaining their medical licences; I am talking about people earning vast sums of money while not representing their constituents in this place. I have found that this job is equivalent to two full-time jobs. It is impossible to be a proper Member of Parliament and to do our job properly while constantly being away earning huge sums of money elsewhere. It simply cannot be done, and we need to legislate strongly against that. We also need to do more to enable our constituents to see the difference. Maybe there needs to be greater transparency. I have often wondered if we should clock in and out of the Chamber and report how many surgeries we all hold, and so on, so that people can make fair comparisons and understand who is doing the work and who is not doing the work. Another point we need to address is our debating. Maybe we need to review “Erskine May” and what constitutes parliamentary language. I have been really disappointed at times since I was elected by the things that are deemed acceptable. For example, I thought it was disgusting when the Leader of the Opposition described Members on the Government Benches as “paedo defenders”, and we all know that we got abuse because of that. The things said in this Chamber get repeated to us by our constituents. Members on the Government Benches who are themselves survivors of child sexual abuse had that label attached to them, and it was deeply distressing to them. Frankly, the Leader of the Opposition should have done better, but that was not called out by Mr Speaker because it is apparently deemed to be parliamentary language. We need to address that. We also need to look beyond this place. There are examples—one has been given already—of where the public simply do not have the transparency that they would expect at lower levels of government and in public bodies. I was very disappointed to see that the leadership of Durham county council changed the rules on hearing standards complaints, so that a very small committee, on which Reform always has a majority, hears an increasing number of serious complaints. Some former Reform councillors who resigned and sit as independents have described the leadership as shambolic. The Nolan principles predominantly deal with integrity, but do we need to consider principles that address the challenges of 2026? Is it acceptable for people in public life to express racist opinions under the guise of free speech? Before Reform took control of Durham county council, I supplied it and the media with a full dossier of disgusting Facebook posts from accounts that claimed to be their candidates’ accounts and who the administrators of those accounts were. One of those people went on to become a Reform councillor, which was entirely unacceptable. Finally—as I raised with the Leader of the House today—as we look increasingly to devolve power, there needs to b

First, I apologise to the hon. Member for Mid Dunbartonshire (Susan Murray) for missing her opening remarks. I was rushing to the Chamber from another meeting. I very much welcome a debate about the Nolan principles. To start with a point that the hon. Member for Bishop Auckland (Dr Rushworth) made at the beginning of his speech, it is indeed surprising and perplexing that we would regard nearly 100% of the colleagues in this Chamber—from whichever party—as careful, diligent and morally upstanding people. There is a tiny minority who we perhaps do not trust, but basically, although we might not be able to remember the seven principles of public life by heart, that is the way we want to live our lives. That is the example we want to demonstrate in the work we do, yet the more paraphernalia created around the enforcement of standards in the House of Commons, the worse the reputation of politicians seems to become. I think that is because we think of ourselves as legislators, and the hon. Member for Bishop Auckland fell into that trap: “We need more rules about this. We need more rules about that. We need rules to address this.” I spent the previous Parliament on the Standards Committee, and I participated in producing the report that came out in May 2022. That report was a complete revision of the House of Commons code of conduct, and was trying to start a different conversation. One witness, who was a Chief Whip of a major political party, told us in evidence, “The seven principles are quite simple, and if you do not understand them, you should not be in public life.” On the face of it, they are very simple, but is navigating conflicts of interest as a Member of Parliament simple? We all have them; whether we are paid as an outside director or sponsored by a trade union, everybody has conflicts of interest. What about the conflicts of interest—even if they are not necessarily declarable—between our parties’ programmes and the interests of our constituents? We all have to deal with conflicts of interest. The image we were given in one piece of evidence from the Westminster Abbey Institute was that we are trying to navigate our way across a stormy sea, with lots of conflicting pressures and priorities, and it is not always easy to decide what to do in a given set of circumstances. If any hon. Member present thinks it has been easy, they probably do not realise what they have stumbled into. Yes, we want transparency, and yes, there need to be rules, but the rules should not be the culture. If you go into the Tea Room and talk about the House of Commons code of conduct, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am sure that you find—like everyone else—that people discuss how to stay clear of the rules. That is what the conversation appears to be about; it does not tend to be about how to deal sincerely and honestly with conflicts. The problem with the way in which the House of Commons has set up the adjudication of the code is that it tends to be a very legalistic process. Anyone who has been under the cosh of an investigation by the Commissioner for Standards finds first that they have got nobody to talk to. I have recommended that we should split the role of the commissioner, with somebody to advise and counsel Members of Parliament about conflicts of interest and the code, and somebody—preferably a former High Court judge—to adjudicate. Of course, I have no criticism to make of the present commissioner, but we could upgrade the juridical process of adjudicating the code as we have done for appeals, which are now presided over by a High Court judge and a panel in a much more strictly judicial process. The advantage of that is a High Court judge is used to adjudicating: judging evidence and facts and coming to a conclusion.

I genuinely think that the hon. Gentleman’s is a voice worth listening to on this. Does he not feel that the growth in rules has been a response to the scandals we have had rather than the producer of them? Is he arguing for less regulation or that we have just got the wrong rules and system in place?

I am not arguing for abolition of the code or anything like that. I am arguing for a system that recognises that conflicts of interest inevitably arise and have to be handled. The system should create a supportive environment for Members of this House to discuss and explore the dilemmas they are confronted with, openly and frankly and without fear. That does not exist at the moment. I also think that the margin of appreciation in interpreting the rules should be much more forgiving. The present commissioner has made it clear that that is not his method, and indeed the House of Commons resolutions do not steer him in that direction. We might think that the guidance accompanying the rules was just guidance, but the official advice from the House Service is that, because it has been approved by the House, along with the code of conduct rules, it has equal force as the law of Parliament. I do not think that is what Parliament really understood when it voted the guidance through, or each time it does so. I would like to see a more flexible and forgiving system: one where there is a more open conversation about the dilemmas we face.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Mid Dunbartonshire (Susan Murray) on securing the debate. Trust in politics is one of the big challenges of our time. It has never been particularly high, but at the moment, Britain’s trust in politics is among the lowest in western Europe. There are obviously many theories as to why that might be, but, from my experience before coming to this place of working on open government in over 70 countries, I recognise that there are ways in which we could reverse the trend. That is part of what this debate is about. My strong belief is that it is about a combination of transparency and accountability plus delivery on the issues that our constituents care about. Those two things do not need to be in tension, although some try to argue that; they can be complementary. The big opportunity coming up for the Government is the White Paper on rewiring the state. I am personally very excited about that, because of the term “taking on unaccountable government”. I hope that there is space in that vision to articulate why open government, transparency and opportunities for public participation lead to better decisions and better government. It is about ensuring that citizens have a voice, and that the state is accountable for decisions and failures are learned from and not covered up. I was therefore really glad that the Prime Minister committed to working with me on justice for Grenfell—a tragedy that would not have happened had the Nolan principles been followed by the leadership of the royal borough of Kensington and Chelsea. I agree with the chair of the Ethics and Integrity Commission and my hon. Friend the Member for Bishop Auckland (Dr Rushworth) that more needs to be done on local government. That is an important commitment in the Government’s anti-corruption plan.

I share the hon. Gentleman’s horror and disgust at what the Moore-Bick inquiry has uncovered about the conduct of quite a number of bodies and people that led to the Grenfell tragedy. It was a system failure, and the question of who takes responsibility for system failures is much more important. The problem with just applying rules is that they do not necessarily address system failures, because they are about culture, attitude and behaviour. That is what we need to address and demonstrate leadership on, as we are figures in public life.

I agree that culture is a huge part of this. The Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea is belatedly undergoing what it calls a culture review, but I fear that it may fall into the category of reviews that may not necessarily lead to the change we want, as the hon. Gentleman mentioned earlier. Let us see what happens; I want to keep an open mind. I also support the idea of a national oversight mechanism —I know the Cabinet Office is doing work on this. If we are going to spend time, energy and resources on inquests and inquiries, it is important that the recommendations are tracked and monitored; otherwise, it feels to me that we may defeat the point. Of course, the Hillsborough law—the Public Office (Accountability) Bill, which I hope will become an Act very soon—may be a big step forward on the duty of candour. I want to cover two areas. First, there is a huge amount to welcome in the Representation of the People Bill, particularly on foreign money in politics and the Rycroft recommendations, and we will shortly get that Bill back from the other place. There were so many good suggestions that could not find their way into the Bill, which is why the Government were right to set up a task and finish group. I hope the ideas that come through that group will see the light of day, potentially in future legislation. I really welcome the Bill, but I do not want to lose the ideas that we could not get through this time. I really hope that when the Electoral Commission looks at spending caps during the regulated period, it will take an expansive view and think about whether we need to have wider ones, given the nature of modern campaigning, which is essentially permanent. The second main area that I want to cover is lobbying reform. The July report from the Ethics and Integrity Commission was a really thorough and good piece of work that contained lots of recommendations about lobbying. At the moment, the public record captures only 4% of lobbyists, because it is restricted to consultant lobbyists, and information is captured in disparate databases across Government, making it hard to track and make useful. We know from Greensill and the covid contracts that modern lobbying happens in lots of different ways, not just through formal meetings. This is not about policing who the Government meet, because they should be meeting businesses, stakeholders and so on. It is about having the right to know what voices are informing major decisions, so that the public can make a judgment on whether the requirement to consult widely has been met. An initial step would be to clean up the number of different lobbying databases that we have, and to make them easier to understand and view. The report calls for legislation, and I asked at Cabinet Office orals a few weeks ago whether the Government were open to legislation. The Minister confirmed that they were, so I hope that is something we will see. As my hon. Friend the Member for Bishop Auckland said, it has too often taken a crisis to create the urgency to act on matters of ethics and integrity in politics. We can all name them: Greensill, the previous ambassador to the United States, the covid contracts, Owen Paterson and, of course, the multiple ongoing investigations by different bodies into Reform UK’s funding and the hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage)—I have informed him that I would say this. We now have an opportunity to create a reset moment for standards in public life, and the rewiring the state White Paper is a great opportunity to do so.

My hon. Friend refers to the wider rewiring of the state. As we move towards further devolution, does he agree that our local councillors need to be much more accountable? At the moment, even when they are sanctioned, all they are asked to do is apologise. That gets nowhere, because they do not bother to do so.

I completely agree. I am a huge supporter of devolution, but it is important that the Government’s anti-corruption plan calls for a local audit office to look at finance and at codes of conduct for local councillors and senior officers. Of course, local government is required to follow the Nolan principles, but I am not sure that we have all the systems in place to track and monitor that, so I agree with my hon. Friend. The first opportunity is to finish the job on the Representation of the People Bill and the Public Office (Accountability) Bill, and the second is the White Paper on rewiring the state. My third and final suggestion is to have a “clean up Westminster” Bill in the next Session. It would bring together all the different elements on which we know action is needed, such as lobbying and second jobs, finishing the job on money in politics and sending a clear message to the public that open and accountable politics is central to this Government’s mission of rewiring the state in a way that delivers growth, opportunity and hope across the country.

It is a pleasure to speak in this debate on the Nolan principles; I congratulate the hon. Member for Mid Dunbartonshire (Susan Murray) on securing it. As chair of the APPG on anti-corruption and responsible tax, let me say that it is on all of us to speak truth to power in a spirit of constructive criticism, regardless of which party is in power. I wish to focus my remarks on two topics where, collectively, it is my view that we are falling short of the Nolan principles: lobbying reform, which is long overdue, and MPs’ outside employment. Let me say from the outset that lobbying is a vital part of public discourse in driving workable policy solutions. It ensures that differing viewpoints are heard by the Government before decisions are made, but we need to know who is being lobbied by whom so that politicians, the public and the media can accurately scrutinise the machinery of government. Regrettably, that is not the case in the United Kingdom in 2026. In July, the Ethics and Integrity Commission published its review “Lobbying, Business Appointment Rules and Disclosure: Access to Government Decision Making”, which details 37 recommendations to modernise the regime. Doug Chalmers, the EIC’s chair, wrote in that report that the lobbying system “fails to deliver the required level of transparency and, in doing so, falls short of meeting the Nolan Principles.” Over the years, review after review and scandal after scandal have shown that the current system is broken. Only about 4% of all lobbying activity is required to be declared on the register of consultant lobbyists. That means that 96 out of 100 lobbying interactions simply fall outside the disclosure requirement, including in-house lobbyists, lobbyists with a turnover of below £90,000, non-VAT registered foreign businesses, the activities of special advisers, and informal comms such as WhatsApp.

People can mostly see who lobbies me because I often cannot resist putting their pictures on my Facebook page when I meet them. However, I do have to correct my hon. Friend. He is wrong to say that lobbying is not taken seriously in the UK, because in Scotland there is a register of lobbyists, so there are things we can learn even from inside the UK. What is in place in Scotland is not perfect, but does he agree that there is something we can learn from?

I am always willing to learn from comparative analysis of what works elsewhere, including in other jurisdictions across the United Kingdom. The Government have it in their power to bring about a culture shift, and the time to do so is now. Not all of the EIC’s recommendations require primary legislation. There is recommendation 8, which is that the Government simply refuse to meet any organisation seeking to lobby them unless that organisation is on the lobbying register. Recommendation 10 on having one digital repository for transparency releases is a simple fix. How about recommendation 13, which is that transparency releases include informal communication channels, including the likes of WhatsApp? If we are to address the deficiencies in our system, I urge the Government to find time to overhaul the register of consultant lobbyists so that we have a truly representative register that closes the loopholes I have mentioned, that empowers the regulator to levy significant fines for systemic offences of the registration requirement, that is properly resourced, and that documents interactions between the Government and organisations in sufficient detail that it serves as more than a mere box-ticking exercise. Let me turn to MPs’ outside employment, colloquially known as second jobs. This Government pledged in the 2024 manifesto that they would “task the Modernisation Committee to take forward urgent work on the restrictions that need to be put in place to prevent MPs from taking up roles that stop them serving their constituents and the country.” In November 2024, my right hon. Friend the Member for Manchester Central (Lucy Powell) tasked the Committee on Standards to look at how “to conduct further work into how changes to the rules on outside interests and employment might be implemented”. The Standards Committee opened its inquiry on 8 January 2025 and took oral evidence in public through to July 2025, yet—more than a year later—no report has been published, and no recommendations have been forthcoming, and no action has been taken in Government due to this delay. Despite my writing to the Standards Committee requesting an update, I have yet to receive a substantive response. Having advised—for the good part of more than a decade, in my old job before being elected to this place —on conflicts of interest, and on outside employment and related matters, I have been incredibly patient and so have other Members of this House. The Standards Committee has a broad remit and does good work, but after almost 24 months of waiting for a report, after my mentioning this matter previously in the House and after writing to the Standards Committee, there seems to have been no progress. I said in Westminster Hall more than four months ago that this House is moving at a glacial speed. My fear is that the glaciers will have melted by the time the report is published. The lack of progress is simply not good enough.

May I suggest that the questions about lobbying and Members’ outside interests might have turned out to be a little bit more complicated than the Labour manifesto considered them to be? May I also suggest that the hon. Gentleman approaches the Chair of the Standards Committee? The Chair is a Member of Parliament, so he is not difficult to find. We are in the same House—there are only 650 of us. May I suggest he does that, rather than getting on his high horse and criticising the Committee because he does not know what it is doing?
