While I share his ambition, I am sorry to say that the Government are unable to support his Bill, because we do not think that its provisions are necessary. Ultimately, the hon. Gentleman’s Bill rests on two principles: that there should be a clear national strategy for improving cancer outcomes; and that the Government should be transparent about the progress we are making.

Will the Minister arrange for me and the charities who support the Bill to see the Minister who will be responsible for the national cancer plan, so we can work together to ensure there is proper parliamentary scrutiny?

I feel sure that the Minister responsible for this area of policy will arrange such meetings. I will make available to him a copy of this debate so he can read for himself how important it is. I would say in a supportive way to the hon. Gentleman that we now have a cancer strategy that will improve outcomes over the next 10 years. I hope colleagues will also recognise that we have been unflinchingly honest about the scale of the challenge we face. We will always do so. We cannot sugarcoat the current situation, even while we all want to offer our constituents some hope. We have a 10-year national cancer plan to make England a world leader in cancer outcomes. It is very important that it succeeds. It is a plan that sets out more than 100 actions to improve cancer survival, increase earlier diagnosis, recover performance against waiting time standards, and improve the quality of life for people living with and beyond cancer. We published the plan in February this year and, starting on its first anniversary, we will publish an annual report that will measure our progress against each of these targets every year. It will be freely available online and accessible to all. At the end of three years, we will also publish a complete and honest account of what we have got right and where we need to go further. When it comes to improving the plan, no options are off the table. I want to express my sincere thanks to our friend, my hon. Friend the Member for West Lancashire (Ashley Dalton). I am delighted that she has agreed to rejoin us as an adviser on the national cancer plan’s implementation. She knows how important it is that we get this right and she has already done some pretty inspirational work on the first draft of the plan. But I know she would be the first say that wherever the plan is falling short we should and we will improve it. It is not a question of creating new legislation or statutory requirements when we have a cancer plan; our priority should be to crack on with the job. While we get on with that job, I welcome scrutiny from the hon. Member for Wokingham and from all other Members in this place as they rightly hold the Government to account. Accountability is already being built into the way we deliver the plan. For example, in September we followed through on a commitment to establish a new National Cancer Board, bringing together leaders from across the cancer community, to set strategic direction, give independent challenge and make sure we are keeping up momentum towards our goals. A few weeks ago, the hon. Member for Wokingham asked the Prime Minister to look at this proposal, and his suggestion was shared with the National Cancer Board. I can update the House that the board has now provided its views to Ministers, and those views have helped shape the Government’s position today. As I have said, the board deliberately brings together people with different roles and different perspectives. We would not expect every member to agree on this issue. Some members have noted support for the Bill and its ambitions to put cancer strategy and reporting on a statutory footing, while others have concerns and worry that creating a parallel statutory framework could duplicate the national cancer plan, cause confusion for patients and the public and create additional reporting requirements without necessarily improving delivery. Board members, however, share a clear expectation that reporting on the national cancer plan must provide a transparent account of progress, including where delivery is off track and, importantly, what action is being taken to get it back on track.
I thank the Minister for taking the intervention. On that note, will she look at the issues with recruiting cancer specialists, particularly in coastal towns and cities such as Portsmouth?

As the hon. Lady says, recruitment is very important—I am sure that the Minister with responsibility for the plan will look at that issue. Our commitment to publishing an annual report on progress against the national cancer plan is intended to deliver these insights into where the plan is off track, and to spur action to address any problems. The hon. Member for Wokingham has recognised that commitment, but I understand that he is worried that a future Government might choose to stop these annual reports. Even if today’s Bill is passed, a future Government, if they were intent on ceasing annual reports, could undo what the hon. Gentleman’s Bill seeks to do with a simple vote, just as commitments made in legislation on child poverty were undone. However, we have listened carefully to the wider point that the hon. Gentleman is making about accountability. Following the views of the National Cancer Board, we are strengthening our approach further. We have taken on board suggestions from Macmillan and Cancer52 that the annual national cancer plan progress report should not simply be published, but laid before Parliament and accompanied by an oral statement from the Secretary of State. We will make that further commitment, which I hope reassures the hon. Gentleman that we share his determination to ensure that Parliament can scrutinise our progress and hold us to account. The national cancer plan was written by a collective of people who care about this issue, and it takes action across the whole pathway. We are supporting the NHS to transform diagnostic services with £1.65 billion-worth of spending, including through new surgical hubs and state-of-the-art diagnostic scanners. Just last week, we announced that a world-leading new cancer blood test trial is being launched across at least 200 GP practices in England. We have invested £70 million into new cutting-edge radiotherapy machines, and exciting progress has been made on research with the cancer vaccines launchpad, which has now been expanded to support eight clinical trials. If I may test your patience, Madam Deputy Speaker, I also congratulate the world-leading research that is done at the Clatterbridge cancer centre in Liverpool, which is very close to my heart. We are also delivering commitments to improve quality and consistency of care. The Royal College of Physicians and Macmillan Cancer Support have recently published what is called a clinical consensus statement on acute and supportive oncology, establishing a common framework for service development. We are developing a new generation of cancer manuals and treatment. I could go on, but I just want to mention that, for children and young people with cancer, the Government are committing up £10 million a year to a new fund to help with the cost of travelling to and from principal treatment centres, for reasons that will be obvious to Members. We are giving rarer cancers the dedicated attention and leadership that they deserve. We have appointed Dr Robert Metcalf as the national clinical lead for rare cancers, giving patients a powerful voice and clinical leadership. This work also includes renewing our focus on brain cancer. Last month, my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister and the Health Secretary met Archie Goodburn to discuss new action that we are taking on brain cancer. We will appoint a new national brain tumour clinical lead in the coming months. This subject is of great importance to us all, and I therefore thank the hon. Member for Wokingham for bringing his Bill forward, and for the very constructive way in which he and his colleagues have approached the matter. I hope he can see that he has impacted the decisions that the Government have made. It is not the Government’s view that we need further legislation, but it is our view that we must work collectively to do much better with independent checks to improve treatment outcomes and to help people live better with cancer.

I beg to move, That the Bill be now read a Second time. It is my privilege to introduce this Bill today. I thank the Clerks from the Public Bill Office for their support in bringing it to life, and colleagues from along our coastline for their expressions of support for it. Along our coast, people live sicker and die younger. Five years ago, the chief medical officer laid out the evidence, and today this House has an opportunity to act on it. Fresh from steering the nation through the pandemic, Professor Sir Chris Whitty sought to tackle another major challenge: he published a seminal report outlining the health inequalities faced by coastal communities across our country, which include mine in North Norfolk. The findings are stark and shocking, but clear: across a range of measurable factors, those living in coastal communities were worse off—higher rates of coronary heart disease, lung conditions, obesity, substance abuse and addiction, and mental ill health. Their life expectancies were lower, and the percentage of those lives lived in good health was lower, too. We are an island nation. For an island nation to have poorer health outcomes in coastal areas is an unacceptable failing. The evidence exists, and the recommendations exist. What is missing is a system that turns them into action and makes someone answerable when that action falls short. The things that Professor Whitty outlined are not news to many of us in coastal communities. We understand the challenges we face, and we live with them daily. What they exposed is how much coastal communities have in common in facing down these challenges, and how much more we have in common with our coastal neighbours than we do with many of our inland neighbours. Our coastal communities could be a powerful force, and they need to be if the Government are to deliver their ambitions for growth, green energy, strengthened industry, and national defence and security. If our communities are sicker, those aims will all be harder to achieve. For too long, the issues of health and wellbeing in our coastal communities have not been part of the wider conversation about tackling health inequality. I introduced this Bill because I am determined to ensure that my community in North Norfolk, and communities anywhere on our nation’s coast, is being properly represented. Let us look at the inarguable facts. Professor Whitty’s findings continue to stack up with more recent research. An article published just weeks ago in the Journal of Public Health found that coastal communities in the south-east have life expectancy four years lower than their inland neighbours. In the east of England, it is three years lower. I have spoken before about how these inequalities can even be seen within counties; there are notable differences in life expectancy at either end of the Acle Straight in Norfolk, between Broadland and Great Yarmouth, despite their being only a few miles apart. Research from University College London, published in the British Medical Journal over the summer, also shocked me. It spoke of “people who grew up and stayed in coastal areas becoming more likely to develop morbidity from midlife compared with those staying in inland areas and…the people who move to coastal areas are sicker compared with those who move away from coastal areas.” I want the House to reflect on that for a moment. We have evidence that suggests that for people in coastal communities, the best way to stay healthy could be to leave—and for those who are not there currently, not to move there. This is an existential threat to coastal communities as we know them. Action is not a choice any more; it is a necessity. This matters to the Minister with responsibility for health inequalities, the right hon. Member for Kingston upon Hull North and Cottingham (Dame Diana Johnson), who is not in her place today. She is a respected champion and hard worker for the fine city of Hull. In her area, people will live only 53 years of t

I congratulate the hon. Member on introducing an important debate on health inequalities to the House. My constituency is inland but largely rural, and shares similar issues with health inequalities to those that he raises, because of transport and access to services. Does he think that by confining the discussion to coastal communities he is stifling a much more important debate about health inequalities across the country more generally?

In fact, I would say to the hon. Member that in order to tackle inequality truly we need to work from the outside in. In doing so, we would surely bring into line all the rural inland communities of which he speaks, which I do not doubt share many of the same issues that I am discussing today. If we start with the places the system finds hardest to reach, then we can design services that work there and work inwards. Otherwise, a national average can improve while the communities with the greatest barriers are left exactly where they were.

Does the hon. Member agree that the men’s health strategy is working from within, and that having diagnostic, GP and mental health services available at farming auctions is a great move forward by this Government?

That is a wonderful example of how designing from the outside in can work. We have seen that with buses and with broadband, and it is plain that we suffer the same with all forms of health services. The former Health Secretary, the right hon. Member for Ilford North (Wes Streeting), said: “If Australia can effectively serve communities living in the remote outback, we can meet the needs of people living in rural and coastal England.”

In my constituency it can take a very long time to get to the nearest hospital because of small, narrow lanes, and it can be almost impossible in the summer when there is heavy holiday traffic. The integrated care board has talked about merging emergency cardiac care between three hospitals, which would make the journey so long that people would literally die en route to the hospital. We have been campaigning hard for the ICB not to do that. Does my hon. Friend agree that while merging some services may be the way forward to enable ICBs to cover their costs, choosing a service like emergency cardiac care, where the time taken to get to the hospital, and therefore the distance travelled, is absolutely crucial to survival, is the wrong area to start when looking at service provision?

That surely defies all sense. I understand, as my hon. Friend alluded to, that for reasons of professional development and training it may not be possible to deliver all services in all areas, but acute and emergency care is surely beyond reproach. I am yet to hear any understanding or potential safeguards for that risk from the Government, either here or in the other place. There was no acknowledgment of it when I brought forward and spoke to an amendment on the Health Bill, or when Lord Patel did so in the other place. Coastal communities deserve an explanation of why the Government are not ensuring that health services are delivered for them.

The east of England has one of the longest coastlines of any region, so we too are familiar with the challenges faced by coastal communities. The University of Essex has an exemplary centre for coastal communities, led by Dr Emily Murray, an epidemiologist and public health expert. Will the hon. Gentleman join me in commending the work of that centre and in encouraging Ministers to meet representatives from the centre to hear their recommendations?

I surely would, on condition that the hon. Lady allows me to join them, because I would really like to hear more about that work. I am sure it would have a great impact on my part of the east of England, which is quite a big part of the United Kingdom. When I have tried to question the Government on the specifics of their work, I have not received anything substantive. In July, I asked how many meetings the Minister for health disparities had attended in relation to coastal health inequalities this year, and I was told: “Ministers in the Department meet regularly on a range of topics, including tackling health inequalities, to which coastal inequalities are closely linked.” I asked which meetings had taken place; I received a general assurance. I asked what specific work was being done, and I was referred back to that general assurance. Ministers must be able to tell Parliament what they are doing, who is responsible and what has changed. It is becoming a worrying theme that coastal health inequality is being kicked out to sea, so I hope the Minister can provide some straight answers on what the Government have done and will do to make a difference. People in coastal communities want the reassurance that this House, which has more than 100 MPs who represent coastal communities, is placing a legal duty on Ministers responsible for tackling the issues that matter to them. This lack of action or record of delivery is growing more and more worrying. The other part of my Bill relates to a cross-governmental coastal health strategy. It is rare for politicians to admit when an idea is not theirs, but I will admit that this is not my idea. In fact, it is not even very new. It was a core recommendation of the Chris Whitty report in 2021. I am sure that the Government will be keen to point out their existing health plans and strategies. While those do important work in places, they will not do enough to recognise the specific challenges of delivering coastal healthcare. Coastal communities suffer from the challenge of the half-compass effect when seeking access to healthcare. It might sound obvious, but when residents in Mundesley or Cley seek to access healthcare, half the compass directions they could travel in would take them straight into the North sea. To my knowledge we are not yet building GP surgeries or dentists there. Yet we still risk planning services as though patients can travel in every direction. This morning I received a letter from a constituent in Holt, who had been referred by his GP for an MRI scan but was told there was only availability at the Norfolk and Norwich hospital, some 25 miles away. It is a six-hour round trip on public transport. He cannot afford a taxi and there is no hospital transport available, so he has declined the test. He asked me, rightly, how many other constituents find themselves in this situation because of inadequate access to healthcare on the coast. Geography has to shape provision. If we take a one-size-fits-all approach to healthcare delivery, it will only be half as effective for coastal communities. A strategy that pulls together all parts of government that have an impact on and interest in tackling coastal health inequality is important to bring together the action necessary to face up to this challenge. This speaks to the core of my vision for a country that works for people, to rewire Westminster around the lives that people lead. A patient misses an appointment because there is no bus. Their health deteriorates because their home is damp. They cannot get the help that they need because the local service cannot recruit. Westminster files those problems under different Departments, but that person experiences one life. We should organise government around that life. We should give people responsibility for the outcome, the resources to deliver it and the funding and authority to work meaningfully across Departments, not just within annual budgets. Tackling coastal health inequalit
Colleagues know what time this debate has to end, so they should be mindful of time keeping.

In my constituency, our coastal towns of Clevedon and Portishead are places of real character, with Clevedon’s grade I listed pier, Portishead’s maritime and dock heritage, and communities with a fierce sense of pride and belonging. As many Members of the House know, before I was elected I worked as a community pharmacist for nearly 20 years across the south-west. Behind the pharmacy counter I saw the health inequalities between coastal and inland communities first hand. The Chief Medical Officer’s report exemplifies that disparity. Five years ago, Chris Whitty warned that if health problems in coastal communities were not tackled vigorously and systematically, we would face “a long tail of preventable ill health.” It is a problem that will only get worse as populations age. That warning matters in North Somerset. Today, 11% of our population is over 75, but by 2043 that will rise to 14%. The 2021 census showed that people in coastal areas are more likely to report bad or very bad health. In Clevedon, 6.7% of people said that their day-to-day activities were limited a lot by their health, and the figure was 5.2% in Portishead. As the hon. Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) mentioned, coastal communities are harder to recruit in when it comes to health. My first-hand experience of trying to recruit pharmacists and health care professionals, such as pharmacy technicians and dispensers, across coastal communities in the south-west has shown me that it is problematic in those areas to get the healthcare professionals we need. That is also true of GP surgeries. The south-west has the highest community pharmacy vacancy rate at 14%, and workforce planning needs to reflect the ageing population in coastal communities, which will fuel the demand for healthcare. I hate to agree with the hon. Member one more time, but I believe the Government need to have a Minister specifically responsible for coastal communities, to push a cross-Government and cross-Department strategy to try to bring those inequalities in coastal communities closer to those of their inland neighbours. Transport and access to health hubs in coastal communities are more difficult, and that can be problematic not just for attending a GP appointment or getting to a pharmacy, but for getting to work for those working in a healthcare establishment. Pharmacy tends to map towards deprivation and health inequalities in this country, with higher numbers of pharmacies located where inequalities are greatest, and that links to coastal communities and rural areas. When pharmacy is impacted by funding cuts and closures, that tends to hit those communities worse, such as with the closure of the Jhoots pharmacies in Portishead. We lost two of the three pharmacies in that area, meaning that one pharmacy was left to serve a population of around 25,000. Thankfully, with the help of Magna Pharmacy, we have managed to reopen those two pharmacies, but closures make coastal communities particularly vulnerable due to the health inequalities.

I have put on the record my support for particular initiatives around coastal communities. Clause 4 of the Health Bill gives the Secretary of State a duty to have regard to reduce inequalities in access to health services for people in England. Does my hon. Friend agree that Ministers should be mindful of the needs of coastal communities when looking at that clause?

I agree with my hon. Friend’s wise intervention. As I have said, I would go further and put in place a Minister with a responsibility for coastal communities, so great are the health inequalities. They require such a focus. The 2021 report by Chris Whitty made several recommendations, and I urge the Government to take them forward. We need a cross-Government strategy for coastal health. We must ensure there are sufficient healthcare staff in coastal areas as recruitment levels are often lower than the national average, which, as I say, I have personal experience of. Finally, we must undertake better research. Coastal communities have been chronically understudied in public health research, and that gap leads to worse inequalities. An ageing population adds to pressures on local services, from getting appointments at GP surgeries to access to Pharmacy First at community pharmacies. I welcome the hon. Member for North Norfolk raising this issue. Someone’s postcode should never dictate their health outcomes, and I will continue to champion the health of North Somerset’s coastal communities today and for the years ahead.

I greatly appreciate my hon. Friend the Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) for bringing forward this Bill on behalf of coastal communities around the country. Hundreds of families in North Devon have now spent three months without an operational maternity unit, and more than 200 births have been redirected over two hours inland to Exeter. It is not acceptable that an expectant mother in coastal towns such as Ilfracombe, Combe Martin or Lynton should have to travel so far to reach a hospital. It clearly amounts to a massive inequality in NHS healthcare. Many of my constituents feel that if this crisis had struck in Exeter, Bristol or London, things would be very different. We would not have just warm words of sympathy from the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State; we would already have a solution. Many women have told me that the anxiety and worry that the travelling time has caused them is not acceptable and that it has caused many families to feel that the worst could happen while travelling, especially because our areas have a heavy volume of tourists and the roads are narrow.

My hon. Friend is making a fantastic speech. I pay tribute to him for all his hard work campaigning on North Devon district hospital; it is a national disgrace that we have not seen its maternity unit reopen. Does he agree that in areas like both our constituencies, poor rural transport is locking our constituents out of accessing healthcare? In North Cornwall, not a single town has a direct bus to a major hospital, which I find incredible in 2026.

I thank my hon. Friend for making that point, and I totally agree. People in some areas of my constituency and my hon. Friend’s constituency use the hospital situated in my constituency, and it causes those families lots of worry. I appreciate all the work he is doing to help me on this campaign to get the maternity unit reopened. Many of these coastal towns have only very basic healthcare provision locally, and that is reflected in people’s quality of life and life chances. Coastal healthcare is a crisis that overlaps with poor housing, few economic opportunities, limited transport, as we have just heard, and other disadvantages. In one part of Ilfracombe, life expectancy is a full 10 years lower than in other parts of Devon. This Bill rightly says that the Secretary of State should be made to come to this Chamber and account for those disparities. Coastal towns have so much to offer, but across the country there is a pattern of too many coastal towns ending up in the category of “have nots”. A national strategy should exist to counter that and to deliver good healthcare for every coastal community. First-time parents in my constituency have been left all at sea. The Government must take this Bill seriously.

I thank the hon. Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) for introducing this Bill and, importantly, for shining a light on issues that deserve far greater attention. Our coastal communities are special places, but we know that many face challenges that can have a profound impact on people’s health, wellbeing and, indeed, life expectancy. Deprivation, low wages, poor housing, poor air quality, education opportunities and isolation all play a part. I want to concentrate on one area where these inequalities are particularly concerning, which is mental health. Research shows that young people in England’s coastal towns are three times more likely to experience a mental health condition. Behind that statistic are young people, families desperate for support and people whose conditions worsen because help simply is not available when they need it. These challenges are very real in my constituency of Portsmouth—a coastal city. Too many people in our city are struggling with their mental health. An estimated 15.4% of adults have been diagnosed with depression—above the regional and national average. Behind the figures are people trying to cope, families worried about loved ones and individuals who are not able to get the help they need. Getting this help is also not easy, because Portsmouth has 2,133 patients for every GP, compared with 1,634 nationally. This puts enormous pressure on primary care and makes it hard for people to access support early, when it can make the greatest difference. The picture for children’s mental health is equally concerning. The Hampshire and the Isle of Wight integrated care board spends just £966 per child with an active referral to mental health services—the 10th lowest spend in England. By comparison, north-west London spends £2,410. Even more troubling is that 40% of referrals are closed before a second contact—the third highest rate in the country. These are not figures; they represent children and young people who need someone to listen, families looking for reassurance and people who deserve consistent support, rather than being left to navigate the system alone. I therefore welcome the Government’s commitment to opening 159 new NHS mental health facilities across England, bringing support closer to home and intervening early, because it can make a real difference. When community support is unavailable, people too often experience a mental health crisis and end up in A&E. Our emergency staff do extraordinary work, but A&E cannot replace the specialist ongoing care that people need. We must give people access to the right support in the right place at the right time. That is why I am disappointed that Portsmouth has not been selected for one of these new facilities. Given the level of need in my city, I believe that Portsmouth should have been considered, and I welcome the opportunity to work with the Minister to see how we can make that happen. Behind all these figures are real people and real families. Too many young people, in particular, have lost their life to suicide in Portsmouth. I want to pay tribute to Tegan Hide and everyone involved in the Glade’s law campaign. I thank them for meeting me and sharing their friend’s story. Their determination to honour Glade’s legacy and improve mental health support in our city deserves recognition. Glade Clarke was a 23-year-old woman who sadly died of suicide on 26 August 2026. If we are serious about tackling health inequalities, we must recognise that coastal communities have distinct needs and ensure that they are not left behind. People in my city of Portsmouth deserve the right to access the same timely, high-quality mental healthcare as everyone else in the country, and I hope that this Government will continue to work with local communities like mine to make that a reality.

Torbay is often known as the English riviera, and in my view, it is the premier resort in the United Kingdom. We have incredible beaches, incredible countryside and an outstanding hospitality offer. However, behind the beach huts and the palm trees, we have high levels of deprivation—in fact, Torbay has the highest level of deprivation of any constituency that has a Liberal Democrat MP. I pay tribute to Lincoln Sargeant, who is our director of public health. He was also in that role at the time of the Chris Whitty report, and he wrote a chapter on Torbay. I was leader of the council at the time that it was written, so I am only too aware of the issues, and had conversations with him about the deaths and about the diseases of despair that plague our communities across Torbay, whether they relate to drugs, alcohol or depression. Only this morning, I was speaking to a lady in Torbay who attempted suicide because of the challenges in her world, and was trying to support her. I would also like to mention Kate Lissett, the chief medical officer at Torbay hospital. She has shared with me how many patients who come into Torbay hospital say that they see living into their 60s as a good age in Torbay, which is shocking. The challenges we face include high levels of morbidity due to respiratory issues and—going to the other end of the spectrum—obesity and high levels of teeth extraction among young children. All these things in Torbay paint a very depressing picture. What is the fabric that gives rise to these challenges? It is that we have only 8% social rented housing, compared with a national average of 17%; when Thatcher came into power, the figure for the nation was 35%. As a young Liberal, many years ago, I campaigned on street homelessness, and the sad thing is that the levels of street-attached are worse than ever. In Torbay, we also have the third lowest household incomes in the country in terms of wages. I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) on bringing forward the Bill. If we do not measure health inequalities in coastal communities and develop strategies, we are not going to tackle them.

I thank the hon. Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) for bringing this discussion to the Chamber. He might be asking why, as an inland MP, I am speaking on this Bill—I intend to cover that in the coming minutes. Before I begin, though, I will say that it was lovely to hear from the hon. Member for North Devon (Ian Roome). He reminded me of a holiday I had in his constituency many years ago, which I had more or less forgotten, so it was lovely to be reminded of the weekend I spent in Ilfracombe. I strongly respect the goals of the Bill, but I cannot directly support it. I do not believe that the problems the Bill diagnoses and seeks to recognise are limited to coastal communities, which is why I have chosen to speak today. The issues covered in the Bill and as part of this discussion are ones that affect communities up and down the country, whether they are next to the sea or—like mine—many miles from it. It is not living on the coast that inflicts particular problems on a place; it is people and economy. However, because of the fundamental imbalances that have plagued our country for decades, it is difficult for me to read that a specific strategy is needed to tackle child poverty in coastal communities. My community is nowhere near the sea, but there are children in poverty in Erewash who desperately need help all the same. Half of all the children in Ilkeston live in low-income households—that is nearly double the national figure. Opportunity needs to be created for young people right across the country.

I thank my hon. Friend for mentioning young people. This Government have changed the rules for parents on universal credit; previously, if their child went to college, they would still get universal credit payments. This Government have extended that to young people taking up apprenticeships. Does my hon. Friend agree that is a really helpful way to encourage growth and provide opportunities in deprived areas?

I completely agree. The work that the Government are doing to support young people— especially those not in education, employment or training—is really important. We are doing a huge amount of good in that space. Support should be offered—that is absolutely correct—but on the basis of need, not just geographical location. Why should concerns about poor educational attainment in coastal communities be recognised in law but not the real concern of parents in Erewash about poor school standards where they live? The thing is, basically everywhere in this country has some claim or another to having been left behind. Erewash is, given certain elections and a party politics-focused perspective, an extremely important place. Since my constituency was established in 1983, it has had a Government MP, completely without fail. I am proud to be the most recent in a very long line of Erewash Government MPs.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. May I ask you to clarify that we are discussing the Coastal Communities (Health) Bill at Second Reading rather than the Debt Relief (Developing Countries) Bill, so that it is clear to everybody that we have not suddenly switched to the fifth Bill of the day instead of the third?
The right hon. Member is very Eagle-eyed. [ Laughter. ] She is indeed correct; we will rectify the error on the screens. We are indeed in the correct debate and hearing the correct speech.

I thank my right hon. Friend for making that point of order. I was just talking about being the last in a long line of Government MPs. In 2024, the then Prime Minister, the right hon. Member for Richmond and Northallerton (Rishi Sunak), launched the Conservatives’ 2024 election campaign in Ilkeston, where he took some planted questions from local Conservative councillors dressed in hi-vis jackets—that definitely made them look like ordinary members of the public—and the current Prime Minister kicked off his August listening tour in Ilkeston as well. As per the accounts of one Peter Thorne—one of my fantastic former local members, sadly now passed—even Clement Attlee once stood on a soapbox in Long Eaton market place. Indeed, many Labour party and Conservative party leaders have done so over the intervening years. Has Erewash’s status as a perennial key marginal done it any great service? Sure. Long Eaton was in the first round of levelling-up funding under the previous Government, but Ilkeston got rejected in the second round. The particular formulation of my constituency and its demographics mean that it has never been described as part of the “red wall”, but parts of it—especially Ilkeston—can really be considered as such. Ironmaking at Stanton—one of the smaller parts of my constituency—started at the dawn of the industrial revolution, and it carried on for more than 200 years, but sadly it did not survive beyond 20 years after it was privatised. A deep point of pain for my constituents is what happened in Stanton after it was privatised. I have spoken plenty of times in this place about the struggles that our town centres face. The high street banks are abandoning Ilkeston and Long Eaton, without any regard for the one in five people in my community— often elderly and disabled folks—who still do not use online banking and probably never will. Historic industries have left our towns. That is all as true in the midlands as it is on the coasts of Lincolnshire, Yorkshire, Essex, Kent, Dorset and Cornwall—wherever. It is just as true inland as on the coast. I accept that Erewash is almost as far from the sea as it is possible to be in England—I understand that the furthest point away is about 7 miles away from my house, so that is pretty close—but it is not like we do not also have the flooding issues that face our coastal communities. My constituency is bounded to the east by the River Erewash and to the south by the Trent, which is fed by the Derwent. That means that the entirety of my constituency—particularly Long Eaton—is always at flood risk, as I am reminded every year when I struggle to get house insurance. Even before I was a Member of Parliament, when Storm Babet came in 2023, I spoke to people across the constituency in Ilkeston, Long Eaton and especially Sandiacre, where many residents found their homes under water, facing exactly the same issues as their counterparts in coastal constituencies. A few months ago, I was joined by my hon. Friend the Minister of State for Water and Flooding at the new Witches Oak addition to the Severn Trent site at Church Wilne, which is being specifically developed to deal with particularly dirty water sourced from the River Trent. The River Erewash itself, formerly flanked on both sides by heavy industry, as it flowed through Mansfield, Ashfield, Amber Valley, Ilkeston and Long Eaton, was once said to be the most polluted river in Britain. I was particularly bemused by attitudes to regional development and the distribution of economic growth during the Makerfield by-election. Right-wing journalists, perhaps for the first time ever, were looking at ward-level economic data to try to say that the incredible growth they have had in Greater Manchester was all just bundled up in shiny towers in the city centre, but that is not what the evidence showed. That suggests that columnists at The Spectator and The Daily Telegraph were perhaps not engaging with that very real and serious debate in

I thank my hon. Friend for considering our children, our young people and their opportunities. Does he agree that the report by the Children’s Commissioner made for some very stark reading? My own city of Portsmouth was the 12th-worst place in the country to be a child, yet Hampshire was in the top 20 best places. When we talk about red wall seats and areas of deprivation, it is really important that the south-east is not just seen as one block; there are elements of high deprivation in the south-east. We were the worst place in the country for opportunities for 16-year-olds.
Order. Before the hon. Member for Erewash (Adam Thompson) returns to his speech, let me remind him that we are debating the Coastal Communities (Health) Bill, which is about health inequalities.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I will continue to make points about the health system in coastal communities. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) for her intervention. The fact is that coastal communities have suffered for the same reason that the post-industrial midlands and north have: the economy has changed, and the health provision has changed with it. A good part of that change is the swirling nature of markets, consumer interests and all that, but undeniably political choices were made. The route to recovery for those places, whether we live next to the sea or far away from it, is economic growth. That is as true in the health space as it is everywhere else. For that, we need investment. I have no doubt that a great many of our coastal communities suffer from infrequent, expensive and unreliable deregulated services, particularly in the health sector, that have been cut time and time again. There is a lot more that I could talk about, and I know that the various crises are really biting in many coastal communities, but I want to end my speech by saying that I cannot support the Bill as written, because I agree with the Prime Minister. What we need is growth in every postcode, in the health sector and across all of society. Our problems are not created by geography, even if they are reinforced by it. Ultimately, the problem is that our economy and our health service have been imbalanced for too long. Regardless of whether someone is on the North sea, looks out across the channel or, like me, lives in the very heart of the midlands, where they live has been left behind because of political and ideological choices made by successive Governments. I am proud to be part of a Government who recognise that fact and are finally striving to correct our nation’s course—not pitting us against one another, but pulling us all together.

I begin by thanking the hon. Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) for bringing forward this Bill and for giving the House the opportunity to debate, on all sides of the question, the health and wellbeing of our coastal communities. I trust that the hon. Member will be reassured that, as a Minister and a constituency MP for Birkenhead who lives right next to the edge of the country, on the banks of the River Mersey and proximate to the Irish sea, I understand this issue very well. The Government share the concern that lies behind this Bill. We recognise that there are significant and persistent health inequalities in some of our coastal communities, and it is absolutely right that the Government address them. However, having listened to the debate, I am struck by some of the comments that my hon. Friends made about the various health inequalities that persist across our country. I agree with my hon. Friend the Member for Erewash (Adam Thompson) that the underlying economic circumstances are the determinants of health. There should be nothing inevitable about somebody experiencing poorer health, or spending fewer years of their life in good health, simply because of where they live, yet in far too many communities, including coastal communities, poorer health outcomes sit alongside deep-rooted social and economic disadvantage. These challenges are not new. They were set out powerfully in the chief medical officer’s 2021 report on health in coastal communities, and the importance of place to our health has been reinforced by the chief medical officer’s latest annual report on health in rural areas and small towns. We in this House all thank the chief medical officer for his considerable work on this subject. That report is particularly relevant to today’s debate, because rural, small town and coastal communities frequently overlap, and many of the challenges that it identifies will be familiar to Members of this place. It highlights the challenges of accessing and providing services across greater distances, limited public transport, ageing populations, workforce recruitment and retention, housing pressures and hidden deprivation. Importantly, the report also emphasises that health and social care services need to be designed around the needs and circumstances of local populations. That matters, because when we talk about health inequalities, we cannot simply talk about differences in people’s experience of the NHS, as I said yesterday in a speech on the work that we are doing on social care.

Given that we have limited time for a full ministerial response and that the Minister obviously has an interest in this subject, as do I, will she agree to meet me or set up a meeting with the relevant Minister to discuss coastal health inequalities further?

As you know, Madam Deputy Speaker, I never refuse a meeting with any Member of this House. I have my surgeries on Wednesdays, if the hon. Member would like to pop in and talk about mental health or social care. If he wants to talk about general health inequalities, I refer him to the Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety. Of course, high-quality healthcare matters enormously to all of us. Our health is shaped long before we arrive at a GP surgery or a hospital waiting room. It is shaped by the homes in which we grow up and live, by our education and the opportunities available to us, and, as Labour Members know only too well, by whether we have secure and rewarding work. Our health is also shaped by our income, by the transport available to us, by our environment, and by whether the communities in which we live give people the opportunity to lead healthy and fulfilling lives. Place and geography matter for health, but tackling inequalities between places requires action within healthcare and far beyond it. That is an analysis with which this Government agree, and I have not heard dissenting opinion in the House this afternoon.

Thank you for calling me to speak, Madam Deputy Speaker. I also thank the Minister for his time today—he has a very distinguished record of military service. My grandfather, Austin Coghlan, was told that he was too old to serve in the war, so he lied about his age and joined the Navy. On one convoy, he sailed into Havana, met a girl in naval intelligence and, after seven days, married her. He moved fast with Grandma, because he knew he was a lucky man. But he also did not expect to survive. That he did was in many ways due to the codebreakers of Bletchley Park, who diverted convoys away from U-boats. In the process, the codebreakers invented the world’s first computer, Colossus, which went on to power the economic development of the post-war world. The spillover effect from publicly developed military technology to private sector civilian use is one of the most powerful forces for economic growth. We can use it now. I commend the Government’s decision in the Budget to borrow, jointly with our allies, and invest £5 billion in dual-use military technology. It is a great start. We now need the confidence to scale it, knowing that even with extra borrowing, the debt-to-GDP ratio will fall as a result of higher growth. The London Business School’s Paolo Surico has shown that innovations that are funded by the Government, but taken forward by the private sector, develop productivity and economic growth that is eight times larger than for innovations funded by the private sector alone. Just look at how innovations in military train technology have led to disruptions in civilian industries, from 3D land mapping and crop monitoring to rapid cost-effective manufacturing. UK Government support for nuclear submarine technology has led Rolls-Royce to develop small modular nuclear reactors for civilian use. I would like to know whether the Government are open to scaling their £5 billion initial investment. With annual £2 billion increments over 10 years, academic research suggests that, along with improvements in AI, we could choose to double our annual growth, to fulfil our NATO defence spending commitments and, together with our allies, to secure liberal democracy. British politicians in the 1930s were labelled guilty men because they failed to prioritise defence over the deficit. My grandfather’s generation paid the price. As a reservist, an infantry officer and an MP, I want to ensure that our generation does not.

I thank the hon. and gallant Member for Dorking and Horley (Chris Coghlan) for securing this debate and for his continued interest in the role that research and development can play in strengthening our national security and economy. He spoke passionately about his grandparents, about the impact of technology during the war and about the innovations that brought about the victories that ensured our democratic freedoms in the nation we both grew up in. It was a powerful testament to his commitment to democracy. I will share with the hon. Member how highly the Department spoke of him and his work in the run-up to this Bill debate. As a member of the Treasury Committee and a steadfast advocate for innovation-led growth, he has made a valuable contribution to this discussion. This debate comes at a particularly important moment. The world is becoming more contested, more technologically competitive and more uncertain. Emerging technologies, from artificial technologies and quantum computing to advanced cyber capabilities and autonomous systems, are transforming the character of warfare and the nature of economic competition. In this environment defence research and development is not a luxury; it is a necessity. It is how we maintain operational advantage and keep our armed forces ready to face the challenges of the future. More than military capability, it is a catalyst for economic growth, industrial resilience and technological leadership. Innovation must sit at the heart of our national security strategy and our growth agenda. In the 2025 strategic defence review, we set ourselves the goal of the UK becoming a technologically enabled defence power innovating in priority areas, including AI, cyber, space and quantum at a wartime pace. Building on that, the defence industrial strategy recognised that investing in our innovation ecosystem is not simply a security imperative, but a significant opportunity to create jobs, as the hon. Member made very clear. It is central to growing businesses and strengthening our regional economies. Most recently, the defence investment plan provided a clear direction of travel for defence spending. It sent a signal to industry, investors and research institutions about the technologies and capabilities that we intend to prioritise. The plan marks a shift towards readiness and resilience at scale. It combines high-cost and low-cost equipment and integrated networks that make the most of crewed and uncrewed platforms. That commitment must be backed by investment. In answer to the question about whether we are scaling productivity, the Ministry of Defence’s research and development budget will exceed £2 billion in 2026-27 and will rise in each subsequent year. Defence R&D expenditure reached approximately £3.1 billion in 2024-25, representing a significant real-terms increase on the previous year.
I would be grateful if the Minister could comment, as far as he is able, on the extent to which we are integrating R&D with Ukraine.

Perhaps I will come on to that point shortly. Small innovative firms are the bedrock of UK innovation. They are also the bedrock of our commitment and delivery in Ukraine. Ensuring that they have every opportunity to access defence opportunities is a priority for this Government. That is why, as part of the root-and-branch modernisation of the Ministry of Defence, we are establishing UK Defence Innovation, a new team with a ringfenced annual budget of at least £400 million and planned investment of £1.6 billion by 2030. UKDI is helping up-and-coming enterprises to develop new technologies and move them more rapidly into service, maximising the military and economic impact of that investment. UKDI is part of our new National Armaments Innovation organisation, which unites our development accelerator with the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, under the leadership and co-ordination of a three-star director general. DSTL continues to play a vital role in defence research, working with industry and academic partners to look beyond the immediate horizon at threats and opportunities from emerging areas, such as quantum, engineering, biology and future computing. Alongside that, we are bolstering the links between Government, industry and academia. The Defence Universities Alliance is bringing together universities and defence to accelerate research, develop skills and increase the commercialisation of new technologies. At the heart of this agenda are people. We have committed £182 million to defence skills initiatives, supporting education, training and workforce development throughout the country. This investment will help improve science, technology, engineering and mathematics participation, increase capacity in the education system, and ensure that people have the skills they need to succeed in the defence sector. We are investing in defence technical excellence colleges and supporting hundreds of doctoral researchers working on technologies that are vital to the country’s future prosperity and security. We are securing the highly specialised workforce needed to develop and support future nuclear submarine and deterrent programmes, with £290 million committed to developing nuclear skills that support recruitment and training across the defence nuclear enterprise. I am surprised not to hear an intervention from my hon. Friend the Member for Barrow and Furness (Michelle Scrogham). The sector supports around 440,000 jobs and more than 24,000 apprenticeships across the UK. We are creating even more highly skilled, highly valued defence innovation employment opportunities, which will benefit communities for decades to come. Those are not confined to London or the south-east; they can be found in cities, towns and communities across every region and nation of the United Kingdom. We have launched defence growth deals, backed by £250 million, in Plymouth, Yorkshire, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. These partnerships are designed to attract further investment, strengthen local industrial capability, support innovation and create long-term economic growth. By aligning defence investment with regional strengths, we are helping to ensure that the benefits of defence spending are shared across the whole country. Strengthening British exports is key. From day one, we have been clear that this Government view defence through an international lens. The UK has been one of the world’s leading defence exporters over the past decade, with defence exports worth £14.5 billion in 2023, and defence R&D has played an important role in securing that position. Continued investment in research and innovation, and our role in transformational programmes such as AUKUS and the global combat air programme, ensures that British companies remain internationally competitive.

On the international point, does the Minister agree that borrowing jointly with allies is a great way of not only reducing our credit risk in borrowing for investment in defence R&D, but building our relationships and the middle power alliance?

I could not agree more with the hon. Gentleman. I was grateful to see the commitment that the Chancellor made to the multilateral defence mechanism and the efforts that we are making with partners, particularly Finland and other peer nations, to scale money and bring in private capital. I look forward to hearing your comments and views on the defence finance strategy.
Order. Minister, no “you” and “yours”, because you are speaking through the Chair. Please try to rephrase that.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker—of course, I was referring to your views on the defence finance strategy, which I will take back to the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry. That strategy will arrive in December, and will be a staple part of making sure that we can deliver the defence investment plan and the strategic defence review. Of course, we recognise that defence R&D is not a silver bullet for the economic challenges facing the UK. It must form part of the broader strategy, encompassing greater oversight and fiscal responsibility. New funding for infrastructure and a fresh perspective on private wealth funds and venture capital is essential, as the hon. Member for Dorking and Horley made clear. However, innovation investment can provide a golden opportunity to advance two fundamental national objectives—I think these are the points that the hon. Member was making—by strengthening both our security and our growing economy. I will leave hon. Members with an example to illustrate that point. The UK’s DragonFire laser weapon programme did not emerge overnight. It is a product of more than two decades of investment in advanced weapon science and technology led by our scientists at DSTL and delivered in partnership with MBDA, QinetiQ and Leonardo. That long-term commitment and partnership has produced a world-leading directed-energy weapon—one capable of downing drones at a cost of £10 per shot, compared with the hundreds of thousands and, in some cases, millions of pounds that conventional air defence systems cost. The programme is backed by a £316 million contract to accelerate delivery of the capability to the Royal Navy and is sustaining about 560 skilled jobs and 30 apprenticeships across the UK, from Scotland to the south-west. DragonFire demonstrates the hon. Member’s point. It demonstrates why defence R&D matters. A sustained investment in science creates the knowledge, skills and industrial capacity that allows the UK to develop transformational military capabilities. It grows new sectors, supports high-value employment and strengthens our sovereign technological base. DragonFire is a powerful example of how investment in defence research and development can deliver military advantage and economic growth for decades. It supports British scientists, engineers and innovators. It creates highly skilled jobs, drives productivity and strengthens regional economies. It attracts private investment and helps secure the UK’s place as a leading technological nation in an increasingly competitive world, and it ensures that our armed forces have the capabilities they need to meet the threats of today and tomorrow. The Government recognise the critical importance of making the UK a technologically enabled defence power and ensuring that the economic benefits of innovation are felt in every postcode. Once again, I thank the hon. Member for securing this debate and commend the House’s continued interest in this important subject. Question put and agreed to.
